# Associate Degree to Bachelor — The Hong Kong Articulation Pathway Complete Guide 2026

For Hong Kong DSE students whose exam results don't reach the cut-off for direct entry to a UGC-funded bachelor programme at one of the Eight universities, the **Associate Degree (AD)** followed by **articulation (senior-year entry) into a bachelor degree** is the second major pathway into a Hong Kong university education. It is used by roughly **15,000–18,000 students per year** across Hong Kong and is the single most important "second chance" mechanism in the HK higher education system.

This guide explains how the articulation pathway actually works in 2026, which institutions accept senior-year entry students, what GPA cut-offs look like, the realistic timeline from DSE results day to graduation, the known success rates and their caveats, and how the pathway compares to the direct JUPAS admission route. It is written for international students, parents, and counsellors who want to understand the full picture — not just the marketing version.

## What is an Associate Degree in Hong Kong

An **Associate Degree (AD)** in Hong Kong is a **2-year full-time post-secondary qualification** roughly equivalent in depth and scope to the first two years of a 4-year bachelor degree in North American systems. It was introduced in 2000 as part of the Hong Kong Government's target to increase post-secondary participation to 60% of the 17–20 cohort.

Key features:

- **2 years full-time** (some programmes offer 3-year part-time options)
- **Awarded by**: the sub-degree arm of a university (e.g., HKU SPACE Community College, CUHK CCouC, HKBU CIE, PolyU CPCE, CityU CCC) or one of several private providers
- **QF Level 4** on the Hong Kong Qualifications Framework (compared to Level 5 for a bachelor degree)
- **Cost**: typically HK$70,000–90,000 per year tuition — significantly higher than UGC-funded bachelor fees (HK$42,100/year)
- **Funding**: self-financing, with limited government grants/loans available through NMTSS and the Extended Non-means-tested Loan Scheme

An Associate Degree on its own is a recognised sub-degree qualification, but **the overwhelming majority of AD students do not intend to stop at the AD level** — they use it as a stepping stone to a bachelor degree via articulation.

## What is articulation

"Articulation" in Hong Kong higher education means **transferring into Year 2 or Year 3 of a bachelor degree programme after completing an Associate Degree (or Higher Diploma)** with the AD credits recognised toward the bachelor degree.

There are two main articulation targets:

1. **Senior-year entry into a UGC-funded bachelor at one of the Eight universities** — the most competitive and most desired outcome. Admitted students typically enter **Year 3** of a 4-year programme and graduate with a standard UGC-funded bachelor degree after 2 more years.

2. **Senior-year entry into a self-financing bachelor at a HK private university** — HSUHK, Tung Wah College, Caritas IHE, Chu Hai College, Hang Seng University, Saint Francis University, and others. Less competitive, wider capacity, but self-financing tuition fees (typically HK$90,000–130,000/year) and a less prestigious credential on graduation.

For most families, "articulation" implicitly means the first category — getting into HKU, CUHK, HKUST, PolyU, CityU, HKBU, EdUHK, or LingU's senior-year entry pool.

## The numbers — how competitive is UGC articulation

The Hong Kong government allocates a specific **UGC-funded senior-year entry quota** each year, distributed across the Eight universities. In the 2024/25 academic year:

- **Total UGC-funded senior year places**: approximately **5,000 per year**
- **Total Associate Degree + Higher Diploma graduates applying**: approximately **14,000–16,000 per year**
- **Success rate (to UGC-funded bachelor, senior-year entry)**: approximately **30–35%**

By institution (approximate 2024/25 figures):

| University | Senior-year entry quota (per year) | Typical AD GPA cut-off |
|---|---|---|
| HKU | ~800 | 3.7/4.0+ |
| CUHK | ~800 | 3.7/4.0+ |
| HKUST | ~450 | 3.6/4.0+ |
| PolyU | ~1,100 | 3.4/4.0+ |
| CityU | ~900 | 3.5/4.0+ |
| HKBU | ~500 | 3.4/4.0+ |
| EdUHK | ~300 | 3.3/4.0+ |
| LingU | ~200 | 3.3/4.0+ |

**Translation**: To be competitive for HKU/CUHK/HKUST senior-year entry, an AD student needs a **GPA of ~3.7+ out of 4.0** — which means consistently achieving A/A- grades across the 2-year AD programme. For PolyU/CityU/HKBU, **3.4–3.5+** is typically sufficient. For EdUHK/LingU, **3.3+** is competitive.

These cut-offs are approximate — real admission depends on the specific programme, discipline, and year. Some high-demand programmes (business, engineering, law, medicine-adjacent) require 3.8–4.0 even at PolyU and CityU. Some lower-demand programmes may accept 3.2–3.3.

## Timeline from DSE to Bachelor graduation via articulation

**Year 0 (DSE Year 13)**:
- Take DSE, receive results in July
- If DSE results don't meet JUPAS cut-off for desired bachelor programme, apply to AD programmes in August
- AD programmes typically have multiple intakes through August–September
- Start AD in September

**Years 1–2 (AD study)**:
- Complete 2-year AD programme
- Focus on maintaining high GPA
- Build English proficiency (most HK bachelor programmes require IELTS 6.0+ or TOEFL 80+ equivalent)
- Research articulation targets in Year 1, plan application in Year 2

**Year 2 Semester 2**:
- Submit articulation applications to target universities (typically January–March)
- Attend interviews if required (some programmes only)
- Receive offers (typically April–June)
- Complete AD in June

**Years 3–4 (Bachelor senior-year entry)**:
- Enter Year 3 of bachelor programme in September
- Complete 2 more years
- Graduate with standard UGC-funded bachelor degree

**Total time**: **4 years** from DSE completion to bachelor graduation — **the same as direct JUPAS entry**. This is the key marketing point of the AD articulation pathway: "same 4 years, same final degree." The catch is that the first 2 years cost significantly more (self-financing AD at HK$70–90k/year vs UGC-funded at HK$42k/year) and the student bears the risk of not articulating successfully.

## Cost comparison with direct JUPAS entry

**Direct JUPAS route (DSE → UGC-funded bachelor):**
- Year 1–4: HK$42,100/year × 4 = HK$168,400 tuition total
- Living expenses (dorm/transport/food): HK$60,000–100,000/year × 4 = HK$240,000–400,000
- **Total**: HK$408,400–568,400

**AD articulation route (DSE → AD → UGC-funded bachelor senior-year entry):**
- AD Year 1–2: HK$75,000/year × 2 = HK$150,000
- Bachelor Year 3–4: HK$42,100/year × 2 = HK$84,200
- Living expenses: HK$60,000–100,000/year × 4 = HK$240,000–400,000
- **Total**: HK$474,200–634,200

**Additional cost of AD route**: approximately **HK$66,000** more than direct JUPAS over 4 years. Not catastrophic, but meaningful. Plus the articulation risk — if articulation fails, the student either stops at AD level, pays for a self-financing bachelor (even more expensive), or looks overseas.

**Self-financing bachelor route (DSE → AD → self-financing bachelor):**
- AD Year 1–2: HK$150,000
- Self-financing bachelor Year 3–4: HK$110,000/year × 2 = HK$220,000
- Living expenses: HK$240,000–400,000
- **Total**: HK$610,000–770,000

This is the fallback option for AD students who don't articulate into UGC-funded places but still want to complete a full bachelor in Hong Kong.

## Pros of the articulation pathway

**1. Second chance at a UGC-funded bachelor degree.** For students whose DSE results don't make the JUPAS cut-off, this is the most viable route to the same final credential — a HKU/CUHK/HKUST/PolyU/CityU/HKBU/EdUHK/LingU bachelor degree.

**2. Same final degree.** On graduation, the bachelor degree certificate is identical to a direct JUPAS graduate. Employers cannot distinguish "Year 1 JUPAS entry" from "Year 3 senior entry" on a bachelor transcript in most cases. The UGC-funded bachelor is the UGC-funded bachelor.

**3. Time to mature.** Two years of AD study gives students time to improve English, study skills, and personal motivation. Many AD students outperform their DSE results dramatically once they find their footing.

**4. Rebrand opportunity.** If DSE results were weak in specific subjects, AD provides a chance to demonstrate academic competence through a fresh GPA-based assessment.

**5. Lower entry barrier.** AD entry is significantly easier than JUPAS direct entry — most AD programmes accept students who did not meet the 332233 minimum DSE requirement for direct bachelor entry.

## Cons and caveats

**1. Articulation is not guaranteed.** Roughly **one in three** AD students successfully articulate into a UGC-funded bachelor. The other two-thirds either stop at AD, go to self-financing bachelor, or abandon higher education.

**2. Higher cost.** An extra HK$66,000+ compared to direct JUPAS entry. For lower-income families this is non-trivial.

**3. GPA pressure is intense.** To articulate into a competitive programme, students need GPA 3.5–3.8+. This means consistent A-level performance across 2 years — the competitive pressure is arguably higher than JUPAS.

**4. Limited programme choice.** Not all bachelor programmes accept senior-year entry. Some high-demand programmes (law, medicine, dentistry, pharmacy) rarely or never accept AD articulation students. Business, engineering, social sciences, arts are the main targets.

**5. Stigma.** Despite official parity, some employers and graduate schools in Hong Kong still distinguish AD articulation graduates from direct JUPAS graduates when reviewing candidates. This has improved over the last decade but has not disappeared.

**6. Self-financing bachelor as fallback is expensive.** If articulation fails, the self-financing bachelor alternative can cost HK$600,000–770,000 total — more than an overseas bachelor in some cases.

## Which AD provider to choose

The main AD providers in Hong Kong are:

- **HKU SPACE Community College** — largest, widest programme range, strong articulation record to HKU and other UGC universities
- **CUHK Community College (CCouC)** — smaller, close ties to CUHK, especially strong in business and science
- **HKUST Community College (HKUST-CC)** — discontinued; HKUST no longer operates a separate community college
- **PolyU College of Professional and Continuing Education (CPCE)** — large, strong vocational programmes, good PolyU articulation
- **CityU College of Community (CityU CCC)** — close ties to CityU senior-year entry
- **HKBU School of Continuing Education / College of International Education (CIE)** — smaller, HKBU articulation
- **Lingnan Institute of Further Education (LIFE)** — small, close ties to LingU

**General rule**: If you want to articulate into a specific Eight university, study at its affiliated community college. Articulation statistics consistently show that affiliated students have the highest acceptance rates into their parent university (e.g., HKU SPACE → HKU senior year entry is notably higher than other community colleges → HKU).

## How to maximise your articulation chances

**1. Pick programmes strategically.** Look at the articulation statistics before you choose your AD programme. Some AD programmes have 50%+ UGC articulation rates (business at HKU SPACE, science at CUHK CCouC); others have 10–15%.

**2. Target GPA above 3.5 from day one.** Don't treat the AD as "high school extended" — treat it as final-year university work. Every single course grade matters.

**3. Build English proficiency aggressively.** Take IELTS or TOEFL in Year 1, aim for 6.5–7.0 overall. Weak English is the single biggest filter in competitive senior-year entry pools.

**4. Get to know faculty.** Articulation often requires a reference letter. Build relationships with your instructors in Year 1 so that by Year 2 you have credible advocates.

**5. Understand the target programme requirements.** Read the admissions page for your target bachelor programme at each Eight university. Know the GPA cut-off, required subjects, English requirement, and whether an interview is part of the process.

**6. Apply broadly.** Don't apply only to your first-choice programme. Apply to 5–8 programmes across multiple universities to maximise offers.

**7. Consider a second gap semester if needed.** If your Year 2 GPA is borderline, some students take an extra semester to strengthen grades before applying. This is legal but uncommon.

## Articulation success stories and realistic outcomes

In a typical AD cohort at a major community college (e.g., HKU SPACE, 2023/24 data):

- **~10%** articulate to HKU Year 3 senior-year entry
- **~20%** articulate to CUHK/HKUST/CityU/PolyU Year 3 senior-year entry
- **~15%** articulate to HKBU/EdUHK/LingU Year 3 senior-year entry
- **~20%** go to self-financing bachelor (HSUHK, Tung Wah, Caritas, etc.)
- **~15%** go overseas (UK, AU, Taiwan mostly)
- **~15%** stop at AD, enter workforce or vocational training
- **~5%** repeat or transfer within AD

**Total "upgrade to bachelor" rate**: approximately **65%**. **UGC-funded bachelor rate**: approximately **45%**. The rest go to self-financing bachelor or overseas.

For a high-GPA student (3.7+), the UGC-funded articulation rate is closer to **75–85%**. For a borderline student (GPA 3.0–3.4), it drops to **20–30%**.

## AD articulation vs direct JUPAS — which is better?

The honest answer: **direct JUPAS entry is almost always better if you can get it**. It is:

- **Cheaper** (HK$168k vs HK$234k tuition over 4 years)
- **Lower-risk** (guaranteed 4 years to bachelor, no articulation gatekeeping)
- **Less pressured** (no extreme GPA requirement in Years 1–2)
- **Fully UGC-funded** from day one

The AD articulation route only makes sense when direct JUPAS entry is not realistic given DSE results. In that scenario, AD is a legitimate, well-trodden, and successful pathway — but it should be understood as a **Plan B**, not a Plan A. A student who could realistically have scored 5*5*5*5* on DSE with more effort should put that effort into DSE preparation, not into accepting a weaker DSE result and planning to articulate.

**Exception**: AD can be a superior pathway for **late-blooming students** — those whose DSE results don't reflect their actual academic ability (e.g., due to health issues, family crisis, poor school, weak test-taking skills at 18). For these students, AD provides a cleaner second chance with no legacy from DSE on the final transcript.

## What happens after articulation

Once articulated, the student is essentially **indistinguishable from a direct JUPAS entry student**:

- Same UGC-funded tuition (HK$42,100/year)
- Same bachelor transcript and degree certificate on graduation
- Same access to scholarships, exchange programmes, and career services
- Same IANG visa pathway for post-graduation work (for non-local students)
- Same graduate school eligibility

The only difference is that the articulated student has 2 years of AD coursework on their academic record, which is viewable in full transcripts but not on the bachelor degree certificate itself.

## Practical conclusion

The Associate Degree to Bachelor articulation pathway is a **legitimate, well-established, and reasonably successful** route into a Hong Kong UGC-funded bachelor degree for students whose DSE results don't make the direct entry cut-off. Approximately 30–35% of AD students succeed in articulating into the Eight, with much higher rates for high-GPA students at well-connected community colleges. The cost is modestly higher than direct JUPAS entry (~HK$66k more over 4 years), the timeline is identical (4 years to bachelor), and the final degree is the same credential employers recognise.

It is not a magic second chance — it requires 2 years of hard work at GPA 3.5+ to be competitive — but it is the single most important "second-chance" pathway in the Hong Kong higher education system, and for the right student, it is a perfectly reasonable route to a top Hong Kong university degree.

## Hong Kong Student Visa Extension & Change of Programme — Complete Guide 2026
URL: https://dsedaquan.cn//en/admission/hk-visa-extension

# Hong Kong Student Visa Extension & Change of Programme — Complete Guide 2026

> Summary — Non-local students in Hong Kong must apply for an extension of stay within 4 weeks before their current limit of stay expires, using **Form ID91**, a Letter of Certification from their institution, and a HK$330 change-of-condition fee. From **1 January 2026**, a new **HK$800 Student Visa Handling Fee** applies to any non-local student who needs a fresh student visa after deferment, reinstatement or visa expiry. Switching university, programme or degree level is **not an extension** — it requires a brand-new student visa application via Form **ID995A**.
>
> This article is independently written by the the editorial team AI editorial team, citing primary sources from the Hong Kong Immigration Department (ImmD), CityU, HKU, CUHK and THEi. License: CC BY 4.0.

---

## 1. Who this guide is for

If you are a non-local student — mainland Chinese, international or otherwise without the right of abode in Hong Kong — your ability to remain in Hong Kong is tied to a student visa / entry permit issued by the **Hong Kong Immigration Department (ImmD)** and sponsored by a recognised local institution. That visa is:

- Granted on entry and tied to **one specific programme at one specific institution**
- Usually issued for **one year or the full programme duration**, whichever is shorter
- Capped at a maximum of **six years of cumulative stay** under the same programme at the same institution

You will need to interact with ImmD in four common scenarios:

1. **Extension of stay** — your visa is about to expire but you are continuing the same programme at the same school.
2. **Change of programme / level** — you are moving from bachelor → master, or switching majors with a new admission offer.
3. **Change of institution** — you are transferring from, say, PolyU to HKU.
4. **Deferment, reinstatement or expired visa** — you paused studies and are now returning.

Each of these is handled differently. This guide walks through all four, with fees, timelines and the exact forms required.

---

## 2. Scenario A — Simple extension of stay (same programme, same institution)

This is the most common case. Your programme runs longer than the limit of stay that ImmD originally granted (typical for 4-year bachelor degrees where the first visa is issued for only one year, or for postgraduate research students on year-by-year renewals).

### 2.1 When to apply

ImmD's published rule is that you must apply **within 4 weeks before your current limit of stay expires**. Some institutions (notably HKU) advise students to begin preparing paperwork **4–6 weeks in advance** to account for school certification turnaround. Applying too early will lead ImmD to reject the application as premature; applying late puts you out of status, which can jeopardise future immigration matters and, from 2026, can force you into the HK$800 new-visa fee route.

**Rule of thumb**: request your school Letter of Certification 4–6 weeks ahead, submit Form ID91 within the final 4-week window, and keep a buffer of at least 2 weeks before your visa's expiry date.

### 2.2 Required documents

Based on ImmD, CityU and the Technological and Higher Education Institute of Hong Kong (THEi) guidance, you need:

| # | Document | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Form ID91** — Application for Extension of Stay | Downloadable from the ImmD website; can be filled online |
| 2 | Valid travel document (passport / MTP / Home Return Permit) | Bring the original + a photocopy of the biodata page and the latest visa/landing slip |
| 3 | Hong Kong Identity Card | Mandatory for anyone who has been in HK longer than 180 days |
| 4 | **Letter of Certification** from your school | Must explicitly state: (a) you are currently enrolled, (b) the remaining duration of the programme, and (c) the expected graduation date |
| 5 | Proof of financial support (as requested) | Bank statements, scholarship letter, or sponsor's affidavit |
| 6 | For dependants | Sponsor's travel document + proof of current permission of stay |

The Letter of Certification is the single most important document — without it, ImmD will not process the application. Undergraduate students at CityU, for example, obtain the letter from the Academic Regulations and Records Office; postgraduate students use the Chow Yei Ching School of Graduate Studies. At HKU, this is handled through the Admissions Office (Registry). Lead time is typically 3–5 working days.

### 2.3 How to submit

You have two options:

1. **Online** — via the GovHK online portal for extension of stay (non-permanent residents). You will need to create an account and upload scans. After approval, you collect your new visa label at Immigration Headquarters.
2. **In person** — at the Extension Section, 5/F, Administration Tower, Immigration Headquarters, 61 Po Yap Road, Tseung Kwan O, New Territories.

Note two hard requirements that catch students out every year:

- **You must be physically present in Hong Kong** on both the submission date and the collection date for a label endorsement. You cannot apply for an extension from the mainland or abroad.
- **Payment is made after approval**, not at submission. ImmD will notify you and offer payment via FPS, credit card, the online portal, or in-person at any immigration office.

### 2.4 Fees

Student visa extension is treated by ImmD as a **"change of condition of stay"**. Per the official fee table:

| Fee type | Amount (HKD) |
|---|---|
| Change of condition of stay — other applications | **HK$330** |
| Change of condition — specified scheme, over 180 days | HK$1,300 |
| Change of condition — specified scheme, 180 days or less | HK$600 |

For a standard undergraduate or taught-postgraduate student, the fee is **HK$330**. Specified-scheme rates apply only to talent and employment schemes, not ordinary student visas.

### 2.5 Processing time

ImmD states that routine extension applications are **normally finalised within 2 to 3 weeks** upon receipt of all necessary documents. Expect significant slippage during the **June–August summer rush**, when postgraduate admissions and undergraduate cohort turnover drive peak demand. Apply before the rush if your visa lapses between late June and early September.

### 2.6 What "extension" does not change

- Your extended visa is still tied to the **same programme at the same institution**.
- The cumulative stay counter does not reset — the six-year cap runs continuously from first entry.
- Part-time work rules remain the same (on-campus: up to 20 hours per week during term; internships: subject to programme approval).

---

## 3. Scenario B — Bachelor → Master (progression to a new programme)

This is where students most often trip up. **Moving from a bachelor's programme to a taught master's programme is not an extension** — it is a new student visa application, even when both programmes are at the same university.

Why? Because your original student visa was issued for a specific programme. Once you graduate, that programme ends, the sponsoring arrangement ends, and any continuation of studies must be authorised under a fresh visa tied to the new programme.

### 3.1 What you need to do

1. **Receive your unconditional offer** from the new master's programme.
2. **Submit a new student visa application** using:
   - **Form ID995A** (Part A — applicant) and
   - **Form ID995B** (Part B — local sponsor, usually the admissions office of the new programme)
3. The new institution acts as your sponsor and usually routes the application on your behalf.
4. **Surrender your old visa status** / let it expire naturally; do not attempt to "extend" a bachelor's visa into a master's programme — ImmD will reject it.

### 3.2 Timing pitfall

Taught-master's offers from HK universities typically arrive between March and May for a September start. Your bachelor's visa may still be valid into October or November. Do **not** rely on the residual bachelor's visa to cover the summer gap — if you travel out of Hong Kong after graduating and try to re-enter on the old student visa without holding the new one, ImmD officers at the border may refuse entry.

Best practice:

- Apply for the new student visa **as soon as you receive the unconditional offer letter** — typically April/May.
- Plan for 6–8 weeks processing for the new visa.
- Avoid international travel between bachelor's graduation and master's enrolment unless you already hold the new entry permit.

### 3.3 Fees

The new visa application costs **HK$330** (standard visa fee, effective 8 September 2025). In addition, if your institution acts as sponsor, the school will usually charge its own visa handling fee, which varies by institution.

---

## 4. Scenario C — Change of institution

Transferring from one UGC-funded university to another (e.g. PolyU → HKU) is rare at undergraduate level but common for self-financed students re-admitting into a different cohort.

Rules:

- **A new student visa is required.** Your existing visa is tied to the previous institution and cannot be "transferred" directly.
- Apply via **Form ID995A / ID995B**, sponsored by the new institution.
- If your previous programme has already ended and your limit of stay expires before the new visa is issued, you must leave Hong Kong and re-enter under the new visa once it is issued — or, if your old visa is still valid, you may remain in Hong Kong while the new application is processed, but you **cannot switch schools** until the new visa is in hand.

The transfer cannot be used to bypass the six-year maximum-stay cap. That cap is calculated from the cumulative duration of student visas, not per-institution.

---

## 5. Scenario D — Deferment, reinstatement and expired visas (the new 2026 rule)

This is the single biggest change for 2026 and affects many mainland students who defer a semester for medical, family or personal reasons.

### 5.1 The HK$800 Student Visa Handling Fee

With effect from **1 January 2026**, ImmD has introduced a **Student Visa Handling Fee of HK$800** that applies to non-local students requiring a new student visa **before resumption of studies after**:

- a **deferment of study**, or
- **reinstatement** of enrolment (e.g. after academic suspension), or
- **expiry of a previous student visa**.

This fee is **in addition to** the ordinary visa fee (HK$330) and any institutional sponsor fees. In practical terms: if you defer a year of study and need to return to HK to resume your programme, your direct ImmD cost is **HK$800 + HK$330 = HK$1,130**, plus whatever your school charges.

### 5.2 Why this matters

Previously, students who deferred could often reuse their original visa if the limit of stay had not expired. Under the 2026 rules, ImmD treats any gap in enrolment as a trigger for a **fresh visa assessment**, not a simple extension. This means:

- Deferment is no longer "free" from an immigration standpoint.
- Students who let their student visa expire while abroad during a gap year must apply for a new visa before re-entry — they cannot simply fly back.
- Reinstatement after academic suspension now carries a clear, non-trivial immigration cost.

### 5.3 How to apply

Use **Form ID995A (applicant) + ID995B (sponsor)**, submitted through your institution's admissions or registry office. Expect the same 6–8 week processing window as a first-time visa, and plan your return travel dates accordingly.

---

## 6. Common mistakes to avoid

| Mistake | Consequence |
|---|---|
| Applying more than 4 weeks before visa expiry | ImmD returns the application as premature; clock ticks down before you can re-apply |
| Missing the Letter of Certification | Application rejected; you must restart and may fall out of status |
| Trying to "extend" a bachelor's visa into a master's programme | Rejected — requires a new visa under ID995A |
| Travelling out of HK while an extension is pending without the label | You may be refused re-entry; physical presence is required |
| Assuming deferment preserves your original visa (2026+) | You will still owe the HK$800 handling fee + new visa on return |
| Letting the 6-year cap lapse | No further extension possible under the same programme/institution; must apply under a different visa category |
| Using a tourist visa to "tide over" a gap in student status | Illegal for any form of study; ImmD will void and potentially blacklist |

---

## 7. Frequently asked questions (FAQ)

**Q: Can I apply for a visa extension from outside Hong Kong?**
A: No. Both the submission and label-collection steps require your physical presence in Hong Kong. If you are outside HK when your visa expires, you must apply for a brand-new student visa via Form ID995A through your institutional sponsor.

**Q: How long does a student visa extension normally take?**
A: ImmD states 2 to 3 weeks for routine applications. Allow 4–6 weeks during the June–August summer rush, and always build in a buffer before your visa's expiry date.

**Q: What is the difference between Form ID91 and Form ID995A?**
A: **ID91** is for **extending** an existing permission of stay under an already-approved programme. **ID995A** is for a **new** student visa application — whether because you are entering HK for the first time, switching programme, switching school, or resuming studies after a deferment.

**Q: I am a mainland student on a Two-way Permit (EEP). Does the same process apply?**
A: Yes, with one procedural twist: EEP holders submit applications at the Quality Migrants and Mainland Residents Section (6/F, Administration Tower, Immigration HQ), not the general Extension Section on the 5th floor. The forms, documents and timeline are otherwise the same.

**Q: Does a visa extension reset my six-year maximum stay?**
A: No. The six-year cap is cumulative from first entry under the same programme at the same institution. An extension does not reset it.

**Q: If I switch from a taught master to a PhD at the same university, do I need a new visa?**
A: Yes. Research postgraduate (PhD/MPhil) programmes are a different programme from taught master's (TPG) programmes, even within the same university. You need a new ID995A application under the research studentship sponsorship.

**Q: Can I work in Hong Kong during the gap between my bachelor's graduation and my master's enrolment?**
A: Not under a student visa. If your bachelor's visa is still valid, you remain bound by student visa conditions (on-campus 20 hours/week limit, no general employment). For full-time work in the gap, you would need to apply separately under the **IANG** (Immigration Arrangements for Non-local Graduates) scheme once your bachelor's degree is formally conferred.

**Q: Does the HK$800 handling fee apply if I only defer for one semester?**
A: Based on ImmD's published wording, the fee is triggered by any **new student visa required before resumption of studies after deferment**. If your existing visa's limit of stay remains valid through the entire deferment period and no new visa is needed on return, the fee may not apply. Confirm with your institution's admissions office before booking return travel.

**Q: I am applying for an extension of stay. Do I need to buy medical insurance?**
A: ImmD does not strictly require proof of medical insurance for a visa extension, but most HK institutions mandate comprehensive medical insurance as a condition of continued enrolment. In practice, your Letter of Certification may be withheld until insurance is in place.

---

## 8. Quick-reference checklist

- [ ] Check your visa's "Limit of stay" date on your passport label or HKID-linked record.
- [ ] Identify your scenario: extension / progression / transfer / deferment return.
- [ ] Request Letter of Certification from school registry (4–6 weeks ahead).
- [ ] Prepare documents: passport, HKID, Form ID91 (or ID995A for new visa), financial proof.
- [ ] Submit online via GovHK or in person at Immigration HQ, Tseung Kwan O.
- [ ] Stay physically present in Hong Kong until the new visa label is issued.
- [ ] Pay the fee after approval notice (HK$330 extension; +HK$800 from 2026 if new visa after deferment).
- [ ] Collect the new visa label at ImmD and keep a scan on file.

## IELTS vs TOEFL for Hong Kong University Admission — Which to Take in 2026
URL: https://dsedaquan.cn//en/admission/ielts-vs-toefl-for-hk

# IELTS vs TOEFL for Hong Kong University Admission — Which to Take in 2026

> **Summary** — All eight UGC-funded Hong Kong universities accept both IELTS Academic and TOEFL iBT, but minimum scores differ sharply: HKU demands IELTS 6.5 / TOEFL 93, while HKUST and PolyU accept IELTS 6.0 / TOEFL 80. The January 2026 TOEFL scoring overhaul (new 1–6 band scale) adds a conversion layer applicants must understand. This guide compares both tests side by side, maps every university's requirements, and helps you decide which exam to sit.
> 本文由 the editorial team AI 編輯團隊獨立撰寫，引用 official university admission pages, HKEAA, ETS, and British Council sources. License: CC BY 4.0.

---

## Why English Proficiency Matters for Hong Kong Admission

Hong Kong's eight UGC-funded universities — HKU, CUHK, HKUST, PolyU, CityU, HKBU, Lingnan, and EdUHK — teach almost entirely in English at the undergraduate level. Whether you are a mainland Chinese student applying through the Gaokao or independent admission track, an international school graduate, or a local DSE candidate seeking a non-JUPAS route, you will need to prove English proficiency through a recognised standardised test.

The two dominant tests are **IELTS Academic** (administered by the British Council, IDP, and Cambridge) and **TOEFL iBT** (administered by ETS). Both are accepted at all eight universities, but the minimum required scores, accepted test formats, and practical logistics differ. Choosing the wrong test — or misunderstanding the new TOEFL scoring system introduced in January 2026 — can delay your application or force a costly retake.

---

## The 2026 TOEFL Scoring Overhaul — What Changed

On **21 January 2026**, ETS launched a redesigned TOEFL iBT with a new **1–6 band score scale** (in half-point increments) aligned to the Common European Framework of Reference (CEFR). This replaces the legacy 0–120 total score.

### Key changes at a glance

| Feature | Old TOEFL (pre-Jan 2026) | New TOEFL (from 21 Jan 2026) |
|---|---|---|
| **Overall score range** | 0–120 (sum of four sections) | 1–6 bands (average of four sections) |
| **Section score range** | 0–30 per section | 1–6 per section (half-point increments) |
| **CEFR alignment** | Indirect concordance | Direct band-to-CEFR mapping |
| **Test duration** | ~2 hours | ~85 minutes (shorter, adaptive format) |
| **Score reports** | 0–120 only | Both new 1–6 band AND old 0–120 shown side by side (transition period 2026–2028) |
| **Score availability** | 4–8 days | ~72 hours |

### Score conversion reference

During the transition period, both old and new scores appear on your score report. Here is the official ETS concordance:

| New Band | Old 0–120 Equivalent | Approximate CEFR |
|---|---|---|
| 6.0 | 114–120 | C2 |
| 5.5 | 107–113 | C1+ |
| 5.0 | 95–106 | C1 |
| 4.5 | 86–94 | B2+ |
| 4.0 | 72–85 | B2 |
| 3.5 | 58–71 | B1+ |
| 3.0 | 44–57 | B1 |

**Why this matters**: A university that previously required "TOEFL 80" now states a new-scale equivalent. The numbers are not always a clean match — for example, old 80 falls in the Band 4.0 range, but old 86 pushes into Band 4.5. Read each university's updated requirement carefully.

---

## All 8 Hong Kong Universities — English Requirements Comparison (2026 Entry)

The table below covers **undergraduate** admission for non-JUPAS / international applicants. JUPAS candidates fulfil the English requirement through DSE results and do not need IELTS or TOEFL.

| University | IELTS Academic (min.) | TOEFL iBT — Old Score (pre-Jan 2026) | TOEFL iBT — New Band (from Jan 2026) | Sub-score Requirements | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **HKU** | **6.5** | **93** | **~5.0** | None stated | Highest bar among the 8. IELTS Indicator / IELTS Online / TOEFL Home Edition NOT accepted. |
| **CUHK** | **6.5** | **80** | **~4.0** | None stated (PTE: 64, no band < 60) | IELTS One Skill Retake and TOEFL Best Scores NOT accepted. IELTS Indicator / TOEFL Home accepted for reference only — a centre-based test is still required. |
| **HKUST** | **6.0** | **80** | **4.5** | None stated | HKUST explicitly states 4.5 for new-scale tests, which corresponds to old ~86. This is effectively a slight increase from the previous old-scale 80 requirement. |
| **PolyU** | **6.0** | **80** | **~4.0** | None stated | IELTS Online / Indicator / One Skill Retake NOT accepted. TOEFL Home NOT accepted. Must be in one sitting. |
| **CityU** | **6.5** | **79** | **~4.0** | None stated | IELTS Online / Indicator NOT accepted. TOEFL Home NOT accepted. Results must be within 2 years of Semester A start. |
| **HKBU** | **6.0** | **79** | **~4.0** | None stated | Check individual programme pages for higher requirements in language-intensive degrees. |
| **Lingnan** | **6.0** | **79** | **~4.0** | None stated | Notably, Lingnan **accepts** IELTS One Skill Retake — one of the few HK universities to do so. |
| **EdUHK** | **6.0** | **80** | **~4.0** | None stated | Duolingo, TOEFL Home, TOEFL MyBest, IELTS Indicator / Online / One Skill Retake all NOT accepted. Test must be dated on or after 1 Jan 2024. |

### Important observations

1. **HKU is the outlier**: IELTS 6.5 and TOEFL 93 is significantly higher than every other university. If HKU is your top choice, you need to prepare for a higher bar.
2. **CityU and CUHK sit in the middle**: They require IELTS 6.5 (like HKU) but accept a lower TOEFL of 79–80. This creates a gap — if you are stronger at TOEFL, CityU/CUHK is relatively more TOEFL-friendly than HKU.
3. **HKUST's new TOEFL band of 4.5**: On the old scale this equates to approximately 86, which is higher than the previous 80. If you are targeting HKUST with a TOEFL taken after January 2026, aim for Band 4.5 or above.
4. **Home editions and online tests are almost universally rejected**: The only exception is that some universities accept them "for reference" — they do not satisfy the formal requirement. Always book a centre-based test.

---

## IELTS vs TOEFL — Head-to-Head Comparison

| Feature | IELTS Academic | TOEFL iBT (2026) |
|---|---|---|
| **Administering body** | British Council / IDP / Cambridge | ETS |
| **Test format** | Paper-based or Computer-delivered | Computer-based (adaptive) |
| **Total duration** | ~2 hours 45 minutes | ~85 minutes |
| **Sections** | Listening, Reading, Writing, Speaking | Listening, Reading, Writing, Speaking |
| **Speaking format** | Face-to-face with a human examiner | Recorded responses (AI-scored from 2026) |
| **Writing tasks** | Task 1: describe data/chart; Task 2: essay | Task 1: email response; Task 2: academic writing |
| **Score scale** | 1–9 bands (0.5 increments) | 1–6 bands (0.5 increments) from Jan 2026 |
| **Score validity** | 2 years | 2 years |
| **Results turnaround** | 3–5 days (computer) / 13 days (paper) | ~72 hours |
| **Test frequency (HK)** | ~48 dates per year | Multiple dates per month |
| **Test fee (HK, approx.)** | HK$2,150 (~US$275) | ~US$215–235 (varies) |
| **HK test centres** | 14+ locations via British Council & IDP | HKEAA centres in Kowloon & Tsuen Wan |
| **UK visa accepted?** | Yes (IELTS for UKVI specifically required) | No — UKVI requires IELTS |
| **Mainland China availability** | Widely available in 40+ cities | Available in major cities via NEEA |

---

## Which Test Should You Take? Decision Framework

### Choose IELTS if:

- **You are also applying to UK universities** — UK Visas and Immigration (UKVI) requires IELTS for Tier 4 student visa applications. If Hong Kong is your backup and the UK is your primary target, taking IELTS covers both.
- **You prefer face-to-face Speaking** — IELTS Speaking is a 11–14 minute conversation with a human examiner. Many test-takers find this more natural than speaking into a microphone.
- **You are stronger at British English conventions** — IELTS reading passages may include British spelling and vocabulary. If you studied in a British-curriculum school, this can feel more familiar.
- **Your target university requires IELTS 6.0** — For HKUST, PolyU, HKBU, Lingnan, and EdUHK, IELTS 6.0 is a moderate bar that many applicants can clear with 4–8 weeks of preparation.
- **You want more test centre options in Hong Kong** — IELTS offers 14+ venues across Hong Kong and Macau through British Council and IDP.

### Choose TOEFL if:

- **You are also applying to US or Canadian universities** — TOEFL is the default in North America. One test covers HK + US/Canada applications.
- **You want a shorter test day** — At 85 minutes (2026 format), TOEFL is nearly half the duration of IELTS. Less fatigue, especially for younger test-takers.
- **You prefer typing over handwriting** — All TOEFL responses are typed. IELTS Writing is also typed on computer-delivered tests, but paper-based IELTS still requires handwriting.
- **You perform better on multiple-choice Reading/Listening** — TOEFL Reading and Listening are predominantly multiple-choice, while IELTS includes sentence completion, matching, and short-answer formats.
- **You want faster results** — TOEFL 2026 delivers scores in approximately 72 hours, compared to 3–13 days for IELTS.

### Consider taking BOTH if:

- You are applying to HKU (TOEFL 93 / IELTS 6.5) AND UK universities (IELTS only for UKVI). You might sit IELTS for your UK applications and TOEFL as a backup for HK if your IELTS score falls short of 6.5.
- You sat one test and scored below your target. Rather than retaking the same test, switching to the other format may play to different strengths (e.g., switching from IELTS Writing Task 1 chart description to TOEFL's email-response format).

---

## Test Preparation Tips Specific to Hong Kong Admissions

### 1. Start early — at least 6 months before the application deadline

Most Hong Kong universities close non-JUPAS applications between November and January for September entry. Work backwards:

- **September–October**: Take the test for the first time
- **November–December**: Retake if needed (scores usually arrive in 3–8 days)
- **January**: Submit application with final scores

### 2. Understand the "one sitting" rule

HKU, PolyU, HKUST, and others explicitly require scores achieved "in one sitting" or "in the same attempt." TOEFL's MyBest Scores feature (which combines best section scores across multiple tests) is **not accepted** at most Hong Kong universities. Similarly, IELTS One Skill Retake is rejected at all universities except Lingnan.

### 3. Check validity windows

Both IELTS and TOEFL scores are valid for **2 years** from the test date. Most universities require the score to be valid as of September 1 of the entry year. A test taken before September 2024 will not be valid for 2026 entry.

EdUHK has a stricter rule: the test must be dated **on or after 1 January 2024** for 2026/27 entry.

### 4. Register through official channels only

- **IELTS in Hong Kong**: British Council (britishcouncil.hk) or IDP (ielts.idp.com/hongkong)
- **TOEFL in Hong Kong**: HKEAA (hkeaa.edu.hk) is the authorised administrator; register via the ETS website
- **IELTS in mainland China**: British Council via the NEEA IELTS portal (ielts.neea.cn)
- **TOEFL in mainland China**: NEEA TOEFL portal (toefl.neea.cn)

### 5. Aim above the minimum

Published minimums are the floor, not the target. Competitive applicants to HKU and CUHK typically hold IELTS 7.0+ or TOEFL 100+ (old scale) / Band 5.0+ (new scale). A score at the minimum may not be enough when competing against applicants from English-medium international schools.

---

## Frequently Asked Questions (FAQ)

**Q: Can I submit Duolingo English Test (DET) scores to Hong Kong universities?**
A: As of 2026, no UGC-funded university in Hong Kong accepts Duolingo as a primary English qualification for undergraduate admission. EdUHK explicitly rejects it. Some universities may accept it "for reference" alongside a centre-based IELTS or TOEFL, but it cannot replace them. If Duolingo is your only English test, you will need to sit IELTS or TOEFL before applying.

**Q: Is PTE Academic accepted?**
A: CUHK accepts PTE Academic (minimum 64, no band below 60). Other universities may accept it on a case-by-case basis, but IELTS and TOEFL remain the safest choices across all eight institutions.

**Q: I took TOEFL before January 2026. Will my old 0–120 score still be valid?**
A: Yes. Scores remain valid for two years regardless of the scoring change. During the 2026–2028 transition period, ETS score reports display both the legacy 0–120 score and the new 1–6 band score side by side. Universities will accept either format as long as the score was obtained within the validity window.

**Q: My IELTS is 6.0 but HKU requires 6.5. Can I still apply?**
A: You can apply, but your application may be automatically screened out if HKU enforces the minimum strictly. It is strongly recommended to retake the test and achieve 6.5 or higher before the application deadline. Some faculties at HKU may exercise discretion for borderline scores if other credentials are exceptional, but this is not guaranteed.

**Q: Does the IELTS score need sub-scores above a certain level for HK universities?**
A: At the undergraduate level, most Hong Kong universities state only an overall minimum band score without sub-score requirements. However, individual programmes (especially in law, journalism, or education) may set higher sub-score requirements. Always check the specific programme's admission page.

**Q: Can I combine IELTS and TOEFL scores from different sittings?**
A: No. Each university requires the English proficiency requirement to be met by a single test result from one sitting. You cannot combine an IELTS Writing score with a TOEFL Speaking score, or combine scores from two different IELTS sittings (except at Lingnan, which accepts IELTS One Skill Retake).

**Q: I already have a high DSE English score. Do I still need IELTS/TOEFL?**
A: If you are applying through JUPAS using DSE results, you do not need IELTS or TOEFL — the DSE English exam fulfils the English requirement. IELTS/TOEFL is required for non-JUPAS applicants, international qualifications holders, and mainland Chinese students applying through direct admission schemes.

**Q: How does the new shorter TOEFL format affect my preparation?**
A: The 2026 TOEFL is approximately 85 minutes (down from ~2 hours), uses an adaptive format, and includes revised task types (e.g., an email-writing task replaces the independent essay). Study materials published before 2026 may not reflect the new format. Use official ETS practice materials updated for the January 2026 changes.

# Complete Guide for International Students Applying to Hong Kong Universities 2026

Hong Kong has quietly become one of Asia's most compelling destinations for international undergraduates. Four of its universities consistently place in the global top 100. The city operates under a common law framework, conducts most degree programmes in English, and sits at the intersection of mainland China and the wider world — a combination that is genuinely difficult to replicate elsewhere.

For students educated outside Hong Kong's local curriculum (HKDSE), the admissions landscape is navigable but requires deliberate planning. This guide covers every stage of the journey: selecting the right pathway, meeting qualification thresholds, submitting a competitive application, budgeting for four years, securing a student visa, and understanding your options after graduation.

---

## 1. Why Study in Hong Kong?

### Academic standing

The 2025 QS World University Rankings place the University of Hong Kong (HKU) at 17th globally, HKUST at 47th, and CUHK at 51st. These are not honorary placements — research output, employer reputation scores, and faculty-to-student ratios all contribute to consistent top-50 results across major ranking systems.

### Language

The majority of degree programmes at HKU, HKUST, and HKBU are delivered entirely in English. At CUHK, PolyU, and CityU, English is the medium for most programmes with Cantonese or Mandarin appearing in specific professional or local-oriented streams. International students who are not Cantonese speakers function comfortably in academic and professional settings.

### Location and career access

Hong Kong is the world's third-largest financial centre by assets under management. Graduates from HK universities have structured pathways into finance, technology, logistics, and trade roles across both the Hong Kong and Greater Bay Area job markets. The IANG visa (covered in Section 11) allows graduates a renewable 24-month post-study work period with no employer sponsorship requirement.

### Costs relative to peers

Tuition fees for international students run approximately HKD 145,000–198,000 per year depending on programme and institution. This is meaningfully lower than equivalent programmes at UK Russell Group universities (GBP 30,000–45,000/year) or comparable US institutions.

---

## 2. The Eight UGC-Funded Universities

Hong Kong's University Grants Committee (UGC) funds eight publicly-supported institutions. All offer undergraduate programmes open to international applicants.

| University | Abbreviation | International admissions page |
|---|---|---|
| The University of Hong Kong | HKU | [admissions.hku.hk](https://admissions.hku.hk) |
| The Chinese University of Hong Kong | CUHK | [admission.cuhk.edu.hk](https://admission.cuhk.edu.hk) |
| The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology | HKUST | [ug.hkust.edu.hk](https://ug.hkust.edu.hk) |
| The Hong Kong Polytechnic University | PolyU | [www.polyu.edu.hk/arro/admissions](https://www.polyu.edu.hk/arro/admissions/) |
| City University of Hong Kong | CityU | [www.cityu.edu.hk/ao/non-jupas](https://www.cityu.edu.hk/ao/non-jupas/) |
| Hong Kong Baptist University | HKBU | [ar.hkbu.edu.hk/non-jupas](https://ar.hkbu.edu.hk/non-jupas/) |
| Lingnan University | LU | [www.ln.edu.hk/admissions](https://www.ln.edu.hk/admissions/) |
| The Education University of Hong Kong | EdUHK | [www.eduhk.hk/admissions](https://www.eduhk.hk/admissions/) |

Each university manages its own non-JUPAS admissions independently. There is no common application platform for international students — you apply directly to each institution.

---

## 3. Application Pathways for International Students

### 3.1 Non-JUPAS Direct Application

JUPAS (Joint University Programmes Admissions System) is the centralised platform used by students sitting the Hong Kong Diploma of Secondary Education (HKDSE) examination. **International students who hold non-HKDSE qualifications do not use JUPAS.** They apply through each university's own Non-JUPAS admissions channel.

Accepted qualifications under Non-JUPAS vary by institution but broadly include:

- **International Baccalaureate (IB) Diploma**
- **GCE A-Level** (UK, Singapore, and other international variants)
- **SAT + AP courses** (US curriculum)
- **Australian Tertiary Admission Rank (ATAR)** with applicable subject prerequisites
- **National Certificate of Educational Achievement (NCEA)** — New Zealand
- **Canadian provincial transcripts** (Ontario OSSD and equivalents)
- **European Baccalaureate**
- **Other nationally-recognised secondary leaving certificates** assessed on a case-by-case basis

Each university publishes specific minimum entry requirements for each qualification type. These can be verified on the relevant admissions pages linked above.

### 3.2 Mainland China Gaokao Route

The National College Entrance Examination (Gaokao / 全国高考) is treated as a distinct admissions route — separate from the general Non-JUPAS process. HKU, CUHK, HKUST, PolyU, CityU, HKBU, and LU all accept Gaokao applicants.

Key features:

- **Quota-based**: Each university has a fixed annual intake quota for Gaokao applicants. Total Gaokao intake across all eight UGC universities is subject to UGC guidelines.
- **Score benchmark**: Most HK universities require scores significantly above the national 一本线 (First-tier cut-off line). Indicative requirements are 一本线 + 30 to 100 points depending on programme and university, though exact thresholds are announced each year by each institution.
- **Direct application**: Gaokao applicants apply directly to HK universities using their 高考成绩单 and relevant supporting documents. Applications typically open in June after national scores are released.
- **Interview**: Several programmes at HKU and HKUST require a Mandarin or English-medium interview for Gaokao applicants.
- **Scholarship overlap**: Gaokao applicants are eligible for the same scholarship pools as other Non-JUPAS applicants at most institutions.

Mainland students enrolled in international curricula (IB, A-Level) or studying at international schools in China should apply via the Non-JUPAS pathway, not the Gaokao route.

### 3.3 IB Direct Entry

The IB Diploma is among the most widely recognised and strongly preferred qualifications at HK universities. IB applicants apply through the Non-JUPAS system (not a separate stream), but are typically assessed with higher admission rates relative to other qualification types, particularly at HKU and HKUST.

---

## 4. Required Qualifications by Programme Area

### 4.1 Medicine and Health Sciences

Medical programmes in HK are among the most competitive in Asia.

**HKU MBBS (Medicine)**
- IB: Minimum 38–42 points; mandatory HL Biology and Chemistry at grade 6 or above
- A-Level: A\*A\*A with Chemistry and Biology required
- SAT: 1540+ with strong AP Chemistry and AP Biology (5s expected)
- Gaokao: Top provincial scorers only; science stream required; typically within top 0.5% of provincial candidates
- Additional: BMAT or HKUMSQ entrance assessment; English interview

**CUHK Medicine (MBChB)**
- IB: 38–42 points; HL Chemistry and Biology (grade 6+)
- A-Level: A\*AA minimum
- Additional: UCAT ANZ strongly recommended; medical interview mandatory

### 4.2 Business and Finance

**HKU BBA (Business Administration)**
- IB: 35+ overall; HL Mathematics (Analysis and Approaches) grade 5+
- A-Level: AAB minimum; Mathematics preferred
- SAT: 1480+ with Mathematics score 750+

**CUHK Business Administration**
- IB: 34–36; HL subjects in relevant disciplines
- A-Level: ABB–AAB
- SAT: 1430–1500

**HKUST Business (incl. BBA, Finance)**
- IB: 36–40; HL Mathematics required for quantitative tracks
- A-Level: AAA for most BBA programmes; Mathematics required
- SAT: 1500+

### 4.3 Engineering and Computer Science

**HKUST Engineering / Computer Science**
- IB: 36–40; HL Mathematics and Physics required; Chemistry advantageous
- A-Level: AAA; Mathematics and Physics required
- SAT: 1500+ with 780+ in Mathematics

**HKU Engineering**
- IB: 35–38; HL Mathematics and Physics required
- A-Level: AAB–AAA; Mathematics and one science required
- SAT: 1470+

**CityU Computer Science**
- IB: 32–36
- A-Level: ABB–AAB

### 4.4 Arts, Humanities and Social Sciences

Requirements are generally lower than for STEM and professional programmes, with greater emphasis on written assessments, portfolios (for fine arts, design), and the personal statement.

**HKU Arts (BA programmes)**
- IB: 32–36
- A-Level: ABB–AAB; relevant humanities subjects preferred

**HKBU Communication / Journalism**
- IB: 30–34
- A-Level: ABB

All minimum scores above are indicative and based on published institutional guidelines and historical data. Verify directly with each university's admissions office before applying, as thresholds can change year to year.

---

## 5. English Language Requirements

### Standard requirements

Almost all UGC universities require proof of English proficiency for applicants whose medium of prior education was not English. Standard benchmarks:

| Test | Typical minimum | Competitive score |
|---|---|---|
| IELTS Academic | 6.0–6.5 overall (no band below 5.5) | 7.0+ for top programmes |
| TOEFL iBT | 80–90 | 100+ for top programmes |
| Cambridge C1 Advanced | Grade C | Grade B or A |
| Cambridge C2 Proficiency | Grade C | Any grade |
| Duolingo English Test | 105 | 120+ |

Programme-specific requirements frequently exceed institutional minimums. HKU Medicine, for example, typically requires IELTS 7.0+ or TOEFL iBT 100+. Always confirm requirements for your specific target programme.

### English proficiency waivers

You are generally exempt from English tests if:

1. Your secondary education was **conducted entirely in English** for at least three years immediately prior to applying (this includes students at English-medium international schools)
2. You hold qualifications from a country where English is an official language and the medium of instruction — this commonly includes the UK, Ireland, USA, Canada, Australia, New Zealand, Singapore, and South Africa
3. You have completed (or are completing) GCE A-Levels or IB Diploma in English — these are often treated as sufficient evidence of English competency

Submit documentary evidence (school transcripts noting language of instruction, or a letter from your school principal) alongside your application if claiming a waiver.

## 6. Application Timeline — Month by Month

The admissions cycle for most UGC universities follows a common pattern, though specific deadlines vary. Plan for the following:

| Month | Action |
|---|---|
| **August–September** (Year 12 / final year) | Research programmes; shortlist 5–8 universities and programmes; request teacher recommendation letters |
| **October** | Most universities open Non-JUPAS applications; begin drafting personal statement; request predicted grades from school |
| **October–November** | Submit applications to early-closing programmes (HKU typically closes in late November/early December for most programmes) |
| **November–December** | Submit remaining applications; confirm English test booking if not yet taken |
| **December–January** | Receive conditional or unconditional offers from some universities; respond to any document requests |
| **January–February** | Sit final examinations (IB, A-Level internal assessments); final English tests |
| **February–March** | Supplementary admission rounds; some universities issue further offers |
| **March–April** | IB and A-Level predicted grades submitted; accept preferred offer |
| **May–July** | Final IB/A-Level results released; universities confirm places; arrange student visa |
| **August** | Arrive in Hong Kong; orientation programmes; register for courses |

Gaokao applicants follow a compressed timeline: Gaokao takes place in early June; scores are released mid-June; HK university applications for Gaokao applicants open in June–July with offers typically made by July–August.

## 7. Required Documents Checklist

Prepare all documents well before the application deadline. Most universities require:

- [ ] **Online application form** completed via the university's admissions portal
- [ ] **Application fee** (typically HKD 200–400 per programme application)
- [ ] **Certified copies of academic transcripts** (years 10–12 or equivalent; official translation to English if originals are in another language)
- [ ] **Predicted grades / school report** (issued by your school on official letterhead)
- [ ] **Personal statement** (500–1,000 words; programme-specific motivation and fit)
- [ ] **Teacher reference letters** (typically 1–2; written in English on school letterhead; sealed and submitted directly or via the application portal)
- [ ] **English language test score report** (IELTS/TOEFL certificate; or proof of waiver eligibility)
- [ ] **Copy of valid passport** (main page)
- [ ] **Proof of nationality** (national ID or passport)
- [ ] **Programme-specific materials**: supplementary portfolio (Design, Architecture, Fine Arts), research proposal (certain BBA or senior entry programmes), BMAT / UCAT score (Medicine)
- [ ] **Photograph** meeting official specifications
- [ ] **Gaokao score notification** (高考成绩单) — Mainland applicants only

Documents must typically be submitted as PDF uploads through each university's portal. Physical certified copies may be required at the point of enrolment confirmation. Keep originals safe.

## 8. Cost Breakdown for International Students (2026)

### Tuition fees

International students (non-local students) pay higher tuition fees than domestic HKDSE students. Published annual fees for 2025/26 (indicative; confirm with each institution):

| University | Annual tuition (non-local, 2025/26) |
|---|---|
| HKU | HKD 182,000–198,000 |
| HKUST | HKD 173,000–180,000 |
| CUHK | HKD 145,000–175,000 |
| PolyU | HKD 140,000–168,000 |
| CityU | HKD 138,000–165,000 |
| HKBU | HKD 130,000–155,000 |
| LU | HKD 120,000–140,000 |
| EdUHK | HKD 108,000–130,000 |

Medical and dental programmes typically carry the highest fees within each institution; arts, education, and social sciences the lowest.

### On-campus housing

University halls of residence are available for international students and are generally the most affordable and convenient option in Year 1. Costs:

- Shared room (two-person): HKD 18,000–22,000 per academic year
- Single room: HKD 22,000–30,000 per academic year
- Guaranteed for Year 1 students at most universities; competitive allocation thereafter

Demand far exceeds supply from Year 2 onwards. Budget accordingly.

### Off-campus rental

Private rentals near major campuses (Pokfulam for HKU, Sha Tin for CUHK, Clear Water Bay for HKUST) average:

- Studio apartment: HKD 8,000–14,000/month
- Shared flat (per person): HKD 5,000–8,500/month

### Other living costs

| Category | Estimated monthly | Annual |
|---|---|---|
| Groceries and household | HKD 2,000–3,500 | HKD 24,000–42,000 |
| Dining out | HKD 2,500–4,500 | HKD 30,000–54,000 |
| Transport (MTR/bus) | HKD 500–900 | HKD 6,000–10,800 |

| Personal and leisure | HKD 1,500–3,000 | HKD 18,000–36,000 |

**Realistic total budget (excluding tuition):** HKD 90,000–140,000 per year depending on lifestyle and accommodation choice.

**Combined annual budget (tuition + living):** Approximately HKD 230,000–340,000 per year, or roughly USD 29,500–43,500.

## 9. Scholarships for International Students

Financial support for non-local undergraduates has expanded significantly in recent years. Below are the major university-administered scholarships that international students are typically eligible for:

### HKU

**HKU Foundation Entrance Scholarship**
- Value: Up to HKD 120,000 per year (renewable for up to 4 years)
- Eligibility: Exceptional academic achievement; open to all non-local students
- Application: Automatically considered upon full application to HKU; no separate form

**HKU Presidential Scholarship for Global Excellence**
- Value: Full tuition coverage for the degree period
- Eligibility: Highest-achieving applicants globally; requires additional nomination

### CUHK

**Vice-Chancellor's Scholarship**
- Value: HKD 120,000 per year (renewable)
- Eligibility: Top non-local undergraduate applicants; GPA equivalent 3.8+ or IB 40+
- Application: Separate scholarship application via CUHK admissions portal

**CUHK Merit Award**
- Value: HKD 40,000–80,000 per year
- Eligibility: Strong academic standing; broader eligibility than Vice-Chancellor's Scholarship

### HKUST

**HKUST President's Scholarship (Non-local)**
- Value: Full tuition waiver + housing subsidy for 4 years
- Eligibility: Top 1–2 candidates per admissions cohort; exceptional academic and extracurricular record
- Process: Invited to a scholarship assessment day

**HKUST Academic Excellence Award**
- Value: HKD 50,000–100,000 per year
- Eligibility: Automatically considered based on admissions application

### PolyU, CityU, HKBU

Each institution offers merit-based entrance scholarships in the range of HKD 20,000–80,000/year for high-achieving non-local students. Applications are typically embedded in the regular admissions process.

### External scholarships

- **Hong Kong Scholarship for Excellence Scheme (HKSES)**: Government-funded; for students from economies with existing bilateral agreements. Check with your home country's education ministry.
- **Belt and Road Scholarship**: Targeted at students from economies along the Belt and Road Initiative; covers tuition and living allowances. See: [www.ugc.edu.hk/eng/ugc/activity/br/scholarship.html](https://www.ugc.edu.hk/eng/ugc/activity/br/scholarship.html)

Apply for all relevant scholarships at the same time as submitting your admissions application. Do not wait for an offer before starting scholarship applications.

---

## 10. Student Visa Application Process

International students admitted to a full-time undergraduate programme in Hong Kong require a student visa issued by the Immigration Department (IMMD).

**Process overview:**

1. **Receive unconditional offer letter** from your university (issued after final results)
2. **University lodges visa application on your behalf** through the Document Submission and Processing Centre (DSPC) system — you do not apply directly to IMMD yourself
3. **Provide documents to the university's admissions or registry office:**
   - Completed visa application form (Form ID 995A)
   - Passport copy (main page)
   - Two recent passport-size photographs
   - Proof of academic qualifications (certified transcripts and certificates)
   - Financial proof — bank statements or sponsorship letter demonstrating ability to fund your studies. IMMD requires evidence of at least HKD 220,000 per year or equivalent for tuition plus living expenses
   - Letter of acceptance from the university
4. **University submits the application** to IMMD via DSPC
5. **Processing time**: Typically 6–8 weeks. Apply no later than 6 weeks before your intended arrival date
6. **Visa granted**: You receive a visa label in your passport. Your study visa is typically valid for the duration of your programme plus a short buffer

Students from certain nationalities may be eligible for visa-on-arrival or pre-clearance arrangements. Confirm your nationality-specific requirements at: [www.immd.gov.hk/eng/services/visas/study.html](https://www.immd.gov.hk/eng/services/visas/study.html)

**Important**: Do not travel to Hong Kong on a tourist visa and attempt to convert to a student visa on arrival. Begin the student visa process as soon as you receive your offer.

---

## 11. After Graduation: IANG Visa

The Immigration Arrangements for Non-local Graduates (IANG) is one of Hong Kong's most graduate-friendly post-study work policies globally.

**Key features:**

- **No job offer required at point of application**: Graduates can apply for IANG immediately upon graduation without having secured employment
- **Initial validity**: 24 months, allowing unrestricted work rights in HK
- **Renewal**: Extendable based on demonstrated employment or evidence of continued contribution to HK's economy. Employment-based renewals have been routinely granted for qualifying graduates
- **Policy trajectory**: The HKSAR Government has periodically expanded the scope and conditions of IANG as part of its talent attraction strategy. The 2023 policy update extended flexibility for graduates from non-local universities with HK campuses — verify current conditions at [www.immd.gov.hk/eng/services/visas/IANG.html](https://www.immd.gov.hk/eng/services/visas/IANG.html)
- **Path to permanent residency**: Graduates who remain employed and ordinarily resident in HK for 7 years may apply for the right of abode as permanent residents

**Eligibility**: Must have completed a full-time locally-accredited degree programme at a HK-based institution (includes all eight UGC universities).

The IANG visa, combined with the breadth of employment opportunities in finance, technology, and trade, makes Hong Kong one of the most direct post-study pathways in Asia from graduation to long-term residency.

---

## 12. Common Mistakes and Rejection Reasons

Understanding why applications fail is as useful as knowing what makes them succeed.

### Academic threshold miscalculations

Many applicants underestimate programme-level requirements. Institutional minimums published on websites are floor thresholds — actual competitive offers are typically made to students meaningfully above those minimums. For top programmes at HKU, HKUST, and CUHK, assume you need to be in the top 5–15% of applicants from your qualification type.

### Applying too late

Applications to HK universities are accepted on a rolling basis in most cases. Early applications receive earlier offers, and strong early candidates lock in places before later applicants receive consideration. Aim to submit all applications before November.

### Weak personal statement

A personal statement that is generic, reads as a list of achievements, or does not address the specific programme and why Hong Kong specifically is your destination will not distinguish you. Admissions tutors read thousands of applications; clarity of motivation and programme fit are weighted heavily.

### Inadequate English proficiency evidence

Submitting an IELTS score of 6.0 for a programme with a stated minimum of 6.0 is technically compliant but weakens your application. Competitive candidates for flagship programmes at HKU or HKUST typically present 7.0+. Retake the test if necessary.

### Missing predicted grades

Many international school students assume their final results will be sufficient. HK universities make conditional offers based on predicted grades during application, before final results are available. Ensure your school submits a formal predicted grades report.

### Not requesting recommendation letters early enough

Experienced referees — particularly at international schools during busy periods — may need 4–6 weeks to write a meaningful letter. Request letters in September for November application deadlines. A generic letter from a busy teacher is worse than a specific, warm letter from one who knows you.

### Ignoring programme prerequisites

Engineering at HKUST requires HL Mathematics and Physics in the IB — not just a general IB score. Submit an application without meeting prerequisite subject requirements and it will be rejected regardless of your total score. Read the subject prerequisites on the programme page, not just the headline score.

### Visa delays due to financial documentation

IMMD requires evidence of financial capacity. Applications delayed by insufficient bank statements or unclear sponsorship letters push visa processing past safe arrival windows. Prepare financial documentation as soon as you receive an offer.

---

## 13. Frequently Asked Questions

**Can I apply to multiple universities simultaneously?**
Yes. There is no restriction on how many non-JUPAS applications you submit. Apply to 4–8 programmes across 3–5 institutions to maintain optionality. Pay each application fee separately.

**Is the application fee refundable?**
No. Application fees at HK universities are non-refundable regardless of outcome.

**Do I need to submit my final IB or A-Level results before receiving an offer?**
No. Most offers are conditional, based on predicted grades. Conditional offers are confirmed or withdrawn after final results are released (July for IB; August for UK A-Levels).

**Can I defer my offer by a year?**
Some programmes permit deferral for compelling personal reasons (medical, family). This is discretionary. Contact the admissions office of the specific programme. Gap year deferral is less commonly granted in HK than at UK universities.

**What if my final results fall slightly below my conditional offer requirements?**
Contact the admissions office immediately. Some programmes will maintain an offer if results miss by a narrow margin, particularly if the rest of your application is strong and you accept quickly. Do not wait.

**Are there part-time work restrictions on a student visa?**
Student visa holders in Hong Kong are permitted to work part-time for up to 20 hours per week during term time and full-time during official vacation periods, without needing a separate work authorisation.

**Can mainland Chinese students apply via both Gaokao and Non-JUPAS routes?**
No. Mainland applicants must choose one route. If you are completing a Gaokao-based curriculum, you apply via the Gaokao route. If you are completing an international curriculum (IB, A-Level, international school), you apply via Non-JUPAS.

**Is there a minimum age requirement?**
No explicit minimum age, but applicants must have completed a full secondary education equivalent to HKDSE Year 12 or equivalent to be considered for undergraduate entry.

**Is studying through Chinese medium possible for international students?**
Yes. CUHK offers significant Chinese-medium teaching, particularly in humanities. Lingnan University has programmes in both mediums. For students fluent in Mandarin or Cantonese, this can be an advantage.

**What is the difference between non-local and international student status?**
In HK, "non-local student" is the official classification used for fee and quota purposes and includes mainland Chinese, Macau, Taiwan, and foreign passport holders. The term "international student" is colloquially used but is not a formal legal classification at HK universities.
