# Lingnan University (LU) Complete Guide 2026

Among Hong Kong's eight UGC-funded universities, **Lingnan University** — LU, or simply *Lingnan* — is the one that does not try to play the comprehensive research-university game. Where HKU, CUHK and HKUST chase global league-table rankings on the back of giant labs and medical schools, Lingnan has spent the last quarter-century sharpening a single, very deliberate identity: **a small, residential, liberal-arts university where the ratio of students to faculty stays low, almost every undergraduate spends a term abroad, and the curriculum forces breadth across the humanities, business and the social sciences**.

Internationally, Lingnan is the only Hong Kong member of the **Global Liberal Arts Alliance** and is one of the very few institutions in Asia that the international press routinely lists among the region's top liberal-arts universities. If you are a DSE candidate, a mainland Gaokao student or an international applicant whose interests sit in language, literature, translation, cultural studies, economics, philosophy, politics, sociology, business or data science — and who values small classes, mandatory hostel life and exchange opportunities over giant lecture halls — Lingnan offers something its larger peers genuinely cannot.

This guide covers the 2026/27 admissions cycle: what kind of university Lingnan really is, where it sits in the 2026 rankings, the three faculties and the School of Interdisciplinary Studies, the JUPAS and non-JUPAS application routes, tuition fees and scholarships, the flagship programmes you should know about, and what graduates actually do after they leave the Tuen Mun campus.

---

## 1. What kind of university is Lingnan?

Lingnan traces its lineage to the **Christian College in China** (格致書院), founded in **Canton (Guangzhou) in 1888**. The institution moved to Hong Kong in **1967** as Lingnan College, and was granted full university status in **1999**. The main campus sits in **Tuen Mun**, New Territories, on Castle Peak Road, hugging the foothills of Castle Peak. It is reached most easily via the West Rail Line to Siu Hong station and then a short bus or taxi ride, or via the Light Rail. The campus is the most "liberal-arts-college" in feel of any in Hong Kong: low-rise red-brick buildings, courtyards, a single central plaza, and dormitories that house roughly 80% of full-time undergraduates.

The "Christian" origin reflects the institution's founding mission, but Lingnan today operates as a fully secular public university. The motto, **"Education for Service"** (作育英才・服務社會), has remained unchanged since the Canton era and is reflected in the university's strong emphasis on community engagement and a mandatory **Service-Learning** component for many programmes.

### Size and campus character

- Around **3,500 undergraduates** and **5,000 postgraduates**, total enrolment of roughly **8,500** — comfortably the smallest of the eight UGC-funded universities
- **Student-to-faculty ratio of approximately 17–18:1 overall, but small-class seminars of 20–35 are standard** for arts, languages and social sciences subjects
- **Hostel guarantee for all four years** for non-local students and at least three years for local students — almost no other Hong Kong public university offers this
- Around **270 exchange partner institutions in over 50 countries**, with **more than 80% of undergraduates** taking part in a credit-bearing exchange, summer programme or winter institute
- Compact campus: the entire ground can be crossed end-to-end in under ten minutes, which means students bump into their classmates and professors daily

For an applicant who wants to know what life on a Hong Kong public university actually feels like, Lingnan is the closest thing to a North American liberal-arts college.

---

## 2. Lingnan's place in 2026 rankings

The 2026 ranking cycle is genuinely strong for Lingnan, especially given that for many years the university opted out of submitting data to the major league tables.

- **QS World University Rankings 2026: 701–710** — the rise reflects Lingnan's deliberate decision in recent years to participate fully in the global rankings.
- **Times Higher Education (THE) World University Rankings 2026: 301–350** — Lingnan is one of only six Hong Kong institutions in the global top 350.
- **THE Asia University Rankings 2026: #84** — the university's first time participating, landing immediately in the Asia top 100.
- **THE International Outlook 2026: #47 globally** — one of the most internationally diverse universities in the world by faculty and student composition.
- **QS World University Rankings by Subject 2026: nine broad and individual subjects ranked**, more than half of which moved up versus 2025; Computer Science enters for the first time.

The headline takeaway: in pure overall research-volume rankings Lingnan will never catch HKU or CUHK, and applicants chasing a top-100 brand should not expect that here. But on the metrics where a liberal-arts university *should* shine — international outlook, teaching reputation, and named subject areas in the humanities and social sciences — Lingnan now performs very respectably indeed.

---

## 3. Faculties and academic structure

Lingnan organises its undergraduate teaching into **three faculties** plus a **School of Interdisciplinary Studies**. There are 16 academic departments and a handful of language and disciplinary centres. Across the four units, Lingnan offers roughly **29 honours bachelor's degree programmes**.

### Faculty of Arts
- Departments: Chinese, English, History, Philosophy, Translation, Visual Studies, Cultural Studies (joint with Social Sciences in some programmes)
- Flagship majors: **BA in Chinese**, **BA in Translation** (one of the longest-established translation programmes in Hong Kong), **BA in English**, **BA in Cultural Studies**, **BA in Visual Studies**, **BA in Philosophy**, **BA in History**

### Faculty of Business
- **AACSB-accredited** — Lingnan's business school sits in the top ~5% globally that hold this accreditation
- Departments: Accountancy, Finance, Management, Marketing & International Business, Operations & Supply Chain Management, Computing & Decision Sciences
- Programmes include the **BBA (Honours)** with majors and concentrations in Accounting, Finance, Marketing, HRM, Risk and Insurance Management; and the standalone **BSc in Risk and Insurance Management** and **BSc in Data Science**

### Faculty of Social Sciences
- Departments: Economics, Political Science, Sociology & Social Policy, Psychology, Health and Social Services Management
- Programmes include **BSocSc (Honours)** with concentrations in Economics, Political Science, Sociology and Psychology, plus the **BSocSc in Data Science** and the **BSocSc in Health and Social Services Management** offered in collaboration with health-services partners

### School of Interdisciplinary Studies
- Houses Lingnan's newer cross-faculty programmes such as **BA in Animation and Digital Arts**, **BSc in Data Science**, the joint major in **Philosophy, Politics and Economics (PPE)**, and the **BA in Interdisciplinary Studies in Humanities** which lets students design their own major from across the Faculty of Arts
- Closely linked to the Wong Bing Lai Music and Performing Arts Unit and to the Science Unit, which together provide quantitative literacy and arts electives across the entire university

The takeaway: **Lingnan is not the place for medicine, dentistry, civil engineering or pure science as a major** — those programmes simply do not exist here. It is the place for languages, humanities, business, social sciences, data science and the new interdisciplinary humanities-plus-tech mix.

---

## 4. JUPAS admission for HKDSE candidates

Lingnan participates fully in **JUPAS**, with all UGC-funded undergraduate programmes available through the system.

### Minimum entrance requirements
- **English Language**: Level **3**
- **Chinese Language**: Level **3**
- **Mathematics (Compulsory Part)**: Level **2**
- **Citizenship and Social Development**: **Attained**
- One elective at Level **3** (or two at Level 2 for some arts programmes)

### Score profiles in recent admissions
Lingnan's JUPAS median score for the **best five subjects** typically falls in the **18–22 range**, depending on the programme:
- Most BA Faculty of Arts majors: **median best-five around 18–20**
- BBA and BSc Data Science: **median best-five around 20–22**
- BSocSc programmes (Economics, Politics, Sociology, Psychology): **median best-five around 19–21**
- The most competitive concentrations (PPE, Data Science, Marketing & International Business): **median best-five around 22–24**

These are noticeably more accessible than HKU/CUHK/HKUST cut-offs and broadly comparable to HKBU and EdUHK. For DSE candidates whose final score lands in the **18–22 best-five band**, Lingnan is realistically a Band A–B target.

### JUPAS entrance scholarships
Lingnan operates a generous entrance scholarship scheme. Any JUPAS applicant achieving **22 or above in the best five subjects** who is admitted to a JUPAS-participating programme is awarded an entrance scholarship — single payment for one-time awards or renewable for the full four years for higher scoring bands. Top scorers (best five 30+) can receive full tuition plus a hostel and living allowance.

---

## 5. Non-JUPAS admission routes

Lingnan accepts non-JUPAS applicants through three main streams.

### Mainland Chinese students (Gaokao)
Lingnan participates in the **Mainland China Undergraduate Admission Scheme**, which is **independent of the Gaokao national enrolment system** — applicants apply directly to Lingnan and admission decisions are based on Gaokao score, English subject score and (for some programmes) interview. Indicative score floors:
- **Gaokao total**: above the **first-tier (一本)** line in the applicant's province, typically with a margin of 30–60 points
- **Gaokao English**: 120/150 or above (recommended)
- Direct application to Lingnan opens in **January–May 2026** for September 2026 entry

### International qualifications
- **A-Levels**: typical offer 3 A-Levels at grades **BBB to ABB**, with at least a B in any subject directly relevant to the chosen major
- **IB Diploma**: typical offer **28–32 points** total, with English at HL or SL Grade 5+
- **SAT / ACT**: SAT 1300+ (1600 scale) or ACT 28+ in addition to school transcripts
- **English requirement** for non-local applicants: IELTS **6.5** (no band below 5.5), or TOEFL **iBT 88+**, or equivalent

### Senior-year transfer
Lingnan accepts senior-year transfer applicants (Year 2 or Year 3 entry) holding an Associate Degree, Higher Diploma, or completed first/second year of a recognised bachelor's degree. Cumulative GPA of **3.0/4.0 or above** is recommended; transfer credits are assessed individually.

---

## 6. Tuition fees and cost of attendance (2026/27)

| Item | Local students | Non-local students |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Tuition (UGC-funded undergraduate, per year)** | **HK$47,000** | **HK$175,000** |
| Caution money (refundable) | HK$450 | HK$450 |
| Student union, hall and amenities fees | HK$1,000–1,500 | HK$1,000–1,500 |
| Hostel (compulsory residence, per year) | HK$13,000–18,000 | HK$13,000–18,000 |
| Estimated living costs (food, transport, books, personal) | HK$45,000–55,000 | HK$50,000–70,000 |

For a non-local student, the all-in budget for one academic year at Lingnan is roughly **HK$240,000–265,000** (≈ US$30,500–34,000 / RMB 220,000–245,000). That is **slightly below** the comparable budget at HKU, CUHK or HKUST, mostly because the Tuen Mun area is meaningfully cheaper than Pok Fu Lam, Sha Tin or Clear Water Bay.

### Scholarships beyond JUPAS
- **Entry scholarships for non-JUPAS and mainland applicants**: tiered scholarships covering tuition (full or partial) plus a hostel and living allowance for top applicants
- **Exchange scholarships** to subsidise the mandatory or recommended international experience
- **Need-based bursaries** through the HKSAR Government's Tertiary Student Finance Scheme for eligible local students

---

## 7. Flagship programmes worth knowing about

### BA in Chinese
One of the most respected Chinese-language and literature programmes in Hong Kong, with concentrations in Chinese literature, Chinese linguistics, and Chinese language teaching. Particularly strong choice for students considering careers in publishing, secondary teaching or graduate study in Chinese studies.

### BA in Translation
Lingnan was one of the first Hong Kong universities to offer a dedicated translation degree. The programme covers Chinese-English and English-Chinese translation across literary, legal, business and audiovisual contexts, with simultaneous and consecutive interpreting modules. Graduates routinely enter government, professional translation firms, publishing houses and the major broadcasters.

### BA in Cultural Studies
The first dedicated cultural studies undergraduate degree in Asia, founded in the 1990s. Combines critical theory, media studies, urban studies and political economy. Strong feeder for graduate study at top-tier UK, US and Asian institutions.

### BSocSc (Hons) in Economics
A small, rigorous economics programme with closer faculty access than at HKU or CUHK Economics. Recent graduates have moved into central-bank graduate schemes, financial-services research desks and top US/UK postgraduate economics programmes.

### BBA (Hons) — Marketing & International Business / Finance / Risk and Insurance Management
The AACSB-accredited business school punches above its weight, with the Risk and Insurance Management programme in particular feeding graduates into the major Hong Kong insurance and reinsurance firms. The Marketing & International Business concentration enjoys very high placement rates with consumer-goods, retail and digital firms across the Greater Bay Area.

### BSc in Data Science (Faculty of Business and the School of Interdisciplinary Studies)
Lingnan's newest flagship, designed to combine Python and R programming, statistics, and machine learning with humanities-side data interpretation. The programme deliberately positions graduates as "data translators" between technical teams and business or policy decision-makers.

### BA in Animation and Digital Arts
A relatively young School of Interdisciplinary Studies programme that has rapidly attracted attention. Combines storytelling, 2D and 3D animation, game design and immersive media. Studio-style teaching with industry mentors from the Hong Kong creative cluster.

---

## 8. Hostel and campus life

Lingnan operates **ten residential halls** clustered on the main Tuen Mun campus. Hostel life is genuinely central to the Lingnan experience:
- **All non-local undergraduates** are guaranteed a hostel place for the full four years
- **Local undergraduates** are guaranteed three years of residence
- Each hostel has its own master, tutors, hall culture, hall colours, hall song and an annual programme of academic, sports and community-service activities
- Mandatory **integrated learning programme** credits (community service, leadership, arts and sports) are tracked against hostel residency

The flip side: Tuen Mun is a 45–55 minute MTR ride from Central, and weeknights on campus are quiet. Students who want easy access to the bars, restaurants and gigs of Causeway Bay or Lan Kwai Fong should plan around it. Students who value a self-contained campus community where you actually know everyone in your year usually love it.

---

## 9. Graduate outcomes

Lingnan publishes annual graduate employment surveys. Recent figures show:
- Overall employment / further-study rate of **roughly 95%** within six months of graduation
- Median starting salary across all programmes of approximately **HK$20,000–22,000 per month**
- BBA and BSc Data Science graduates: median starting salary closer to **HK$22,000–25,000**
- Translation, Chinese and Cultural Studies graduates: strong placement into government, NGO, secondary-school teaching and publishing roles, with a meaningful share (15–20%) progressing to taught masters in Hong Kong, the UK or the US
- A growing share of mainland graduates use the **IANG visa** to remain in Hong Kong and work in the Greater Bay Area's media, marketing, insurance and education sectors

---

## 10. Who should apply to Lingnan?

**Lingnan is right for you if**:
- You want **small classes, close faculty contact and a true residential experience** more than you want a top-100 brand on your CV
- Your interests sit in **languages, humanities, cultural studies, social sciences, business or data science** rather than medicine or hard engineering
- You actively want to **spend a term or year abroad** as part of your degree
- You are a mainland or international student who wants to live in Hong Kong but cannot afford the rent of Pok Fu Lam, Sha Tin or Clear Water Bay
- You value an AACSB business school with an undergraduate-first culture rather than a giant MBA-driven research factory

**Lingnan is probably wrong for you if**:
- You want to study **medicine, dentistry, law (LLB), pharmacy, civil/mechanical engineering or architecture** — none of which are offered
- You measure a university entirely by its overall QS or THE world rank
- You strongly prefer an urban-core campus over a suburban residential one

For the right student, Lingnan can be one of the most rewarding undergraduate experiences in Hong Kong — and one of the most internationally connected. For the wrong one, the Tuen Mun location and the absence of professional schools will eventually grate. Knowing which student you are is the single most important question in any Lingnan application.

# Hong Kong Metropolitan University (HKMU) Complete Guide 2026

When DSE candidates and international applicants think about Hong Kong's universities, the conversation almost always starts with the eight UGC-funded institutions — HKU, CUHK, HKUST, PolyU, CityU, HKBU, EdUHK and Lingnan. Yet sitting outside that "Group of Eight" is a university that quietly enrols around 12,000 full-time undergraduates, runs the largest nursing pipeline in Hong Kong, and in 2024 became the territory's first ever University of Applied Sciences (UAS): **Hong Kong Metropolitan University (HKMU)**.

In 2026, HKMU is no longer a niche option for second-chance learners. It debuted in the QS World University Rankings 2026 in the 781–790 band — the first self-financing institution and first UAS in Hong Kong to be ranked — and six of its subjects appeared in the QS World University Rankings by Subject 2026, three of them in the global top 150. For a university that began life in 1989 as the distance-learning Open Learning Institute, that arc is striking.

This guide walks through HKMU's identity, its five schools, the JUPAS and non-JUPAS application routes, tuition after government subsidy, scholarships, campus and accommodation, and where graduates actually end up. If you are weighing a self-financing offer against a UGC programme, or considering HKMU as your insurance choice, this is the context you need.

---

## 1. What HKMU Is — and Why Its Status Matters

HKMU is unique in Hong Kong in three ways simultaneously:

1. **It is the only self-financing university established by the Hong Kong Government.** Other self-financing institutions (such as Hang Seng University, Saint Francis University, or Tung Wah College) were founded by private bodies. HKMU traces its statutory origin to the 1989 Open Learning Institute Ordinance.
2. **It is Hong Kong's first University of Applied Sciences (UAS).** In March 2024, the Education Bureau formally designated HKMU as the city's inaugural UAS, modelled after the German *Fachhochschule* tradition: degree programmes built around industry practice, applied research, and credentials valued by employers rather than purely academic prestige.
3. **It is Hong Kong's largest self-financing university by enrolment**, with around 12,000 full-time students plus a sizeable part-time and distance-learning population that traces back to its open-university roots.

The UAS designation is the most important development for prospective students. It signals a deliberate policy direction: the Government wants HKMU to anchor a parallel, application-oriented degree track alongside the research-heavy UGC sector. In practice that translates into more compulsory internship hours, closer ties with regulators (Nursing Council, Physiotherapy Board, Civil Aviation Department), and programmes deliberately scoped to address Hong Kong's skills shortages.

In 2021 the institution also rebranded from "Open University of Hong Kong" to "Hong Kong Metropolitan University" to reflect that more than 90% of its students are now full-time, on-campus learners — the open-learning legacy is no longer the dominant identity.

---

## 2. The Five Schools and Their Programme Portfolio

HKMU organises its undergraduate teaching across five schools. Each one has carved out a clear niche rather than trying to mirror the UGC universities.

### School of Arts and Social Sciences

Programmes in creative writing, film, animation and visual effects, journalism and communication, applied psychology, social sciences, sports and recreation management. The creative-media offerings are particularly well-regarded: graduates are visible in Hong Kong's animation, post-production and gaming industries, and the school operates one of the few dedicated motion-capture and VFX studios on a Hong Kong campus.

### Lee Shau Kee School of Business and Administration

Bachelor of Business Administration programmes with concentrations including accounting, finance, marketing, international business, and the flagship **Aviation Services Management** programme — built with Hong Kong's airport ecosystem in mind and supported by a dedicated cabin training simulator. The school is named after the late property magnate whose foundation funded the building.

### School of Education and Languages

The largest provider of pre-service language teachers among self-financing institutions. Five-year double-degree programmes pair a BEd with a BA in Chinese, English or Putonghua education — graduates qualify directly as registered teachers in Hong Kong primary or secondary schools without needing a separate PGDE. There are also stand-alone language and translation degrees.

### School of Nursing and Health Sciences

This is HKMU's defining strength. The School produces more nursing graduates each year than any other Hong Kong institution — a critical pipeline given chronic shortages in the public hospital system. Programmes include the five-year Bachelor of Nursing (with both general and mental-health streams), the Bachelor of Science (Hons) in Physiotherapy launched in recent years, and the Bachelor of Science (Hons) in Medical Laboratory Science. These are all SSSDP-subsidised and lead to professional registration.

### School of Science and Technology

Engineering and computing programmes positioned around the UAS philosophy. Offerings include Computer Science, Cybersecurity, Data Science, Building Services Engineering and Sustainable Development, Civil Engineering, Electronic and Computer Engineering, Testing and Certification, Environmental Studies, and Life Sciences. Many programmes are accredited by the Hong Kong Institution of Engineers or by professional bodies in their respective sectors.

For the 2026/27 academic year, HKMU is offering **50 JUPAS programmes** across these five schools, plus a wider portfolio when non-JUPAS, top-up, and senior-year-entry options are counted.

---

## 3. JUPAS Admission to HKMU

HKMU has been a full participating institution in the **Joint University Programmes Admissions System (JUPAS)** since 2007. Local DSE candidates apply through the same JUPAS portal, slot HKMU programmes into Bands A–C, and receive offers in the same Main Round as the eight UGC universities.

A few HKMU-specific rules are worth memorising:

- **Best-of-multiple-sittings, no penalty.** HKMU considers the best grade attained in each subject across any HKDSE sittings. Re-takers are not penalised, which is a meaningful contrast with some UGC programmes that prefer single-sitting candidates.
- **Subject weighting varies by programme.** Most BBA programmes weight English and Mathematics; the BEng programmes weight Mathematics and a science subject; nursing and physiotherapy weight Biology or Chemistry. Always read the programme-specific weighting on the JUPAS site rather than relying on a generic 4C+2X assumption.
- **Interview is common but not universal.** Nursing, physiotherapy, education, and aviation programmes typically require interviews; many BBA and arts programmes use grades alone.
- **Lower published score thresholds than UGC.** Indicative median admission scores for many HKMU programmes sit in the **15–22 (4C+1X)** range, depending on programme. Nursing, physiotherapy, and the popular BEd double degrees typically demand the upper end of that range, while less competitive arts and BBA streams are accessible with the JUPAS minimum.

For DSE students who fall short of UGC offers but still want a recognised, government-supported degree, HKMU is one of the most logical insurance choices precisely because the JUPAS process is identical and the funding is parallel.

---

## 4. Non-JUPAS, Sub-degree Articulation, and International Routes

HKMU runs three other inflows worth knowing:

- **Non-JUPAS (Local).** For local applicants holding qualifications other than current-year DSE — IB, A-Level, GCE, HKALE, Associate Degrees or Higher Diplomas. Applications are submitted directly through the HKMU admissions portal.
- **Sub-degree articulation.** Holders of Associate Degrees or Higher Diplomas from HKCC, CCCU, IVE, HKU SPACE, and other local providers can apply for senior-year (Year 3) entry into a matching bachelor programme. This is one of the most common pathways into HKMU and is responsible for a significant share of each year's intake.
- **International / Mainland applicants.** Mainland students apply via the HKMU Mainland Admissions route (separate from the Gaokao single-track scheme used by UGC universities). International students apply through the Non-JUPAS portal and submit IELTS/TOEFL or equivalent. HKMU programmes are eligible for Hong Kong student visas, and graduates qualify for the **IANG** post-study work scheme on the same basis as UGC graduates.

---

## 5. Tuition, SSSDP, NMTSS, and the Real Cost

This is the area most prospective students misunderstand. "Self-financing" sounds like "expensive" — but in HKMU's case the headline tuition is heavily offset by Government subsidy.

All HKMU full-time undergraduate programmes are funded under one of two Government schemes:

- **SSSDP (Study Subsidy Scheme for Designated Professions/Sectors).** Targeted at programmes addressing manpower shortages — nursing, physiotherapy, medical laboratory science, building services, computer science, testing and certification, creative industries, and several BBA streams. Students pay an annual tuition comparable to the standard UGC tuition (HK$44,500/year for the 2026/27 cohort, subject to confirmation).
- **NMTSS (Non-means-tested Subsidy Scheme).** Applies to most other full-time self-financing degree programmes. For 2025/26, the annual subsidy was raised to **HK$35,120**, with a further review for 2026/27 indexed to the Composite Consumer Price Index. Net tuition typically lands in the HK$45,000–60,000/year range depending on programme.

In practical terms, a Hong Kong student admitted to HKMU through JUPAS into an SSSDP programme pays roughly the same out-of-pocket tuition as a CUHK or HKU student in a comparable subject. The financial penalty for choosing HKMU over UGC is much smaller than the "self-financing" label suggests.

Government student finance (TSFS, NLSFT, EFAS) is fully available to eligible local students at HKMU on the same terms as UGC institutions.

---

## 6. Scholarships — The DSE Star Scholarship

HKMU runs an aggressive entrance scholarship policy designed to attract high-DSE candidates who might otherwise default to a UGC offer:

- **HKDSE Star Scholarship.** Since the 2022/23 cohort, JUPAS-admitted students who achieve **5\* or 5\*\* in any Category A subject** in the year of admission receive **HK$40,000 per qualifying subject**. There is no cap on the number of subjects — a student with three 5\*\* grades receives HK$120,000. The scholarship is awarded on top of any other merit award.
- **Other entrance scholarships** include the President's Scholarship, dean's-list awards, and programme-specific awards in nursing, physiotherapy, aviation, and the creative arts.
- **Continuing scholarships** are available each academic year for high-GPA students.

For a DSE candidate hovering at the boundary between a competitive UGC programme and an HKMU offer in their target field, the Star Scholarship plus government subsidy can produce a financial package that is materially better than the unsubsidised cost of attending a less-competitive UGC degree.

---

## 7. Campus and Student Life

HKMU's main campus sits in **Ho Man Tin, Kowloon**, on Good Shepherd Street, supplemented by the **Jockey Club Campus** nearby. Both are within walking distance of Ho Man Tin MTR station on the Tuen Ma and Kwun Tong Lines, putting students fifteen to twenty minutes from Mong Kok, Kowloon Tong, and the cross-harbour core.

Smaller annexes house specialist facilities — the cabin simulator for aviation services, the nursing skills laboratories, the VFX and motion-capture studios, and the building services labs. The compactness of the urban campus is a trade-off: students don't get the green expanse of CUHK or HKUST, but they do get genuinely central Kowloon, with internships and part-time work realistically reachable by MTR.

**Accommodation.** Historically a weakness for HKMU. The 2024 acquisition of a former hotel in Hung Hom, rebranded as **MU88**, added 255 rooms and around 400 beds, primarily for non-local and exchange students. Local students typically commute from home — a normal pattern across most Hong Kong universities.

**Student life.** Around 80 student societies cover academic, cultural, religious, and sporting interests. The HKMU Students' Union runs the central social calendar; sports facilities include a multi-purpose hall and access to government recreation grounds. The university's competitive sports teams, particularly in basketball and dragonboat, regularly feature in inter-university tournaments.

---

## 8. Graduate Outcomes and Industry Recognition

HKMU does not publish a single headline employment-rate figure to match the UGC standard, but a few signals are robust:

- **Nursing graduates** enter the Hospital Authority pipeline directly upon registration. Demand has consistently exceeded supply for more than a decade. Starting salaries for newly registered nurses in HA are around HK$32,000/month (Master Pay Scale Point 14).
- **Physiotherapy graduates** are similarly absorbed by HA, private clinics and elderly-care providers, with starting pay at a similar level subject to professional registration.
- **Education graduates** with the BEd double degree enter Hong Kong primary and secondary schools as registered teachers without further qualification — the same status as EdUHK BEd graduates. Starting pay on the Master Pay Scale Civil Service Salaries is around HK$36,000/month.
- **Aviation Services Management graduates** are a deliberate feed for Cathay Pacific, Hong Kong Airlines, the Airport Authority and ground-handling operators.
- **Creative arts graduates** populate Hong Kong's animation, gaming, and post-production firms — notable employers include local studios working on regional broadcast and feature-film projects.

The QS subject rankings 2026 placed three HKMU subjects in the global top 150 — a useful signal for international recognition, particularly for students considering postgraduate study abroad.

---

## 9. HKMU vs UGC Universities — When Does It Make Sense?

HKMU is the right choice rather than a fallback in several specific scenarios:

- **You want to be a registered nurse, physiotherapist, or medical laboratory scientist** and your DSE results put you below the cut-off for the equivalent CUHK, HKU or PolyU programme. HKMU produces more nursing graduates than any UGC institution and the professional registration outcome is identical.
- **You want to be a primary-school or kindergarten language teacher** and the EdUHK BEd is out of reach. The HKMU double-degree route delivers the same registration outcome.
- **You want a creative-industries career** and you have a strong portfolio. The applied, studio-based approach often suits creative practitioners better than the more theoretical art-history orientation at UGC institutions.
- **You are an international or Mainland student** seeking a Hong Kong qualification with IANG eligibility at lower published tuition than the UGC top tier.
- **You hold an Associate Degree or Higher Diploma** and need a clean senior-year articulation route.

HKMU is a weaker choice if you want a research-heavy academic career (the UGC universities offer deeper research mentoring), if you specifically need Hong Kong's most prestigious institutional name on your CV for finance or law recruitment, or if your target programme (Medicine, Law, Architecture) is simply not offered at HKMU.

---

## 10. Application Timeline for the 2026/27 Cycle

For DSE candidates targeting HKMU through JUPAS:

- **December 2025**: JUPAS application opens; programme rankings can be revised through to the deadline.
- **Late February 2026**: Final deadline to revise programme choices (subject to JUPAS-published date).
- **April–May 2026**: HKMU may invite you for interview for nursing, physiotherapy, education and aviation programmes. Interviews are typically held in May–June.
- **July 2026**: HKDSE results released; JUPAS Main Round offers issued shortly after.
- **August 2026**: Confirmation, registration, and orientation.

For non-JUPAS, sub-degree articulation, and international applicants, HKMU operates rolling admissions through its dedicated portal at admissions.hkmu.edu.hk, with main intake decisions issued from spring through to summer 2026.

---

## Bottom Line

Hong Kong Metropolitan University is no longer correctly described as a "second-tier alternative" to the UGC eight. It is Hong Kong's first University of Applied Sciences, its largest self-financing institution, and the dominant supplier of nursing, language-teaching and aviation graduates to the local economy. With government subsidies aligning net tuition with UGC rates, an aggressive merit scholarship for high-DSE candidates, and QS-ranked academic recognition arriving in 2026, the case for HKMU has shifted from "fallback" to "specifically chosen". For DSE candidates whose career target lies in nursing, physiotherapy, language teaching, creative media, aviation, or applied engineering, an HKMU offer in 2026 deserves to be evaluated on its own merits — not as a runner-up.

---

# The Hong Kong Polytechnic University (PolyU) Complete Guide 2026

Among Hong Kong's eight UGC-funded universities, PolyU occupies a distinctive position. It is not the oldest — that honour belongs to HKU. It is not the highest-ranked overall — HKU and HKUST tend to sit above it on the QS table. But on a number of practical measures that matter to undergraduates — the quality of professional accreditation, the calibre of design education, the strength of hotel and tourism management, and the size of the campus right in the centre of Kowloon — PolyU is genuinely first among Hong Kong's universities, and in some subject areas it is first in Asia.

In QS World University Rankings 2026, PolyU sits in the global top 60, having climbed steadily over the past decade. More importantly for prospective students, eight of its subjects rank in the global top 50, and the School of Hotel and Tourism Management has been ranked the world's best for hospitality and leisure management for several consecutive years. PolyU's School of Design is the only Hong Kong institution to feature consistently in the global top 20 for Art and Design.

This guide walks through what PolyU is in 2026, the broad-based admission scheme that distinguishes it from HKU and CUHK, the JUPAS and non-JUPAS pathways, tuition and scholarships, the flagship faculties, accommodation, and the career trajectories that follow a PolyU degree. If you are deciding between PolyU and another UGC institution — or weighing PolyU's design or physiotherapy programmes against overseas offers — this is the context you need.

---

## 1. PolyU's Identity in 2026

PolyU traces its origin to 1937 as the Government Trade School, the territory's first publicly funded technical school. It became Hong Kong Polytechnic in 1972, and was granted full university status in 1994 as The Hong Kong Polytechnic University. That trajectory matters: PolyU is fundamentally an application-oriented research university, not a classical liberal arts institution.

Three features define PolyU's identity in 2026:

1. **Professional accreditation density.** PolyU offers more accredited professional programmes than any other Hong Kong university. Civil engineering, mechanical engineering, electrical engineering, building services, surveying, accounting, construction management, optometry, physiotherapy, occupational therapy, radiography, nursing, social work, speech therapy and Chinese medicine all lead directly to professional registration in Hong Kong. For students who want a clear line from degree to licence to career, PolyU is the most efficient route in the city.

2. **Two world-leading specialisations.** The School of Hotel and Tourism Management (SHTM) and the School of Design are not merely strong by Hong Kong standards — they are global leaders. SHTM has held the world number one position in QS subject rankings for hospitality and leisure management for several consecutive years. The School of Design occupies a comparable position for industrial and communication design in Asia.

3. **Broad-based admission.** Unlike HKU and CUHK, where most JUPAS applicants choose a single discipline at the point of admission, PolyU operates a "broad-based admission scheme" for many of its programmes. Students enter a faculty or scheme (for example, "Scheme in Engineering" or "Scheme in Design") and choose their major after a year of common-core study. This delays the discipline commitment and is particularly valuable for candidates who are torn between related fields.

The campus itself is unusual: 94,600 square metres concentrated in Hung Hom, directly opposite the Hung Hom MTR / cross-harbour rail terminus. Few large research universities anywhere are this central. The location explains why PolyU has retained a strong urban, working-city character that is markedly different from CUHK's Sha Tin valley campus or HKUST's Clear Water Bay coastal site.

---

## 2. Faculties, Schools and Flagship Programmes

PolyU is organised into six faculties and two independent schools, all offering undergraduate degrees:

- **Faculty of Business** — accounting, finance, management, marketing, global supply chain management, aviation management.
- **Faculty of Construction and Environment** — building engineering, building services engineering, civil engineering, environmental engineering, surveying, construction management, urban planning, real estate.
- **Faculty of Engineering** — mechanical, biomedical, electrical, electronic and information, computing (computer science, AI, data science, financial technology), industrial systems engineering.
- **Faculty of Health and Social Sciences** — applied social sciences, social work, social policy, nursing, optometry, physiotherapy, occupational therapy, radiography, medical laboratory science, speech therapy, food safety and technology, biomedical engineering.
- **Faculty of Humanities** — Chinese language and bilingual studies, English studies, English and applied linguistics, translation, Chinese culture, Japanese studies.
- **Faculty of Science** — applied biology, applied chemistry, applied mathematics, applied physics, food technology, investment science.
- **School of Design** — independent school. Programmes in advertising design, communication design, environmental design, industrial design, interactive media, product design.
- **School of Hotel and Tourism Management** — independent school. Programmes in hotel management, tourism and events management, integrated convention and event management.

Three programmes deserve detailed attention because they define PolyU's external reputation.

**The School of Design** is the only Hong Kong design school to consistently feature in the global top 20. It runs a four-year BA(Hons) Scheme in Design admitting students into a common first year before they specialise into one of six majors. Admission requires a portfolio interview in addition to JUPAS scores; the design entry score in DSE is consistently among the highest of any creative programme in Asia. Graduates work at firms such as Nike, IDEO, Frog Design, Apple, and Samsung's design studios in Seoul and London.

**The School of Hotel and Tourism Management (SHTM)** offers BSc(Hons) programmes in hotel management and tourism and events management. SHTM runs Hotel Icon, a fully operating four-star teaching hotel in Tsim Sha Tsui East, where students complete supervised placements as part of their degree — a feature unmatched anywhere else in Asia. The school's industry network includes the Mandarin Oriental, Marriott, Hyatt, Peninsula and Shangri-La groups, and a significant proportion of graduates begin their careers as management trainees rather than line staff.

**The Department of Rehabilitation Sciences** offers BSc(Hons) programmes in physiotherapy and occupational therapy. Both are accredited by the relevant Hong Kong professional boards and by the World Confederation for Physical Therapy / World Federation of Occupational Therapists, meaning graduates can practise in the UK, Australia, Canada and Singapore subject to local registration. JUPAS cut-offs for physiotherapy at PolyU regularly sit second only to medicine and dentistry — typically requiring six 5\* grades or equivalent.

---

## 3. Broad-Based Admission Schemes

For many of PolyU's largest programmes, applicants are admitted into a "broad-based scheme" rather than a single named major. The schemes in 2026 include:

- Scheme in Engineering
- Scheme in Computing
- Scheme in Construction and Environment
- Scheme in Business
- Scheme in Hotel, Tourism and Hospitality
- Scheme in Design
- Scheme in Health Sciences
- Scheme in Applied Social Sciences

Inside each scheme, students complete a common first-year curriculum and then declare a major. The scheme structure has two consequences worth understanding before applying.

First, the scheme as a whole has one entrance score, but individual majors inside the scheme may be competitive. A student admitted to Scheme in Engineering with a JUPAS score at the scheme cut-off will need to perform well in the first-year common modules to secure a place in their preferred major (for example, AI and Big Data, which is currently the most oversubscribed engineering major). For risk-averse applicants this can be uncomfortable; for genuinely undecided applicants it is liberating.

Second, some flagship programmes — physiotherapy, occupational therapy, radiography, optometry, accounting and finance, design — operate **outside** the broad-based schemes and admit directly into the named programme. These programmes are typically more competitive at the JUPAS stage and have a clearer admission ceiling.

PolyU also offers a small number of high-prestige niche programmes, including BSc(Hons) Investment Science (a quantitative finance programme), BBA(Hons) Aviation Management and Logistics, and the BSc(Hons) Bioinformatics and Genomics programme run jointly with the Faculty of Science.

---

## 4. JUPAS Admission

For Hong Kong DSE candidates, PolyU is admitted via the Joint University Programmes Admissions System (JUPAS). The 2026 admission rules to know:

- **No compulsory subject requirement at the institutional level.** Beyond the 332233 university-entry minimum (Chinese 3, English 3, Mathematics Compulsory Part 2, Citizenship and Social Development Attained, two electives at level 3), individual programmes may add specific elective requirements — for example, Physics for engineering, Biology for health sciences.
- **Preferred subjects** influence admission selection. Programmes list two to four preferred electives. Achieving a high grade in a preferred subject improves your effective admission score even if you do not declare it as one of your top weighted subjects.
- **Admission score formulae.** Most programmes use one of two formulae: "Best 5 subjects" or "Chinese + English + Best 3 subjects". Some programmes also apply weightings — typically 1.5x for Mathematics Extended Module M1/M2, or 1.5x for the most relevant preferred elective.
- **Programme priority.** PolyU only considers a programme on your JUPAS list if it appears in **Band A** (your top three choices). Programmes outside Band A will not be reviewed by PolyU for admission — a stricter rule than HKU, which considers Band B for many programmes.

The implication for JUPAS strategy is straightforward: if PolyU is your target, you must place its programmes in Band A. The university publishes the median and lower quartile admission scores for each programme on its admission website and the JUPAS handbook each summer; checking the trailing three years is the most reliable basis for a Band A list.

Programmes that require additional assessment beyond JUPAS scores include:

- **School of Design** — portfolio interview, typically in January–March.
- **School of Hotel and Tourism Management** — interview for borderline candidates.
- **Physiotherapy, occupational therapy, optometry, radiography** — interviews and aptitude tests.
- **Nursing** — group interview.
- **Social work** — interview assessing motivation and personal suitability.

---

## 5. Non-JUPAS and International Admission

Non-local applicants — including mainland Chinese (gaokao), International Baccalaureate, GCE A-Levels, US SAT/AP, and other international qualifications — apply directly to PolyU rather than through JUPAS. The 2026 routes:

- **Mainland gaokao admission** — via PolyU's dedicated gaokao admission scheme. Score requirements vary by province, but in 2025 PolyU admitted students at roughly the 985-university line for most programmes and at top-20 mainland university lines for the School of Design and physiotherapy.
- **International / other qualifications** — IB Diploma typically 36–42 points (programme-dependent); GCE A-Levels typically AAA–A\*A\*A\*; SAT 1450+ with strong AP scores. English requirement: IELTS 6.5 (no band below 5.5) or TOEFL iBT 80, unless the applicant's secondary education was conducted in English.
- **Associate degree / Higher Diploma top-up** — PolyU runs a substantial Senior Year Entry intake admitting students who have completed an associate degree or higher diploma. Most major faculties accept top-up applications, with quotas published annually.

The application portal for non-JUPAS first-year admission opens in September of the year before entry and closes in late January, with an early-round deadline in mid-November. Applicants for the School of Design and SHTM should plan for portfolio submission and interview windows before that close.

---

## 6. Tuition and Living Costs in 2026

PolyU is a UGC-funded university, so its undergraduate tuition is regulated by the Government:

- **Local students** — HK$42,100 per academic year for UGC-funded undergraduate places. This figure has not changed since 1997 and is identical across all eight UGC-funded universities. Self-financed places (taught masters, some second-degree programmes) are charged at programme-specific rates.
- **Non-local students** — HK$145,000 per academic year for most undergraduate programmes in 2026/27, raised in line with the Government's 2024 announcement that non-local UGC tuition would rise across the eight institutions. Some programmes (notably the School of Design and SHTM) charge slightly higher rates.

Living costs in Hong Kong remain high. A realistic 2026 budget for a non-local student living on or near PolyU's Hung Hom campus:

- On-campus hall (limited supply): HK$15,000–24,000 per academic year.
- Off-campus shared accommodation in Hung Hom or Ho Man Tin: HK$5,500–8,500 per month for a shared room.
- Food and daily expenses: HK$4,500–6,500 per month.
- Transport: HK$400–700 per month with Octopus student concession.
- Total annual cost (tuition + living) for a non-local student: roughly HK$240,000–290,000.

PolyU's hall capacity is limited relative to its student population. First-year non-local students are generally guaranteed a hall place; senior-year students enter a points-based allocation system. Many senior students live in the Hung Hom and Whampoa Garden area, which is walking distance to campus.

---

## 7. Scholarships

PolyU operates one of the larger scholarship programmes among Hong Kong universities, structured into three tiers.

**Entrance scholarships** are awarded automatically based on JUPAS or non-JUPAS admission scores. The Talent Admission Scheme offers full tuition plus a living stipend (around HK$60,000 per year) for the top tier of admitted candidates — typically those with seven 5\*\* DSE grades or international equivalent, and outstanding non-academic achievements. The Reaching Out Award and Hong Kong Polytechnic University Scholarships provide partial tuition coverage for the next tier.

**Faculty-level scholarships** are awarded by individual schools — particularly the School of Design and SHTM — based on portfolio quality, interview performance, or sustained academic achievement during study.

**Mainland scholarships** include the National Scholarship for Outstanding Self-Financed Students Abroad (administered by the China Scholarship Council) and PolyU's own mainland recruitment scholarships, which are generally awarded to gaokao top scorers from key provinces.

For internationally-funded students, the Hong Kong PhD Fellowship Scheme is research-only and does not apply to undergraduates, but PolyU's Talent Scholarship provides comparable support for outstanding international applicants.

---

## 8. Campus, Student Life and Hall Culture

PolyU's Hung Hom campus is compact and dense — a stark contrast to the sprawling CUHK and HKUST sites. The campus has been subject to significant redevelopment over the past decade, including the Jockey Club Innovation Tower (designed by Zaha Hadid) which houses the School of Design, and the student amenities centre on the western edge of campus.

Student societies are organised through the Federation of Polytechnic University Students (PolySU). The federation has had a complicated political history — it was deregistered in 2022 and operates today as a less politically engaged body than its CUHK and HKU counterparts. Student social life is concentrated around faculty societies (engineering, design, hotel and tourism), residence halls, and the active sports programme.

Hall culture at PolyU is moderately developed: traditional inter-hall sports tournaments, hall dinners, and orientation camps run each year. Halls are co-educational with single-sex floors; most rooms are shared (twin or quad).

The campus is connected by a footbridge to Hung Hom MTR station, and from there students reach Tsim Sha Tsui in two stops, Central in three. PolyU's location gives students unusually easy access to internships and part-time work in Tsim Sha Tsui, Mong Kok and Central — all of which are within 30 minutes of campus by MTR.

---

## 9. Career Outcomes

The PolyU Graduate Employment Survey 2024 reported a 95.4 per cent overall employment rate within six months of graduation, with median monthly starting salaries ranging from approximately HK$22,000 for humanities and applied social sciences to HK$32,000+ for engineering, computing, accounting and finance, and the School of Design. SHTM graduates entering management trainee programmes at international hotel groups typically reported starting salaries of HK$24,000–28,000.

The pattern of PolyU graduate destinations differs from HKU and CUHK in three ways:

1. **Higher proportion entering professional practice immediately.** Because so many programmes are accredited (engineering, surveying, optometry, physiotherapy, nursing, social work), a large share of graduates begin licensed professional careers within their first year. HKU and CUHK graduates more frequently enter business, finance and consulting roles where the discipline of the first degree is less determining.

2. **Strong representation in the design and creative sector.** The School of Design's network places graduates in international design consultancies and in-house design teams at technology companies — destinations that other Hong Kong universities cannot match.

3. **Hospitality leadership pipeline.** SHTM graduates dominate the management trainee pipelines of major hotel groups not just in Hong Kong but across the Greater Bay Area, Singapore, Tokyo and Dubai. The school's alumni network is a meaningful asset for early career mobility.

PolyU's Mainland Affairs Office and Career Services jointly support graduates returning to mainland China — particularly important given that around 25 per cent of PolyU's undergraduates are non-local, with the majority from the mainland. The IANG visa allows non-local graduates to remain in Hong Kong for up to 24 months after graduation to seek work, and a substantial proportion of PolyU graduates use this window to begin careers in Hong Kong before deciding whether to return to the mainland or move on internationally.

---

## 10. Should You Choose PolyU?

PolyU is the right choice if any of the following apply:

- You want a programme leading directly to professional registration (engineering, surveying, physiotherapy, occupational therapy, optometry, nursing, social work, speech therapy).
- You are aiming at the world's leading hotel and tourism management education.
- You want one of Asia's strongest design educations, with a portfolio-based admission process.
- You value a central, transit-connected campus with strong industry access.
- You are undecided between related disciplines and want the flexibility of a broad-based admission scheme with major declaration after a common first year.

PolyU is less likely to be the right choice if you are looking for medicine or dentistry (offered only by HKU and CUHK), if you want a classical liberal arts undergraduate experience (HKU and Lingnan are stronger fits), or if you specifically want a research-doctorate-track route — although PolyU's research output has grown significantly in the past decade and its postgraduate research programmes are now competitive with HKU and HKUST in several engineering fields.

In 2026, with the city's universities all competing aggressively for international students, PolyU's distinctive offer — applied, accredited, professionally networked, internationally recognised in design and hospitality, and sitting on one of the most accessible campuses in Asia — has rarely been clearer. For DSE candidates and international applicants with a clear sense of professional direction, it deserves serious consideration in any Band A list.

# Hong Kong Self-Financing Universities Complete Guide 2026

For most DSE candidates and international applicants, the eight UGC-funded universities (HKU, CUHK, HKUST, PolyU, CityU, HKBU, EdUHK, LingnanU) dominate the conversation. But Hong Kong has a parallel — and rapidly maturing — self-financing degree sector that admits thousands of students every year, including students whose JUPAS scores miss UGC cut-offs by two or three points, mainland Gaokao students who do not clear the UGC bar, and international students looking for English-medium bachelor's programmes at a lower price point than HKU or HKUST.

This guide explains how the self-financing system works in 2026, profiles the six most established degree-awarding institutions, walks through the SSSDP and NMTSS subsidies (and why they matter even when you are not eligible for them), and gives a decision framework for whether a self-financing degree is the right call.

## What "Self-Financing" Actually Means in Hong Kong

In Hong Kong, "self-financing" is a funding label, not a quality label. UGC-funded programmes receive a per-student block grant from the University Grants Committee, which keeps tuition for local students at the standard HK$42,100 per year. Self-financing programmes do not receive this block grant — instead, institutions cover their own costs from tuition, which means published tuition runs anywhere from HK$70,000 to HK$140,000 per year depending on the programme.

Three of these institutions have been granted full university title:

- **The Hang Seng University of Hong Kong (HSUHK)** — granted university title in 2018
- **Hong Kong Metropolitan University (HKMU)** — formerly OUHK, retitled in 2021, designated as Hong Kong's first University of Applied Sciences in 2024
- **Hong Kong Shue Yan University (HKSYU)** — Hong Kong's first private university (2006)

Three others are degree-awarding institutions that do not yet hold full university title but are accredited to award their own bachelor's degrees:

- **Chu Hai College of Higher Education**
- **Caritas Institute of Higher Education (CIHE)** (rebranding to Saint Francis University in some streams)
- **Tung Wah College (TWC)**

THEi (Technological and Higher Education Institute of Hong Kong, part of VTC) also operates a large self-financing degree portfolio, though it sits inside the VTC group structure rather than as a standalone university.

## How JUPAS Treats Self-Financing Programmes

Self-financing degrees do not appear on the standard JUPAS Band A–E list, but they are available through the JUPAS-linked **E-APP (Electronic Advance Application System for Post-Secondary Programmes)**, which lets DSE candidates apply to self-financing degrees and sub-degrees in parallel with their JUPAS choices. Conditional offers from E-APP institutions can be issued before DSE results day, which means candidates who are not confident of clearing UGC cut-offs can secure an insurance offer in advance.

For non-DSE applicants — IB, A-Level, Gaokao, IGCSE-only, mature students, sub-degree top-up — every self-financing institution operates its own direct-application portal, with deadlines staggered between October of the preceding year and August of the entry year. Several offer rolling admissions, and Shue Yan in particular is known for very fast turnaround on direct applications.

## Tuition and the Two Subsidy Schemes That Reshape the Real Cost

Headline tuition is misleading. For local Hong Kong students (including students with right of abode, dependant visa holders meeting residency rules, and certain visa categories) the government runs two subsidy schemes that effectively cut the cost of many self-financing degrees down to UGC levels or below.

### NMTSS (Non-means-tested Subsidy Scheme for Self-financing Undergraduate Studies)

For the 2026/27 cohort, eligible local students receive **HK$35,120 per academic year** (announced December 2025), automatically deducted from tuition. NMTSS applies broadly to most accredited locally-offered self-financing bachelor's programmes. There is no income test and no application — eligibility is determined at admission.

Practical impact: if HSUHK publishes a tuition of HK$95,000 for a non-laboratory programme, an eligible local student pays roughly HK$60,000 net.

### SSSDP (Study Subsidy Scheme for Designated Professions/Sectors)

For 2026/27, SSSDP provides a much larger subsidy — up to **HK$46,780 per year for non-laboratory programmes and HK$81,450 per year for laboratory-based programmes** — but only for designated programmes in sectors with manpower shortages: nursing, allied health (physiotherapy, occupational therapy, medical laboratory science, radiography), early childhood education, architecture and engineering technology, hospitality and tourism, testing and certification, applied sciences, computing, creative industries, and others.

A nursing degree at Tung Wah College or HSUHK with SSSDP can come out at roughly HK$35,000–55,000 net per year for an eligible local student — cheaper than UGC-funded tuition. This is the single most important fact that any local DSE candidate should understand before dismissing self-financing nursing or allied health programmes as expensive backups.

### Important: International Students Do Not Get These Subsidies

Both NMTSS and SSSDP are restricted to local students. International applicants — including most non-permanent-resident mainland and overseas students — pay the full published tuition, which typically ranges from HK$90,000 to HK$140,000 depending on programme and institution. Scholarships are the main route to bring this down, and every self-financing university operates entry, merit-based, and continuation scholarships that can cover 25%, 50%, or 100% of tuition for top entrants.

## Profiles of the Six Major Self-Financing Institutions

### Hang Seng University of Hong Kong (HSUHK)

Located in Siu Lek Yuen, HSUHK has become the most academically competitive self-financing university in Hong Kong. The QS Asia University Rankings 2026 placed HSUHK at 157th in Greater China and the institution has continued to rise in the broader QS Asia table.

HSUHK's flagship strength is its **School of Business**, which holds AACSB accreditation — a credential shared with HKU, CUHK, HKUST and PolyU and rare among self-financing institutions globally. Its BBA in Supply Chain Management, BBA in Financial Analysis, and BA in English are the highest-cut-off programmes; Best 5 of around 18–22 (3322 minimum) is typical of admitted students, though some specialised entry pathways admit lower scores.

Tuition for 2026/27 is approximately HK$95,000 per academic year for most undergraduate programmes. NMTSS-eligible local students pay roughly HK$60,000 net.

### Hong Kong Metropolitan University (HKMU)

HKMU is the largest of the self-financing institutions in headcount. It debuted in the QS World University Rankings in 2025 (781–790 band) and ranked 393rd in the QS Asia University Rankings 2026 — a jump of more than 140 places.

In 2024 HKMU was designated Hong Kong's first **University of Applied Sciences (UAS)**, a new track introduced by the government to formally recognise vocationally-oriented degree institutions. UAS designation matters because the government has signalled that UAS graduates will increasingly receive parity of recognition with UGC graduates in civil service and statutory body recruitment.

HKMU's School of Nursing & Health Studies is the dominant feeder of registered nurses outside the UGC sector, and its programmes in computing, data science, applied AI, and creative arts are heavily SSSDP-subsidised. The university also operates Hong Kong's longest-running and largest distance learning bachelor's programmes through the Li Ka Shing School of Professional and Continuing Education.

### Hong Kong Shue Yan University (HKSYU)

Established in 1971 and granted university title in 2006, Shue Yan is Hong Kong's oldest private institution and is known for its small-class, liberal-arts-style four-year curriculum. Strongest faculties are Counselling and Psychology (the BSocSc Counselling and Psychology programme is widely considered the strongest non-UGC counselling pathway in Hong Kong), Journalism and Mass Communication, Chinese Language and Literature, and Social Work.

Shue Yan's tuition is among the most accessible in the self-financing sector — typically HK$80,000–90,000 per year — and the university is unusual in retaining a four-year structure for all bachelor's programmes from the pre-2012 era, which gives students an extra year of subject depth compared to many self-financing competitors.

### Chu Hai College of Higher Education

Originally founded in 1947, Chu Hai gained degree-awarding status in 2012 and has built a reputation in **Architecture and the Built Environment**. Its BA (Hons) Architecture is one of the few Hong Kong undergraduate architecture programmes accredited by the Hong Kong Institute of Architects (HKIA), giving it a clear professional pathway. Engineering, Business and Communications round out the offering. Tuition runs approximately HK$80,000–95,000 per year.

### Caritas Institute of Higher Education (CIHE) / Saint Francis University

Operated by Caritas Hong Kong (the Catholic Church's social services arm), CIHE focuses on social work, nursing, gerontology, applied psychology, and digital humanities. Several programmes are SSSDP-subsidised, particularly in nursing and social work — fields where Hong Kong has documented manpower shortages. Some programme streams have been rebranded under the Saint Francis University banner as the institution works toward full university title.

### Tung Wah College (TWC)

Operated by the Tung Wah Group of Hospitals, one of Hong Kong's largest charitable healthcare providers, TWC is a specialist health-sciences institution. Its **Bachelor of Health Science (Honours) in Nursing** and BSc programmes in Medical Laboratory Science, Radiation Therapy, and Occupational Therapy are SSSDP-subsidised and lead directly into Tung Wah Group hospitals via clinical placement networks. For DSE candidates aiming at allied health professions whose JUPAS scores fall just short of PolyU or HKU SPACE quotas, TWC is the most direct alternative pathway.

## Rankings Reality Check

Self-financing universities have made unprecedented progress in international rankings in 2026 — HKMU's QS Asia leap and HSUHK's Greater China placement are real signals of institutional development. But ranking parity with HKU or HKUST is not the goal and is not realistic on a five-year horizon. The honest framing for applicants:

- HSUHK and HKMU are now visible in QS World/Asia rankings; the others are not yet
- Programme-level accreditations (AACSB for HSUHK Business, HKIA for Chu Hai Architecture, Nursing Council of Hong Kong registration for HKMU/TWC/CIHE nursing) carry far more weight in graduate hiring and licensure than overall institutional rank
- Employer perception still trails UGC institutions in finance, law and consulting recruitment but is approximately at parity in nursing, allied health, social work, early childhood education, and creative industries

## Decision Framework: When Should You Choose a Self-Financing Degree?

Choose a self-financing degree over a JUPAS Band C UGC offer or a year of retake when:

1. **The programme is SSSDP-subsidised and matches your career target** — particularly nursing, allied health, social work and early childhood education. These subsidised programmes lead to professional registration that is identical to UGC graduates.
2. **You hold a programme-specific advantage** — Counselling and Psychology at Shue Yan, Architecture at Chu Hai, Supply Chain at HSUHK, all of which match or exceed comparable UGC-sector programmes in employability data.
3. **You are an international student priced out of HKU/CUHK** — full-fee international tuition at HSUHK or HKMU runs HK$110,000–140,000, roughly 35–50% below HKU's international rate, and the visa pathway (student visa → IANG graduate visa → Hong Kong PR after seven years) is identical.
4. **You need an insurance E-APP offer before DSE results day** — securing an HSUHK or HKMU conditional offer in March before sitting your final papers reduces stress and gives you a confirmed pathway if your results come in below your JUPAS Band A.

Avoid a self-financing degree when:

- The same career goal can be reached via Associate Degree → UGC top-up at lower total cost (relevant for Business, Arts and Social Science streams)
- You are committed to graduate destinations — investment banking front office, magic-circle law, top-tier consulting — where UGC brand premium remains decisive
- The specific programme is not professionally accredited, in which case the degree functions as a generic bachelor's at premium cost

## Application Timeline for 2026 Entry

For 2026 entry, the typical timeline is:

- **Sep–Oct 2025** — direct admission portals open at all six institutions
- **Dec 2025** — E-APP opens for DSE candidates
- **Mar–Apr 2026** — first round of conditional offers issued
- **Jul 2026** — DSE results released, JUPAS main-round offers, self-financing institutions issue final unconditional offers
- **Aug 2026** — late-round and clearing-style admissions for unfilled places, particularly at Chu Hai, CIHE and TWC
- **Sep 2026** — semester begins

International applicants should add roughly two months for student visa processing through the Immigration Department and aim to submit their final application by April at the latest.

## Final Thoughts

Hong Kong's self-financing sector in 2026 is no longer a fallback option. With NMTSS and SSSDP subsidies bringing local-student net tuition to UGC parity or below in many subsidised fields, with HKMU's UAS designation and QS Asia rise, with HSUHK's AACSB business school visibility, and with established niches in nursing, allied health, architecture and counselling, the question for DSE candidates is no longer "is self-financing good enough?" but "which self-financing programme matches my professional goal?". For international students priced out of HKU or HKUST, it is one of the most under-appreciated value propositions in the Greater Bay Area's higher education landscape.
