# Hong Kong Shue Yan University (HKSYU) Complete Guide 2026

Outside the halo of Hong Kong's eight UGC-funded universities sits an institution that has quietly walked its own road for more than half a century. **Hong Kong Shue Yan University (HKSYU)** was founded in 1971 by Dr Henry Hu Hung-lit and Dr Chung Chi-yung as a private college, became the first institution in Hong Kong to be granted full **private university** status by the Government in December 2006, and in 2026 is celebrating its 55th anniversary and 20 years as a chartered university.

For DSE candidates who want a small-class liberal-arts environment, for mainland students priced out of overseas options, and for international applicants looking for an English-medium Hong Kong degree without the brutal cut-offs of HKU or CUHK, Shue Yan is a serious option that often goes underestimated. This guide covers everything you need: the three faculties, the roughly 15 honours bachelor programmes, JUPAS and non-JUPAS admission, the two SSSDP-subsidised programmes that change the cost calculus, scholarships, accommodation, and graduate outcomes.

---

## 1. What HKSYU Is — and Why Its Status Matters

Shue Yan is unique among Hong Kong's degree-awarding bodies in three ways:

1. **It is Hong Kong's first private university.** When the Government granted university title under the Post Secondary Colleges Ordinance in December 2006, HKSYU became the first private institution in the city allowed to use the word "University" in its name. Other self-financing universities — Hang Seng University, Saint Francis University, the Hong Kong Metropolitan University — were chartered later.
2. **It has insisted on a four-year curriculum since 1971.** While the rest of Hong Kong's higher education sector ran on a three-year British model until the 334 reform in 2012, Shue Yan refused Government subsidy specifically so it could keep a four-year liberal-arts structure modelled on American colleges. That refusal — costly at the time — turned out to be visionary: when Hong Kong moved to a 3-3-4 secondary and four-year tertiary system in 2012, Shue Yan was the only institution that did not need to restructure at all.
3. **It is governed independently of the UGC.** As a self-financing private university, HKSYU is not funded through the University Grants Committee. The Hu family foundation and the university's own council set strategy. The trade-off is that tuition is paid by students (or, for SSSDP-listed programmes, by Government subsidy plus students), but the institution can move faster on programme design than UGC peers.

Crucially, HKSYU's degrees are accredited by the **Hong Kong Council for Accreditation of Academic and Vocational Qualifications (HKCAAVQ)** at Qualifications Framework Level 5, the same level as bachelor's degrees from the eight UGC universities. They are recognised by the Hong Kong Government, the Mainland Ministry of Education, and most overseas universities for postgraduate admission.

---

## 2. The Three Faculties and Around 15 Honours Bachelor Programmes

HKSYU is organised across three faculties and about 11 academic departments, offering approximately 15 honours bachelor programmes for the 2026/27 intake. The portfolio is deliberately humanities-and-social-science heavy, with two strategic STEM/business additions in the form of SSSDP-subsidised programmes.

### Faculty of Arts

- **Bachelor of Arts (Honours) in Chinese Language and Literature** — one of the few programmes in Hong Kong still teaching classical Chinese as a serious system rather than a survey topic.
- **Bachelor of Arts (Honours) in English Language and Literature** — small-class English major; entry requires DSE English Language Level 3 or above.
- **Bachelor of Arts (Honours) in History** — strong on modern Chinese and Hong Kong history.
- **Bachelor of Arts (Honours) in Journalism and Mass Communication** — includes Cantonese broadcasting, video and TV production studios, with placement pipelines into RTHK, TVB and digital media outlets.
- **Bachelor of Social Sciences (Honours) in Arts, Culture and Technology** — a newer interdisciplinary programme combining curatorial studies, digital media and cultural studies.

### Faculty of Commerce

- **Bachelor of Business Administration (Honours) in Accounting** — recognised by the Hong Kong Institute of Certified Public Accountants (HKICPA) for paper exemptions.
- **Bachelor of Business Administration (Honours) in Business Administration** — concentrations in marketing, human resources and international business.
- **Bachelor of Business Administration (Honours) in Economics and Finance** — incorporates CFA Programme curriculum content.
- **Bachelor of Commerce (Honours) in Financial Technology (BCom FinTech) — JUPAS code JSSY01** — listed on the **Study Subsidy Scheme for Designated Professions/Sectors (SSSDP)**. The 2026/27 first-year sticker tuition is HK$80,089; after the SSSDP subsidy of HK$46,780, the **net first-year tuition is approximately HK$33,309**, and the four-year net cost is around HK$133,236.
- **Bachelor of Arts (Honours) in Law and Business** — non-vocational legal studies that articulate to PCLL or overseas JD programmes.

### Faculty of Social Sciences

- **Bachelor of Social Sciences (Honours) in Counselling and Psychology** — accredited by the Hong Kong Psychological Society (HKPS) and arguably HKSYU's flagship programme; consistently the most competitive entry in JUPAS year on year.
- **Bachelor of Social Sciences (Honours) in Psychology with Forensic Investigation** — a Hong Kong-unique pairing of psychology with criminal justice and policing applications.
- **Bachelor of Social Work (Honours)** — accredited by the Hong Kong Social Workers Registration Board (SWRB); graduates qualify directly for Registered Social Worker status.
- **Bachelor of Social Sciences (Honours) in Sociology**.
- **Bachelor of Science (Honours) in Applied Data Science — JUPAS code JSSY02** — also listed on **SSSDP**. With the 2026/27 subsidy ceiling of HK$46,780 applied against tuition, students pay a substantially reduced net fee.
- **Bachelor of Science (Honours) in Digital Entertainment and Game Application** — partnerships with local game studios; covers Unity and Unreal Engine pipelines.

> The two SSSDP-subsidised programmes (FinTech, Applied Data Science) are HKSYU's strategic answer to Hong Kong's Innovation and Technology talent shortage. Because the subsidy is paid per student per year, net tuition for these two programmes is comparable to a UGC-funded place — which materially changes the value calculation for cost-sensitive applicants.

---

## 3. Admission Requirements

HKSYU runs three parallel admission tracks for undergraduate entry: JUPAS (for HKDSE candidates applying to the two SSSDP programmes), non-JUPAS Direct Application (for HKDSE candidates applying to non-SSSDP programmes, sub-degree holders, IB/A-Level/SAT candidates, and mainland Gaokao students), and articulation entry from associate degree or higher diploma.

### 3.1 JUPAS (HKDSE) Route

JUPAS is the route for the two SSSDP programmes, JSSY01 (BCom FinTech) and JSSY02 (BSc Applied Data Science). The general minimum entry requirement is the standard Hong Kong "**3-3-2-2**" matrix:

- Chinese Language: Level 3
- English Language: Level 3
- Mathematics Compulsory Part: Level 2
- Citizenship and Social Development: Attained
- Plus one elective at Level 2 or above (one elective subject at Level 3 may be required for individual programmes)

HKSYU accepts **combined results from multiple HKDSE sittings**, which is unusual and welcome — retake candidates can mix their best papers across two sittings.

For the two SSSDP programmes, real-world Band A intake medians have historically clustered around **score 14 on the best-five elective method** (reading the JUPAS programme catalogue figures), with applied data science slightly lower than FinTech. Counselling and Psychology, although offered through non-JUPAS, typically takes its strongest cohort at a similar effective score.

### 3.2 Non-JUPAS Direct Application

For all programmes outside SSSDP, **HKDSE candidates apply directly to HKSYU** rather than through JUPAS. Direct applications are also the route for:

- IB Diploma holders (typically 24 points or above, with English at HL 4 or SL 5)
- GCE A-Level / IAL candidates (typically two A-Level passes plus three GCSEs including English)
- Mainland Gaokao candidates (no fixed national line — HKSYU evaluates Gaokao English score, total score relative to provincial first-tier line, and a personal statement and interview)
- International applicants with equivalent qualifications such as SAT, IBE, or recognised national matriculation exams

Non-JUPAS applications open in November and run on a **rolling basis** until programme places fill. Applying earlier is materially advantageous, especially for Counselling and Psychology and Social Work.

### 3.3 Articulation Entry (Senior-Year Entry)

Hong Kong sub-degree holders (Associate Degree, Higher Diploma) can apply for **Year 2 or Year 3 senior entry** with credit transfer, on a programme-by-programme basis. Many Counselling and Psychology, Sociology and Business Administration cohorts include articulation students. This route is particularly important for Hong Kong Community College and HKBU CIE graduates.

### 3.4 English Language Requirement

For English-medium programmes, applicants whose qualifications are not in English typically need IELTS 6.0, TOEFL iBT 70, College English Test (CET) Band 6, or Gaokao English at 110+ depending on the programme. The English major requires higher minima.

---

## 4. Tuition and the SSSDP Subsidy in Detail

For 2026/27 entry, sticker tuition at HKSYU varies by programme but typically falls in the range **HK$73,000 to HK$96,000 per academic year** for full-time honours bachelor programmes. This is comparable to other Hong Kong self-financing universities and well below international undergraduate fees in the UK, US, Australia or Singapore.

The **SSSDP subsidy** materially changes the picture for two programmes. The 2026/27 SSSDP subsidy ceiling is **HK$46,780 per student per year** (announced by the Education Bureau in September 2025). Applied to BCom FinTech, that brings the net first-year tuition down to roughly HK$33,309 and the four-year net programme cost to around HK$133,236. Applied to BSc Applied Data Science, it produces a similarly large reduction. SSSDP funding is awarded automatically with the JUPAS offer — students do not apply for it separately.

For non-SSSDP programmes, scholarships and Government student finance schemes (the Non-means-tested Subsidy Scheme for Self-financing Undergraduate Studies, NMTSS) help eligible Hong Kong-domiciled students reduce the net cost.

---

## 5. Scholarships and Financial Aid

HKSYU operates a substantial entrance and continuing scholarship pool. Key items:

- **Entrance Scholarships for high-scoring DSE applicants** — full or partial tuition waivers for top JUPAS / non-JUPAS entrants. Typical thresholds: full waiver for DSE best-five score of 25 or above; half waiver for 22 or above; quarter waiver for 20 or above. Continuing eligibility requires maintaining a stipulated GPA.
- **Mainland Outstanding Student Scholarships** — separate awards for top Gaokao entrants; Gaokao scores at or above the provincial first-tier line plus competitive English typically secure consideration.
- **Faculty Dean's Scholarships** for second-year and beyond, awarded on cumulative GPA.
- **NMTSS / Non-means-tested Subsidy Scheme** (for eligible Hong Kong residents, around HK$36,000 per year; not applicable to Mainland or international students).
- **Government Tertiary Student Finance Scheme — Publicly-funded Programmes (TSFS) does not apply to HKSYU**; eligible Hong Kong students should look at the FASP / NMTSS schemes instead.

International and mainland students should also check HKSYU's hardship grants and named donor scholarships, several of which are reserved specifically for non-local students.

---

## 6. Campus, Accommodation and Student Life

HKSYU's campus sits at **6 Wai Tsui Crescent, Braemar Hill, North Point**, on Hong Kong Island, with adjoining academic buildings on Wai Man Road. The location is one of the most attractive in the Hong Kong higher-education sector — a hillside campus surrounded by greenery, looking across Victoria Harbour, on the same Braemar Hill ridge as the Chinese University of Hong Kong's Chung Chi College on the opposite side. It is a 15-minute bus ride from Tin Hau MTR station and around 25 minutes from Central.

The campus is compact (roughly 4,000 full-time undergraduates) and almost all classes are taught in groups of fewer than 30 students — a sharp contrast to the lecture-hall format common at the eight UGC universities. The library, Lady Hu Tin-yuet Library, holds around 300,000 print volumes plus digital resources.

**Student residence** is offered in two halls — the Lady Lily Shaw Hall and the Research Complex residences — with priority given to non-local (Mainland and overseas) and remote-domicile Hong Kong students. Residence is not guaranteed for all years; many local students commute. Off-campus rentals in North Point, Quarry Bay and Tin Hau typically run HK$5,000–9,000 per month for a shared room or studio.

Student societies are active across academic departments, with notable strength in journalism (the JMC Society runs a campus newspaper and broadcast unit) and counselling/psychology (peer-counselling and forensic-investigation clubs). The Christian heritage of the founding family is visible in chapel programmes, but the university is non-denominational and students of all backgrounds are welcome.

---

## 7. Graduate Outcomes

Because Shue Yan is small and humanities-heavy, its graduate destinations look different from the eight UGC universities, but they are well-defined:

- **Counselling and Psychology graduates** typically progress to a master's in clinical, counselling, or educational psychology — at HKSYU itself, at the eight UGC universities, or overseas — to qualify as registered psychologists. A meaningful share proceed directly into school counselling, NGO casework, and corporate HR roles.
- **Social Work graduates** qualify directly as Registered Social Workers and move into Social Welfare Department posts, NGO casework, and elderly/family service agencies. Pass rates and registration outcomes are consistently strong.
- **Journalism and Mass Communication graduates** are visible in RTHK, TVB, HK01, Now TV and digital-native outlets, including in production, news and corporate communications.
- **BCom FinTech and BSc Applied Data Science graduates** (the two SSSDP programmes) target Hong Kong's banking IT, insurtech and Greater Bay Area technology companies. As the first cohorts complete their degrees, the early-career signal is positive given the heavy compulsory internship loading.
- **Accounting graduates** with HKICPA paper exemptions feed into the Big Four and second-tier audit firms, particularly into private-company and SME assurance roles.
- **Postgraduate study** is a common path: HKSYU graduates regularly enrol in master's programmes at HKU, CUHK, HKUST, the National Taiwan University, and UK and Australian institutions.

The university's alumni include several public figures in journalism, broadcasting, social work and the Legislative Council, and Hu family alumni networks remain influential in Hong Kong civic life.

---

## 8. How HKSYU Compares — and Who It Suits

HKSYU is not trying to be a research-led UGC university, and prospective students should evaluate it on its own terms.

**Choose HKSYU if you want**:

- A small, four-year, English-medium liberal-arts environment in Hong Kong.
- A flagship Counselling and Psychology, Social Work, Journalism, or Chinese Language programme with professional accreditation and small classes.
- A Hong Kong undergraduate degree at a substantially lower sticker price than overseas options, with SSSDP-net tuition for the two designated programmes that approaches UGC levels.
- A non-JUPAS pathway with rolling admissions and acceptance of combined HKDSE sittings.

**Look elsewhere if you need**:

- Heavy laboratory-science programmes such as Medicine, Dentistry, Engineering or Pure Sciences — Shue Yan does not offer these.
- A large research university brand for a research-track career.
- A campus with a high proportion of international exchange students; HKSYU's exchange network is smaller than the UGC universities'.

---

## 9. Application Timeline at a Glance (2026/27 Intake)

- **September–October 2025**: SSSDP and JUPAS programme catalogues released; HKSYU Open Day in November.
- **November 2025 onward**: HKSYU non-JUPAS Direct Application opens; rolling admissions begin. Mainland Gaokao early enquiry channel opens.
- **December 2025**: JUPAS application closing for SSSDP programmes (JSSY01, JSSY02).
- **June 2026**: Gaokao results; HKSYU mainland admissions interviews.
- **July 2026**: HKDSE results released; JUPAS results offered for SSSDP programmes; non-JUPAS DSE applicants are typically interviewed in July.
- **August 2026**: Non-local students' visa applications submitted; final non-JUPAS offers.
- **Early September 2026**: Term commences.

---

## 10. Bottom Line

In a city defined by its "Group of Eight" UGC universities, Hong Kong Shue Yan University has built an enduring identity that does not depend on UGC validation. As Hong Kong's first private university, the institution that pioneered the four-year liberal-arts model long before the 334 reform, and the home of accredited Counselling and Psychology and Social Work programmes that consistently feed Hong Kong's helping professions, HKSYU deserves a serious look from any DSE, Gaokao or international applicant whose priorities are small classes, professional accreditation and a humanities-and-social-science focus.

The 2026/27 intake brings two SSSDP-subsidised programmes — BCom FinTech and BSc Applied Data Science — that bring net tuition close to UGC levels, a rolling non-JUPAS admissions process that rewards early applicants, and a 55-year-old institution celebrating two decades as a chartered university. For the right candidate, that is a strong combination.

# The Education University of Hong Kong (EdUHK) Complete Guide 2026

The Education University of Hong Kong (EdUHK) is Hong Kong's only publicly-funded university devoted primarily to teacher education and education-related disciplines. Although it is the youngest of the eight UGC-funded universities to attain full university status (granted in 2016), it now occupies a position in global education-discipline rankings that few specialist institutions in Asia can match. For the 2026/27 admission cycle, EdUHK enters as the world's #7 university for Education in the QS World University Rankings by Subject 2026, alongside debut entries in the QS World University Rankings 2026 (#530), QS Asia 2026 (#152), and Times Higher Education World 2026 (#195) — placing it firmly in the global top 10%.

This guide explains everything DSE candidates, Mainland Gaokao students, and international applicants need to know to apply to EdUHK in 2026 — from ranking interpretation, JUPAS Best 5 scoring with interview weighting, Non-JUPAS routes, tuition and scholarships, to flagship programmes and graduate employment realities in Hong Kong's competitive teacher-recruitment market.

## 1. Why EdUHK in 2026: The Numbers Behind the "Education Specialist" Brand

For students considering teacher education or education-adjacent careers (counselling, special needs, early childhood, creative arts, sport science, language teaching, educational psychology), EdUHK is no longer a "regional teachers' college". The 2026 rankings tell a different story:

- **QS World University Rankings by Subject 2026 — Education: #7 globally** (up from #12 in 2025). EdUHK is ahead of NIE Singapore in some sub-indicators and behind only a handful of US/UK/Australian giants like UCL Institute of Education, Harvard, Stanford, Oxford, Toronto and Melbourne.
- **U.S. News & World Report 2026 — Education and Educational Research: #3 worldwide.**
- **QS World University Rankings 2026 (overall): #530**, EdUHK's debut entry.
- **QS Asia University Rankings 2026: #152** — top 10% in Asia, climbing 60 places year-on-year.
- **Times Higher Education World University Rankings 2026: #195** — debut, top 10% globally.
- **QS Sustainability 2026:** climbed over 600 places, entering the global top 30%.

For Mainland and international applicants, the practical reading is this: if your target career involves classroom teaching, education policy, special-needs support, applied psychology, or any role in Greater Bay Area schools, EdUHK gives you a higher subject-rank ceiling than any Hong Kong general-comprehensive university — at substantially lower JUPAS cut-off scores.

## 2. Faculties and Flagship Programmes

EdUHK is organised into three faculties plus the Graduate School. It offers about 45 HKDSE-eligible undergraduate programmes spanning education-major (BEd) tracks and a growing portfolio of non-education BA/BSc/BSocSc degrees.

### 2.1 Faculty of Education and Human Development (FEHD)

The historical core. Five-year Bachelor of Education (BEd) programmes give graduates dual qualification — academic degree plus the Education Bureau's Qualified Teacher status — eliminating the need for a separate PGDE.

Flagship BEd specialisations:
- BEd (Honours) Early Childhood Education — co-tier with NIE Singapore in early-years pedagogy.
- BEd (Honours) Primary Education with majors in Mathematics, General Studies, or English Language.
- BEd (Honours) Special Needs / Inclusive Education — Hong Kong's only full undergraduate programme of its kind.
- BEd (Honours) Physical Education — produces most of Hong Kong's secondary-school PE teachers.

### 2.2 Faculty of Liberal Arts and Social Sciences (FLASS)

The non-teacher-education growth area. Highlights:
- BSocSc (Honours) Psychology — increasingly competitive; useful springboard to clinical/educational psychology master's programmes.
- BA (Honours) Language Studies (English / Chinese / Bilingual).
- BSocSc (Honours) Global and Environmental Studies.
- BA (Honours) Creative Arts and Culture / Visual Arts / Music — co-delivered with strong industry placement.
- BSc (Honours) Sports Science and Coaching.

### 2.3 Faculty of Humanities

Houses Chinese language, literature, history, and Chinese-medicine-adjacent humanities programmes — especially relevant for students intending to teach Chinese language or Chinese history at the secondary level.

### 2.4 Co-terminal Double Degrees

EdUHK's co-terminal BA/BSc/BSocSc & BEd programmes (5 years) are an under-rated route: students earn a content-area degree plus a teaching qualification simultaneously — significantly more efficient than a 4-year bachelor's followed by a 1-year PGDE.

## 3. JUPAS Admission: How EdUHK Calculates Your Score

EdUHK's JUPAS scoring formula in 2026 is straightforward but has two non-obvious twists that catch applicants out.

### 3.1 The Best 5 Formula

EdUHK uses **Best 5 subjects**, regardless of whether they are core or elective, **excluding Citizenship and Social Development (CSD)**. CSD is graded only Attained / Not Attained and counts only as a minimum-met requirement — it does not contribute to your numerical score.

Subject grades convert to scores as follows:
- 5\*\* = 7, 5\* = 6, 5 = 5, 4 = 4, 3 = 3, 2 = 2, 1 = 1.
- M1 / M2 grades are usually weighted at the same scale as a regular elective (i.e., 5\*\* = 7).

Maximum theoretical score: **35 (Best 5)**.

### 3.2 Programme-Specific Weightings

Many BEd programmes apply a weighting to subjects directly relevant to the teaching specialisation. For example:
- BEd English Language: English Language is typically given an additional weight (e.g., x1.5 or x2) up to a stated maximum.
- BEd Mathematics: Mathematics Compulsory Part and M1/M2 may receive enhanced weighting.
- BEd Chinese Language: Chinese Language and Chinese Literature/Chinese History weighted upward.

Always check the programme-specific weighting on the EdUHK Apply portal before finalising your JUPAS Band A choices — the same Best 5 grade profile can yield very different programme-level scores.

### 3.3 Holistic Review and Interviews

For most BEd programmes and several FLASS programmes, EdUHK applies a **genuinely holistic** review. The admission decision considers:
1. HKDSE Best 5 result (after weighting).
2. JUPAS band-choice priority.
3. Interview performance — typically required for most BEd programmes and selected FLASS programmes.
4. School Reference Report (SRR).
5. Other Experiences and Achievements (OEA) — verified extracurriculars, awards, leadership.

The interview is decisive for borderline candidates, especially for teacher-education programmes where communication ability, classroom presence, and articulated motivation to teach matter as much as DSE scores. Group discussions, individual interviews, and sometimes micro-teaching exercises are common formats.

### 3.4 Indicative 2025 JUPAS Median Scores (Best 5)

These are useful 2026 reference points (medians, not minima — you can still be admitted below median if interview and OEA are strong):

- Highly competitive: BEd English Language, BSocSc Psychology, BEd Mathematics — median often around 23–26.
- Mid-tier: BEd Primary Education, BEd Early Childhood, BA Language Studies — median around 19–23.
- Entry-tier: Several FLASS BA programmes — median around 17–20.

For the most current cycle's data, always consult the official EdUHK Apply JUPAS Scores page rather than relying on year-old medians.

## 4. Non-JUPAS Admission for Mainland (Gaokao) and International Students

EdUHK accepts three main non-local admission tracks:

### 4.1 Mainland Gaokao Direct Admission

EdUHK participates in independent Mainland recruitment (not the early-batch government-allocated route used by HKU/CUHK/HKUST). This gives applicants the advantage of **applying directly without affecting Gaokao Mainland admission slots** — your Mainland university applications proceed independently.

Indicative requirements:
- Gaokao total score typically at the **First-Tier (一本) cut-off line** of your home province, with stronger competition for psychology, English-related, and visual-arts programmes.
- English single-subject score: typically **120/150** or above for English-medium programmes; some programmes require 110+.
- Interview (online or in-person) for most programmes.
- Application opens annually around October–November of Year 12, closes around mid-June.
- Tuition: HK$140,000 per year for non-local students (2026/27 standard rate; a small premium applies to some specialised programmes).

### 4.2 International Qualifications

EdUHK accepts:
- IB Diploma: typical conditional offer 28–34 points depending on programme.
- GCE A-Level: typically BBB to AAA.
- SAT/ACT plus 3 AP / SAT Subject scores.
- Other recognised national qualifications (Australian ATAR, Canadian provincial diplomas, etc.).
- English proficiency: IELTS 6.0 (with no sub-band below 5.5) or TOEFL iBT 80 minimum; English-major and language-related programmes require higher.

### 4.3 Senior-Year / Transfer Admission

EdUHK admits Higher Diploma and Associate Degree graduates (from Hong Kong sub-degree institutions) into Year 2 or Year 3 of selected programmes. This is a significant pathway for self-financing-route students who choose to "convert" to a UGC-funded degree.

## 5. Tuition, Scholarships, and Total Cost

### 5.1 Tuition (2026/27 indicative)

- **Local UGC-funded students:** HK$42,100 per year (subject to Government Tuition Fee Subsidy adjustments).
- **Non-local students (Mainland + international):** HK$140,000 per year. EdUHK has historically been the most affordable of the eight UGC universities for non-locals.
- **Self-financing programmes:** vary by programme; check programme-specific pages.

### 5.2 Living Costs

Realistic budget for a non-local undergraduate (2026/27):
- On-campus hall: HK$15,000–22,000 per year (limited supply, demand-allocated).
- Off-campus shared accommodation (Tai Po area, near campus): HK$4,500–7,500 per month.
- Food, transport, insurance, miscellaneous: HK$4,500–6,500 per month.
- All-in annual cost (tuition + living, non-local): roughly **HK$220,000–270,000**.

### 5.3 Scholarships for Non-Local Students

EdUHK operates one of Hong Kong's most generous non-local scholarship pools relative to its size:
- **Entrance scholarships:** Full tuition + accommodation + stipend awards for top non-local entrants (highly competitive).
- **HKSAR Government Scholarship Fund Scholarship for Non-local Students:** worth HK$80,000 per year, with separate Mainland and international quotas.
- **Self-funded faculty / programme scholarships:** typically HK$20,000–80,000 per year, renewable subject to GPA.
- **Belt and Road Scholarship** for eligible nationalities.

For Mainland Gaokao applicants, securing an entrance scholarship significantly narrows the cost gap with a Mainland 985/211 university.

## 6. Campus, Student Life, and Location

EdUHK's main campus is in **Tai Po, in the New Territories** — about 45 minutes from Central by MTR + KCR. The campus is purpose-built (1990s) on a green hillside with:
- Three undergraduate halls + new Northcote Hall extension (limited spaces; non-local students get priority for Year 1).
- Modern teaching blocks including the John Lee Hall, the Mong Man Wai Building, and the Learning Commons.
- Sports facilities including the indoor sports centre, swimming pool, and athletics track — relevant for BEd PE and Sports Science students.
- Practicum schools network: EdUHK has formal practicum partnerships with hundreds of Hong Kong primary and secondary schools.

The Tai Po location is greener and quieter than HKU/CUHK but less "city centre" — many non-local students appreciate the lower cost of living and dedicated campus community, while others find weekend trips to Mong Kok / Central a necessity. The Tai Po Market MTR is a 5-minute shuttle bus from campus.

## 7. Career Outcomes and Graduate Employment

### 7.1 The Teacher Pipeline

EdUHK supplies the majority of newly registered teachers in Hong Kong's pre-primary, primary, and special-education sectors, and a substantial share in secondary. The Education Bureau's Qualified Teacher (QT) status is conferred automatically on BEd graduates, allowing immediate employment in DSS / aided / government schools.

Realistic 2026 graduate-employment context:
- Hong Kong's school-age population is contracting due to cohort declines, leading to school consolidations. Competition for permanent teaching posts has tightened — most fresh BEd graduates start with **contract / supply teaching** before securing a permanent post.
- Starting salary for a permanent Graduate Master/Mistress (GM) post in an aided secondary school is approximately **HK$36,000–42,000 per month** (Master Pay Scale Pt 15–16, 2026 figures), rising to HK$80,000+ with seniority.
- Demand remains relatively strong in **special education, early childhood, STEM (Mathematics, Science, ICT), Putonghua**, and **English Language** specialisations.

### 7.2 Non-Teaching Career Paths

The growing FLASS / Humanities programmes are explicitly designed for non-classroom careers:
- **Psychology graduates** progress to MSocSc/MA in Educational, Counselling, or Clinical Psychology — qualifying as registered psychologists in Hong Kong or Mainland.
- **Language Studies graduates** enter publishing, translation, content, ESL training (highly portable into the Greater Bay Area private-tuition market).
- **Creative Arts graduates** enter cultural institutions, museums, performing-arts companies, and increasingly the games / animation industry.
- **Sports Science graduates** enter the HKSAR Sports Institute, professional clubs, fitness, and corporate wellness.

### 7.3 IANG and Hong Kong PR

All Mainland and international graduates of an EdUHK full-time UGC-funded undergraduate programme qualify for the **Immigration Arrangements for Non-local Graduates (IANG) visa**, currently allowing a 24-month stay after graduation without a job offer. After **7 years of continuous ordinary residence in Hong Kong** (which counts both your study years and IANG/work years), you can apply for **Hong Kong Permanent Residency**.

## 8. Application Timeline and Practical Tips

### 8.1 JUPAS (DSE Candidates) Calendar

- **Early December 2026:** JUPAS application opens.
- **Mid-December 2026:** Band A deadline (do not change Bands after this date).
- **April–June 2027:** EdUHK programme interviews (most BEd programmes). Group + individual format.
- **Mid-July 2027:** DSE results released. JUPAS Late Modification window opens for ~3 days.
- **Early August 2027:** Main Round offer release.

### 8.2 Non-JUPAS / Mainland / International Calendar

- **Mid-October 2026:** Online application opens.
- **Early January 2027:** Main round deadline (programmes with quotas may close earlier).
- **March–May 2027:** Interview windows.
- **Conditional offers** issued from January; final offers after Gaokao results / IB results in July.

### 8.3 Five Practical Tips

1. **Take the interview seriously.** For BEd programmes, the interview can swing the admission decision more than ±2 score points. Prepare authentic answers to "Why teach?" and a short micro-lesson if invited.
2. **Apply for entrance scholarships in your main application** — there is no separate form; selection is automatic from the application file.
3. **For Mainland applicants**: applying to EdUHK does **not** consume any Mainland Gaokao slot, so you can keep both pathways open until July.
4. **Choose your Best 5 strategically** — drop your weakest non-CSD subject; remember M1/M2 count.
5. **Verify programme-specific subject weightings** on the EdUHK Apply portal — a single weighted subject can move your effective score by 1.5–3 points.

## 9. Is EdUHK Right For You? A Decision Framework

Choose EdUHK if you fit at least two of the following:
- You want a clearly defined career identity (teacher / educational psychologist / special-needs practitioner / sports scientist).
- You value a top-10-globally subject ranking in education over a marginally higher overall-university brand.
- Your DSE Best 5 is in the 19–26 range and you want a UGC-funded degree at a publicly-recognised university.
- You are a Mainland student looking for a competitive Hong Kong university at the lowest non-local tuition tier.
- You prefer a smaller, dedicated campus community over a sprawling city campus.

Look at HKU / CUHK / HKUST first if your Best 5 is 30+ and your career goal has no link to education, psychology, language, or creative-arts disciplines.

# HKDSE 2026 Changes: What's New in the Exam This Year

The 2026 Hong Kong Diploma of Secondary Education (HKDSE) examination arrives as part of a broader wave of curriculum reform that has been reshaping secondary education in Hong Kong since 2021. For this year's cohort of candidates — students who entered Secondary 4 in 2023 — several significant structural, syllabus, and assessment changes are now fully in effect. Whether you are a candidate sitting the exam, a parent supporting one, or a teacher guiding a class, understanding these changes is essential for accurate preparation and realistic goal-setting.

This article provides a comprehensive, factual overview of the most important 2026 HKDSE changes, explains their rationale, and offers practical guidance on how to navigate them.

---

## Background: Why 2026 Is a Landmark Year

The HKDSE has undergone incremental reform since the curriculum review initiated by the Education Bureau (EDB) in 2020–2021. The centerpiece of this reform was the abolition of Liberal Studies as a compulsory core subject and its replacement by **Citizenship and Social Development (CSD)** — a change that took effect progressively from 2021. The 2026 cohort is among the first groups for whom CSD has been fully embedded throughout their entire three-year senior secondary cycle (S4–S6), making this the first truly "native" CSD generation to sit the HKDSE.

Beyond CSD, the 2026 exam also reflects refinements to elective subject syllabi, updated school-based assessment (SBA) protocols across multiple subjects, and changes to how certain results factor into JUPAS university admissions calculations.

---

## 1. Citizenship and Social Development: The Biggest Structural Change

### What Changed

The most consequential change in the 2026 HKDSE — and the one most students and parents ask about — is the complete replacement of Liberal Studies with **Citizenship and Social Development (CSD)**.

Liberal Studies had been a compulsory core subject since the launch of the HKDSE in 2012. It was assessed with a traditional grade scale of 1 to 5**, contributing meaningfully to a candidate's JUPAS aggregate and university admission scores. The subject attracted persistent controversy over the years regarding its open-ended nature and the scope of its examination questions.

CSD was formally introduced into the curriculum in September 2021, replacing Liberal Studies for all S4 students entering that year. The 2026 HKDSE candidates completed their full three-year CSD curriculum across S4, S5, and S6.

### How CSD Is Structured

CSD is built around three thematic strands:

1. **Hong Kong** — civic identity, governance, rule of law, and social development
2. **The Motherland** — China's development, national identity, and the relationship between Hong Kong and the mainland
3. **The World** — global issues, international relations, and Hong Kong's role in the world

Rather than the exploratory, argument-driven essays that characterized Liberal Studies, CSD emphasizes factual understanding, civic values, and knowledge of contemporary China and the world. The curriculum includes a **Mainland Study Trip** component in which students visit a city in mainland China as part of their learning experience.

### The Grading Difference: Attained vs. 1–5**

This is the most practically significant difference for JUPAS applicants:

- **Liberal Studies** was graded on the standard HKDSE scale: **1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 5*, 5\*\***
- **CSD is graded as either Attained (AT) or Not Attained (NAT)** — a binary pass/fail result with no numeric grade

The HKEAA assesses CSD through a written examination at the end of S6. A candidate who meets the minimum competency standard receives "Attained"; one who does not receives "Not Attained." There is no distinction between a borderline pass and an exceptional performance — both receive "Attained."

### Impact on JUPAS Scoring

Because CSD produces only a pass/fail result, it **does not contribute numerically to JUPAS Best 5 or Best 6 calculations.** Under the previous system, a strong Liberal Studies grade (e.g., 5 or 5*) could meaningfully boost a candidate's aggregate score. Under the current system, CSD is essentially a threshold requirement: you must Attain it to be eligible for university admission, but once you pass, it adds nothing further to your score.

This has a dual implication:

- **Reduced pressure for high achievers**: Candidates no longer need to invest heavy revision time chasing a top grade in this compulsory subject. Passing is enough.
- **Risk for candidates who underestimate it**: Some students, believing CSD is "easy to pass," under-prepare and fall into the "Not Attained" category. A NAT result can disqualify a candidate from certain JUPAS choices entirely, as many programmes specify minimum entry requirements that include Attained in CSD.

**Practical advice**: Treat CSD seriously enough to secure a comfortable pass. Attend all study trip components, complete the internal assessments diligently, and revise the three thematic strands systematically. Do not leave it until the last month.

---

## 2. Changes to Core Subjects

### Chinese Language

The Chinese Language syllabus for 2026 retains its five papers (Reading, Writing, Listening, Speaking/Oral, and School-Based Assessment), but the EDB confirmed in 2023 refinements to the **reading comprehension passages** to include more contemporary written forms alongside classical texts. The proportion of classical Chinese in the reading paper has been maintained, but the range of text types in the writing paper has been broadened to reflect modern communicative purposes, including analytical reports and structured argumentation tasks.

The oral examination (校本評核 and live oral) remains a graded component. Schools were reminded in 2024–2025 circulars to ensure that speaking tasks reflect updated assessment descriptors emphasizing clarity, coherence, and rhetorical effectiveness rather than only linguistic accuracy.

### English Language

The English Language core subject continues its five-component structure: Reading, Writing, Listening and Integrated Skills, Speaking, and School-Based Assessment. No fundamental structural changes were made for the 2026 examination.

However, HKEAA released updated marking guidelines in late 2024 for the **writing component** that place increased emphasis on task fulfilment and argument coherence over surface-level language accuracy alone. Examiners have been directed to reward candidates who demonstrate genuine communicative purpose and logical development even when some grammatical imperfections are present, reflecting alignment with international English language assessment frameworks.

The SBA component (oral and reading portfolios) remains unchanged in structure for 2026.

### Mathematics (Compulsory Part)

Mathematics Compulsory Part sees no structural changes in 2026. The two-paper format (Paper 1: conventional questions; Paper 2: multiple choice) continues. The EDB's curriculum guide updates from 2022 clarified the boundary between Compulsory and Module content more explicitly, which benefits candidates preparing for the Compulsory Part only — they have clearer guidance on which topics are in scope.

**Mathematics Extended Part (Module 1 and Module 2)** also continues unchanged, though the 2025–2026 past paper analysis suggests a slight increase in the proportion of questions requiring multi-step integration of concepts in Module 2 (Algebra and Calculus). This is an organic trend rather than a policy change, but candidates targeting top grades should be aware.

---

## 3. Changes to Elective Subjects

### New and Revised Electives

The EDB has progressively introduced new elective subjects since 2021 as part of the curriculum reform package. For the 2026 examination, the most notable addition is the continued embedding of **Artificial Intelligence and Data Analytic Strategies** as a recognized elective, though uptake remains limited to schools with the necessary infrastructure. The HKEAA is expected to publish more structured past papers and marking schemes for this subject ahead of the 2027 examination cycle.

Several existing elective syllabi received targeted revisions effective from the 2023 S4 intake (i.e., the current 2026 cohort):

- **Economics**: Updated to reflect post-pandemic monetary policy context and digital economy concepts. New short-essay question formats have replaced some structured data-response questions in Paper 2.
- **Geography**: Additional content on climate adaptation and smart city planning, with updated fieldwork report assessment criteria.
- **Information and Communication Technology (ICT)**: Revised to include cybersecurity concepts and data ethics as assessable topics in the written examination.
- **History**: The China History and World History syllabi retain their structure, but source-evaluation questions have been reweighted to comprise a larger proportion of the examination mark in World History Paper 1.
- **Biology, Chemistry, Physics**: Core syllabi unchanged, but SBA laboratory report assessment forms were updated in 2024 to standardize marking across schools. Teachers were provided new moderation guidelines.

### Business, Accounting and Financial Studies (BAFS)

BAFS — one of the most popular elective subjects — received a notable syllabus update effective for the 2026 cohort. The **Accounting module** now includes introductory content on sustainability reporting and environmental accounting, reflecting global standards. The **Business Management module** has increased coverage of digital transformation, e-commerce strategy, and data-driven decision-making. Examination questions are expected to draw on these updated areas beginning in 2026.

---

## 4. School-Based Assessment (SBA) Changes

School-Based Assessment remains a component in many HKDSE subjects and continues to be moderated by the HKEAA. For the 2026 examination cycle, several procedural updates are in effect:

**Cross-subject SBA standardization**: Following inconsistencies identified in the 2023 and 2024 moderation cycles, the HKEAA issued revised standardization guidelines in early 2024. Schools are now required to submit SBA samples in a structured digital format, and external moderators have access to a wider range of student work per school. This change is intended to reduce grade inflation at individual school level and produce more consistent national standards.

**Chinese and English Language SBA**: Both subjects continue to include SBA as a graded component. For Chinese Language, schools must submit oral recordings; for English, both oral and written portfolio submissions are required. Deadlines for 2026 submissions were set in late 2025, and schools were warned that late or incomplete submissions result in the SBA component being treated as absent.

**Sciences**: Laboratory SBA in Biology, Chemistry, and Physics remains compulsory. Students who were unable to complete laboratory work due to documented medical or other approved reasons were accommodated through alternative assessment pathways, as outlined in the HKEAA's updated Special Circumstances Policy (revised 2023).

**Removal of SBA from some subjects**: It is worth noting that CSD — unlike Liberal Studies before it — does **not** include an SBA component. Assessment is entirely through the terminal written examination and the Mainland Study Trip (which is a curriculum requirement but not directly assessed for the HKDSE grade).

---

## 5. JUPAS University Admission Calculations: What Counts, What Doesn't

With CSD graded as Attained/Not Attained rather than on a numeric scale, the effective "core" subjects contributing numerically to JUPAS aggregates are:

- Chinese Language (best grade counts)
- English Language (best grade counts)
- Mathematics Compulsory Part (best grade counts)
- Up to two elective subjects (for Best 5 calculations)
- A sixth subject if eligible (for Best 6 programmes)

**CSD**: Must be Attained — functions as a gate, not a score contributor.

Most JUPAS programmes at the University Grants Committee (UGC)-funded universities specify **minimum entry requirements** that include:
- Level 3 or above in Chinese Language
- Level 3 or above in English Language
- Level 2 or above in Mathematics Compulsory Part
- Attained in CSD
- Specific levels in relevant electives depending on the programme

Candidates should check individual programme requirements carefully, as some competitive programmes (medicine, law, engineering at top universities) require Level 4 or 5 in specific electives in addition to core requirements.

**Extended Mathematics**: Module 1 or Module 2 results can be used as an elective in JUPAS calculations for programmes that accept them. This remains unchanged for 2026.

---

## 6. Special Examination Arrangements and Accessibility

The HKEAA's Special Examination Arrangement (SEA) policy, which accommodates candidates with documented physical, visual, hearing, or specific learning disabilities, was updated in 2023. The updated policy provides clearer criteria for extended time allowances, rest breaks, and alternative format papers. For 2026, approximately 3,000–4,000 candidates are expected to sit under SEA conditions.

Candidates who applied for SEA and received confirmation letters should have received their specific accommodation details well before the examination period. Those who encountered delays or discrepancies were advised to contact HKEAA's Student Services section directly.

---

## 8. Practical Advice for 2026 Candidates

**Secure your CSD Attained early.** Do not treat CSD as an afterthought simply because it is pass/fail. A "Not Attained" will significantly restrict your JUPAS choices. Engage genuinely with the three thematic strands, complete your Mainland Study Trip reflections thoroughly, and practise writing structured responses to the types of questions that appear in past papers.

**Redirect your energy to scored electives.** Because CSD no longer contributes numerically, every mark you gain in your elective subjects has greater relative weight. If you were previously spending significant revision time on Liberal Studies preparation, that time should now go toward your two strongest electives.

**Understand your JUPAS arithmetic.** Know exactly which five or six subjects constitute your best aggregate for the programmes you are applying to. Use JUPAS's official calculator and simulate different score scenarios. Being strategic about subject entry — for instance, deciding whether to declare Module 1 or Module 2 as an elective — can meaningfully affect your aggregate.

**Check programme-specific CSD requirements.** Some university programmes specify "Attained in CSD" as a minimum requirement explicitly. Do not assume that just because CSD is a binary grade it will automatically be fine — verify your target programmes' entry requirements.

**Prepare for updated question formats.** In subjects like Economics, BAFS, and World History, the examination questions for 2026 will reflect the revised syllabi. Review the subject-specific updates, not just past papers from 2022 or earlier, which may not reflect current question types.

**SBA deadlines are non-negotiable.** If you have any outstanding SBA components, ensure they are submitted to your subject teachers on time. Missing SBA has a disproportionate impact on your final grade in affected subjects.

**Use official HKEAA resources.** The HKEAA publishes updated marking schemes, examiners' reports, and sample papers for all subjects. These are the most reliable guides to what is actually rewarded in marking. Read examiners' reports from recent years — they consistently highlight the same recurring weaknesses that pull grades down.

---

## 9. For Parents: What You Should Know

The shift from Liberal Studies to CSD is the change most likely to prompt questions from parents who sat the old HKDSE themselves or who followed their older children through it. The key points:

- CSD is not "easier" than Liberal Studies in the sense that under-preparation guarantees a fail. Treat it as a subject that requires systematic study.
- The binary grading means a CSD result cannot compensate for weak performance in other subjects — and conversely, excellence in CSD does not boost your child's university admission score.
- JUPAS scoring now leans even more heavily on elective subject performance. If your child is targeting competitive programmes, ensuring strong elective preparation is paramount.
- The Mainland Study Trip is a curriculum requirement. Schools organize and fund these trips. Encourage your child to engage seriously with the experience, as it forms part of the learning process assessed in the terminal exam.

---

## 10. For Teachers: Classroom and Assessment Implications

Teachers in schools with the 2026 cohort will have already completed delivery of the CSD curriculum. Key reminders for the examination period:

- Ensure all SBA materials across applicable subjects have been submitted and moderated per HKEAA's updated digital submission protocols.
- Review the HKEAA's 2025 examiner guidance updates for any subject-specific changes to marking priorities — particularly for Economics, BAFS, English Writing, and History.
- Advise students on realistic JUPAS aggregate calculations now that CSD is non-numeric. Some students (and parents) still carry a mental model based on the Liberal Studies era.
- Post-examination: results release in July 2026 will include CSD as "AT" or "NAT" on the results slip, with no numeric equivalent. HKEAA will not convert CSD to a numeric grade for any purpose.

---

## Key Takeaways

- **CSD replaces Liberal Studies as a compulsory core subject.** It is graded Attained/Not Attained — not on the 1–5** scale. A pass is required for most university programmes but contributes zero to your JUPAS numeric aggregate.

- **JUPAS scoring now relies more on elective performance.** With one fewer numerically-scored core subject, your elective grades carry greater relative weight in admission calculations.

- **Several elective syllabi have been updated** for the 2026 cohort, including Economics, BAFS, ICT, and Geography. Candidates must revise with current syllabus guides, not just older past papers.

- **SBA procedures have been tightened.** Digital submission and expanded moderation mean schools face stricter compliance requirements. Students should confirm all their SBA components are submitted and signed off.

- **The binary CSD grade is a gate, not a booster.** Failing CSD (NAT) can close doors; passing it (AT) opens no additional ones. Aim for a comfortable pass, then focus your energy on scored subjects.

- **Exam timetables, entry requirements, and JUPAS deadlines are set.** Candidates should have all key dates firmly in their schedule and confirm programme-specific entry requirements directly with their target universities.

- **Official HKEAA resources remain the gold standard** for preparation: past papers, marking schemes, and examiners' reports for each subject. There is no substitute for practising with actual examination material under timed conditions.

---

Candidates should verify all specific requirements directly with HKEAA and their target universities, as programme entry requirements may be updated independently.*

# HKDSE Exam Day Logistics: A Complete Guide for International and Non-Local Candidates

The Hong Kong Diploma of Secondary Education (HKDSE) is fully operated by the Hong Kong Examinations and Assessment Authority (HKEAA). While the academic preparation for DSE is similar to other standardized exams, the **logistics side** — where, when, how to register, what you can bring, how Paper 3 Listening works, what to do if you are sick — catches many international and non-local candidates off guard. This article walks you through the full exam day pipeline.

## 1. Who is a "Non-Local Candidate"?

HKEAA categorizes DSE candidates into three groups:

1. **School Candidates**: Students enrolled at HK secondary schools taking DSE through their school
2. **Private Candidates (Self-Study)**: Individuals registering directly with HKEAA without a school
3. **Overseas Candidates**: Candidates registered to sit the exam at overseas centres (limited subjects only)

International students studying in HK international schools typically register as **School Candidates** through their school. Mainland students, Macau students, and self-studying expats register as **Private Candidates**. This article focuses on the Private Candidate pathway since it has the most logistical complexity.

## 2. Registration Timeline

| Month | Action |
|---|---|
| **September (year before exam)** | Registration opens on HKEAA website |
| **Early October** | Registration deadline (regular) |
| **Mid-October** | Late registration window (with surcharge) |
| **November** | Admission form issued by post/email |
| **January** | Mock exams at schools (private candidates not included) |
| **March** | Exam centre and seat number announced |
| **Late March** | Technology & Living practical exam begins |
| **Early April** | Main written papers begin |
| **Early May** | Main written papers end |
| **Mid May** | Speaking assessment for Chinese and English |
| **Mid July** | Results released |

### 2.1 Registration fees (2025 reference)

- **Per subject**: HKD 2,100 – 2,500 (varies by subject)
- **Typical 6-subject entry**: ~HKD 14,000
- **Late registration surcharge**: HKD 500 – 1,000
- **Special arrangement requests**: Free but require medical documentation

## 3. Required Documentation for Private Candidates

You will need:

1. **HKID Card** (if HK resident) OR **Passport** (if non-HK)
2. **Entry Permit** (for Mainland candidates coming to HK for exams)
3. **Previous academic transcripts** (Gr. 10-12 or equivalent)
4. **Proof of English proficiency** (not required for DSE but useful for later uni apps)
5. **Two recent passport-sized photos**

Upload all documents to your HKEAA online registration portal. **Double-check your name spelling** — this name will be on your DSE certificate for life.

## 4. Exam Centre Allocation

HKEAA will assign you an exam centre in March. For **Private Candidates**, you can request one of three geographic zones:

- **HK Island**: Often HK Cultural Centre, HK City Hall, or secondary schools
- **Kowloon**: Often Kowloon Bay International Trade & Exhibition Centre, secondary schools
- **New Territories**: Asia World-Expo, Sha Tin Town Hall, schools

### 4.1 What if your centre is far from your accommodation?

- **Book accommodation near your centre 2 months in advance** (April hotel rates are reasonable)
- Use MTR planner: allow **60 minutes** travel time (buffer for delays)
- Print your admission form — **DO NOT rely on phone screenshots** (some centres don't allow phones during entry)

### 4.2 Centre map and seat allocation

Your seat number appears on the admission form. Arrive **45 minutes before** exam start. Seat allocation is alphabetical by Candidate Number (NOT by name).

## 5. What to Bring to Every Exam

### 5.1 Mandatory

- [ ] **HKID Card or Passport** (primary ID — must match registration)
- [ ] **Admission Form** (printed, showing seat number)
- [ ] **HB or 2B Pencils** (minimum 4 for MC questions)
- [ ] **Black or Blue Ballpoint Pens** (minimum 3)
- [ ] **Eraser** (soft, non-grey)
- [ ] **Pencil Sharpener** (transparent)
- [ ] **Ruler** (15 cm or 30 cm, transparent)

### 5.2 Subject-specific

- **Mathematics / Physics / Chemistry / Biology / Economics / BAFS**: HKEAA-approved calculator (see section 6)
- **Geography**: Compass, protractor
- **Drawing-based subjects**: Coloured pencils (only for specific papers)

### 5.3 Permitted but optional

- **Water bottle** (transparent, label removed)
- **Tissues** (in transparent packet, inspected)
- **Analog watch** (no smartwatch — confiscated if worn)
- **Snack** (sealed, only for multi-paper days, outside exam hall)
- **Lip balm** (transparent tube)

### 5.4 STRICTLY FORBIDDEN

- ❌ Mobile phones, smartwatches, AirPods, Bluetooth earbuds
- ❌ Any paper with writing on it (including prayer cards, cheat sheets)
- ❌ Graphing calculators (most are NOT approved)
- ❌ Correction fluid / tape
- ❌ Highlighters (in some subjects — check rules per paper)
- ❌ Electronic dictionaries (any brand)

**Penalty for having a forbidden item**: Minimum subject mark deduction; maximum full disqualification from DSE.

## 6. Calculator Rules (Critical)

HKEAA maintains an approved calculator list. Only models on this list can be used.

### 6.1 Approved scientific calculators (examples)

- Casio fx-50FH II, fx-50FH, fx-50F PLUS II, fx-82 series, fx-85 series, fx-350 series
- Sharp EL-501W, EL-506W, EL-509WM
- Canon F-502G, F-604

### 6.2 Approved graphing calculators (for M1/M2 only)

- None – graphing calculators **are not permitted** in HKDSE

### 6.3 Pre-exam calculator inspection

- Invigilator will **inspect every calculator** before the exam
- Calculator memory **must be cleared** before entering
- Calculator cover or case must be removed from desk
- Bring **2 calculators** in case one fails

### 6.4 Changes to approved list

Check the latest list at **hkeaa.edu.hk > DSE > Regulations > Approved Calculators** before April every year.

## 7. Subject-Specific Exam Day Notes

### 7.1 English Language (Paper 1-3) + Speaking (Paper 4)

- **Paper 1 Reading**: 1.5 hours, booklet-based
- **Paper 2 Writing**: 2 hours, composition + short writing
- **Paper 3 Listening + Integrated Skills**: 2 hours 10 minutes
  - Audio broadcast via **FM radio** (candidates bring their own FM radio + headphones!)
  - **Bring: FM radio with fresh AA batteries, spare batteries, stereo headphones**
  - **Bring: backup radio** (yes, really)
  - Broadcast frequency announced in admission form
- **Paper 4 Speaking**: Group discussion (4 candidates) + individual presentation, held at designated centres in May

### 7.2 Chinese Language (Paper 1-4 + Speaking)

- **Paper 1 Reading**: Modern Chinese + Classical Chinese (文言文)
- **Paper 2 Writing**: Two long-form essays
- **Paper 3 Listening**: FM radio broadcast (same setup as English)
- **Paper 4 Speaking**: Group discussion or presentation

### 7.3 Mathematics

- **Paper 1**: Long questions (2.25 hours)
- **Paper 2**: Multiple choice (1.25 hours)
- Calculator permitted both papers
- **Geometry set** recommended (compass, protractor, set squares)

### 7.4 Physics / Chemistry / Biology

- **Paper 1A**: Multiple choice
- **Paper 1B**: Structured questions
- **Paper 2**: Essay + optional topic (for some subjects)
- **Data booklet provided** (constants, formulas — DO NOT bring your own)

### 7.5 Citizenship and Social Development (replaces Liberal Studies)

- **Single paper**: 2 hours
- **Pass/Fail only** (no 5** grading since 2024)
- **No materials except calculator and stationery**

## 8. Arriving at the Exam Centre

### 8.1 Timeline for exam day

| Time before exam | Action |
|---|---|
| 2 hours | Final breakfast, light meal |
| 1.5 hours | Leave home / hotel |
| 1 hour | Arrive at centre (buffer for delays) |
| 45 min | Enter centre, find exam hall |
| 30 min | Enter exam hall, desk check |
| 15 min | Last calculator check, settle |
| 5 min | Invigilator final instructions |
| 0 | Exam begins |

### 8.2 Entry procedure

1. Show admission form + ID at centre entrance
2. Security inspection (bag search, metal detector at large centres)
3. Find your desk using seat number
4. Place ONLY permitted items on desk
5. Place bag at designated area (usually front of hall)
6. Mobile phone: placed in **sealed envelope** provided by invigilator, must stay silent
7. Sign attendance sheet
8. Wait for "exam starts" announcement

### 8.3 During the exam

- **No washroom breaks** allowed in the first and last 30 minutes of the exam
- **Raise hand** for any issue (washroom, calculator failure, feeling unwell)
- **No communication** with other candidates
- **No leaning or looking** at nearby desks

### 8.4 End of exam

- When "STOP" is called, put pen down immediately
- Remain seated until answer scripts collected and counted
- Wait for dismissal announcement

## 9. Emergency Situations

### 9.1 You are sick on exam day

- **Minor illness (cough, fever)**: Still go if possible. Tell invigilator before start. You may be allowed to sit the exam in a separate room.
- **Severe illness (cannot attend)**: Get medical certificate from a registered doctor. Within **3 days of exam**, submit to HKEAA with application for "Special Consideration" (cap at ~5% mark adjustment).
- **COVID-19 or infectious disease**: Contact HKEAA hotline immediately (+852 3628 8860). Special isolation centres available.

### 9.2 You miss the exam

- **Transport delay**: Public transport delay receipt from MTR/bus company may be accepted for late entry (up to 30 min into exam).
- **Oversleeping, missed train**: NOT accepted. You will be marked absent for that paper.
- **Passport/ID problem**: Contact HKEAA immediately — emergency ID procedures exist.

### 9.3 Calculator fails mid-exam

- Raise hand
- Invigilator may provide spare calculator from centre stock (very limited)
- Or you use your own backup
- Time is not extended

### 9.4 Bathroom emergency

- Allowed in middle 2/3 of exam
- Escorted by invigilator
- **No phone, no bag, no books** in restroom
- Counted as part of your exam time (no extension)

## 10. Special Arrangements for Candidates with Disabilities

HKEAA provides special arrangements for:

- **Visual impairment**: Large print, Braille, reader, extended time
- **Hearing impairment**: Written instructions instead of verbal
- **Physical disabilities**: Accessible desk, scribe, extended time
- **Specific learning disabilities** (dyslexia, dysgraphia): Assessment report required 6 months in advance
- **Temporary conditions** (broken arm, pregnancy): Case-by-case

### 10.1 Application process

- Submit application **6 months before exam** (deadline early December)
- Include medical documentation or psychological assessment
- HKEAA review committee decides
- Special seating, extended time, or scribe granted

## 11. Results and Regrading

### 11.1 Results release day

- **Mid July**, around 9:00 AM
- Online via **HKEAA Results Portal** using your Candidate Number and password
- **Hard copy** sent by post within 1 week
- JUPAS change-of-choice window opens immediately for 72 hours

### 11.2 Checking / regrading

- **Review of grades**: Available within 1 week of results. Fee: HKD 160 per subject.
- **Rechecking**: Purely administrative (checking if total is correct) — rarely changes result.
- **Re-marking**: Detailed re-marking by independent marker. Fee: HKD 640. Can result in higher OR lower grade.
- **Deadlines are strict**: Miss the 7-day window and you have no recourse.

### 11.3 Retaking DSE

- You can retake the full DSE the following year as a Private Candidate
- Some universities accept your best results across two years
- Most candidates who retake see improvement of 0.5 – 1.5 grades per subject

## 12. Practical Checklist for Exam Week

### One week before:

- [ ] Confirm exam centre address and commute time
- [ ] Print admission form (2 copies — one backup)
- [ ] Test calculator (and backup calculator)
- [ ] Buy fresh AA batteries for FM radio
- [ ] Pack exam bag
- [ ] Review HKEAA rules document

### Night before:

- [ ] Set 2 alarms (phone + clock)
- [ ] Prepare breakfast
- [ ] Go to bed by 22:00
- [ ] Do NOT study new material after 20:00

### Exam morning:

- [ ] Light breakfast (avoid heavy or unfamiliar foods)
- [ ] Dress in layers (exam halls can be cold or hot)
- [ ] Arrive 1 hour early
- [ ] Use restroom before entering hall
- [ ] Deep breathing for 2 minutes before start

### Between papers (if two papers in one day):

- [ ] Quick meal (packed sandwich, fruit)
- [ ] Hydrate (avoid excess caffeine)
- [ ] 10-minute walk outside centre
- [ ] Do NOT discuss previous paper with other candidates
- [ ] Focus on next paper

## 13. Useful Contacts

- **HKEAA Hotline**: +852 3628 8860 (general enquiries)
- **HKEAA DSE Enquiries**: +852 3628 8787
- **Website**: hkeaa.edu.hk
- **JUPAS**: +852 2334 2884, jupas.edu.hk
- **Emergency (HK)**: 999
- **HK MTR Delay Certificate**: Available at any station

## 14. Summary

The HKDSE is as much a logistics test as an academic one. International and non-local candidates face extra challenges: unfamiliar venues, FM radio Listening setup, restrictive calculator rules, and a rigid exam day procedure. Prepare the logistics side as seriously as the academic side — one missed calculator, one forgotten passport, one wrong radio frequency can cost you a grade.

**Six-week-before-exam readiness principles**:
1. **Two of everything**: Calculator, radio, pens, ID photocopies
2. **Know your centre**: Visit it, time the commute, identify restrooms and exits
3. **Rehearse the morning**: Do a full mock on a random Saturday
4. **Sleep is non-negotiable**: 7+ hours for 6 weeks straight
5. **Have a Plan B for every failure mode**: sick day, transport, calculator, illness, lost ID
6. **Relax**: Over-preparing logistics frees your mind for the academic part

Good luck. Remember, DSE is one exam among many life decisions — perform your best, but do not let it define your future.

*This logistics guide is compiled from HKEAA public regulations (2025 edition). Always verify current rules at hkeaa.edu.hk before your exam.*
