# Hong Kong Nursing Bachelor's Programmes Complete Guide 2026

Nursing is one of the most consistently sought-after JUPAS choices in Hong Kong. The territory faces a chronic shortage of registered nurses — the Hospital Authority, private hospitals and an ageing population create a near-guaranteed pipeline of jobs for qualified graduates. For DSE candidates with mid-to-upper-band scores, a strong interest in healthcare and the patience for five years of clinical training, a Bachelor of Nursing is one of the most secure career pathways available outside of medicine.

This guide compares the four universities offering full nursing bachelor's degrees in Hong Kong — The University of Hong Kong (HKU), The Chinese University of Hong Kong (CUHK), The Hong Kong Polytechnic University (PolyU) and Hong Kong Metropolitan University (HKMU) — and walks through admission requirements, tuition, the Nursing Council Licensing Examination, and what graduate life actually looks like in the Hospital Authority and beyond.

## Why study nursing in Hong Kong?

Three structural facts make nursing an unusually high-leverage degree in Hong Kong.

First, **demand is locked in by demographics**. By the early 2030s, more than one in three Hong Kong residents will be aged 65 or above. Public hospitals, private hospitals, residential care homes, community health centres and specialist clinics are all expanding nursing teams, and the government has explicitly identified nursing as a priority manpower area.

Second, **starting salaries are competitive**. New graduates joining the Hospital Authority as Registered Nurses (RNs) start on the master pay scale at roughly HK$40,000–46,000 per month, with a defined ladder up through Advanced Practice Nurse, Nursing Officer, Ward Manager and beyond. Annual leave, training subsidies and a non-contributory provident fund add meaningful value on top of the cash salary.

Third, **the qualification is portable**. A Hong Kong RN registration is well respected in Singapore, the UK, Australia, Canada and the Middle East. Many graduates choose to spend two or three years in HA, sit a bridging exam such as the NMC OSCE in the UK or the NCLEX-RN in North America, and move overseas with significant clinical experience already on their CV.

## The four institutions at a glance

| University | Programme | JUPAS Code | Duration | Intake | Tuition (Year 1) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| HKU | Bachelor of Nursing | JS6468 | 5 years | ~210 (combined with JS6418) | HK$47,000 |
| HKU | Bachelor of Nursing (Advanced Leadership Track) | JS6418 | 5 years | shared with JS6468 | HK$47,000 |
| CUHK | Bachelor of Nursing | JS4513 | 5 years | ~190 | HK$44,500 |
| PolyU | BSc (Hons) in Nursing | JS3648 | 5 years | ~193 | HK$44,500 |
| PolyU | BSc (Hons) in Mental Health Nursing | JS3337 | 5 years | 70 | HK$44,500 |
| HKMU | Bachelor of Nursing with Honours (SSSDP) | JSSU40 | 5 years | ~280 | ~HK$55,150 (after SSSDP subsidy) |

All five undergraduate routes lead to eligibility for full registration as a General Registered Nurse with the Nursing Council of Hong Kong. PolyU's Mental Health Nursing route additionally registers graduates as Psychiatric RNs.

## HKU — Bachelor of Nursing (JS6468 / JS6418)

HKU's School of Nursing sits within the Li Ka Shing Faculty of Medicine and is the smallest of the four programmes by faculty size but draws on the resources of the Queen Mary Hospital teaching cluster. The programme is a five-year full-time honours degree comprising 46 courses across foundational sciences (anatomy, physiology, pharmacology), nursing practice, clinical placements and a final-year capstone or research project.

In 2024/25 HKU launched an **Advanced Leadership Track (JS6418)** alongside the standard JS6468. The Leadership Track admits a smaller number of high-achieving students who follow the same clinical curriculum but receive additional management, research-methods and global-health training, with a guaranteed overseas exchange or internship at a partner institution. Both codes share the 210-seat intake.

Calculation of programme score uses Best 5 with no subject weighting, and applicants must take English, Chinese, Maths and Citizenship & Social Development as the four core subjects. Selection interviews are required for shortlisted candidates, and good working knowledge of Cantonese and English is essential because most clinical placements are in Cantonese-speaking wards.

The 2025 admission score for JS6468 sat in the upper-low-30s on Best 5 (out of 35 with 4-core+2-elective), broadly competitive with CUHK Nursing.

## CUHK — Bachelor of Nursing (JS4513)

CUHK's Nethersole School of Nursing is the largest of the three traditional university programmes by graduating cohort and is consistently ranked as one of the top five most popular JUPAS choices among all CUHK programmes. Clinical placements run primarily through the Prince of Wales Hospital, which is the New Territories East Cluster's flagship and one of the largest acute hospitals in Hong Kong.

CUHK uses 4C+2X weighting for its Best 5 calculation in Nursing, giving extra weight to core subjects. Biology is **not** strictly required, but most successful applicants have taken Biology or Chemistry as an elective, since these subjects directly feed into Year 1 Anatomy and Physiology. The programme integrates simulation-lab teaching, problem-based learning and a mandatory community-health placement, and offers electives in geriatric, paediatric, mental-health and critical-care nursing in later years.

CUHK Nursing's 2025 admission score sat in the low-to-mid 30s for the Best 5 4C+2X calculation. Lower-quartile and median figures vary slightly year on year — applicants should consult the CUHK admissions office's published *Useful Information for JUPAS Applicants* booklet for current data.

## PolyU — School of Nursing

PolyU's School of Nursing is the largest by intake — combined enrolment across JS3648 (general) and JS3337 (mental health) exceeds 260 students per year. PolyU has the deepest historical roots in Hong Kong nursing education, having trained nurses since the 1970s through its predecessor Hong Kong Polytechnic, and runs the most extensive clinical-placement network spanning Hospital Authority hospitals across all seven clusters.

### BSc (Hons) in Nursing (JS3648)

The general nursing track requires Level 3 or above in at least two HKDSE Category A elective subjects, but no compulsory science subject. PolyU uses subject weighting in its score calculation: English, Maths and a science elective (Biology, Chemistry, Physics or Combined Science) typically receive higher weights, which means strong performers in sciences are at a real advantage despite the absence of a hard prerequisite.

In 2024/25 the average admission score for JS3648 was approximately 212.5 (weighted, on a scale roughly comparable to Best 5 × 6 with subject multipliers). The programme launched a new **Global Nursing Leader Distinction** in 2025/26 — high-achieving entrants are invited to participate in WHO Collaborating Centre exchanges in Europe, North America or Australia.

### BSc (Hons) in Mental Health Nursing (JS3337)

PolyU is the **only** university in Hong Kong offering an undergraduate degree dedicated to psychiatric nursing. Graduates are eligible to register as Psychiatric RNs and typically work in psychiatric hospitals (Castle Peak, Kwai Chung, Siu Lam), community mental-health teams and psychiatric units of acute hospitals.

The 2024/25 average admission score was approximately 212.5 — the same band as the general nursing programme, though the smaller 70-place intake means competition can fluctuate sharply between cycles. The programme includes substantial training in psychotherapy basics, addictions nursing, forensic mental health and child & adolescent psychiatry, alongside the general nursing core.

## HKMU — Bachelor of Nursing with Honours (SSSDP, JSSU40)

Hong Kong Metropolitan University (formerly OUHK) is a self-financing institution but its nursing programme is **subsidised under the Study Subsidy Scheme for Designated Professions/Sectors (SSSDP)** — meaning students pay only roughly the same tuition as UGC-funded programmes after the government subsidy is applied. The annual tuition after the SSSDP subsidy of around HK$89,620 is approximately HK$55,150.

HKMU's nursing programme is the largest by absolute intake (around 280 places per year combined across General Health Care and Mental Health pathways), and admission scores are typically lower than the three traditional universities, making it the realistic primary target for applicants in the mid-band-B range. The clinical placement network is extensive — HKMU has formal partnerships with both public and private hospital groups.

HKMU also offers a separate **Higher Diploma in Nursing (HDN)** sub-degree route. HDN graduates can qualify as Enrolled Nurses (ENs), and many later articulate into the bachelor's programme through Pathway 2 to upgrade to RN.

## The Nursing Council Licensing Examination

A bachelor's degree alone does not automatically license you to practise. All graduates must pass the **Nursing Council of Hong Kong Licensing Examination** for either Registration (RN) or Enrolment (EN). Although graduates of the four accredited bachelor programmes are typically granted a streamlined route, all candidates must meet the Council's eligibility standards.

### Examination structure

- **Written part** — multiple-choice and short-answer paper covering general nursing knowledge, clinical practice, ethics and legislation
- **Practical part** — OSCE-style clinical skills assessment, conducted only after the written part is passed
- **Fees (2026)** — HK$860 for RN registration, HK$920 for EN enrolment

### Important rules

Candidates have a maximum of **three attempts**. After three failures, re-sitting requires special permission from the Council. Applicants must make their first attempt within two years of receiving Council approval. Applications submitted by end-October each year are assessed for the following year's examination.

For the four accredited bachelor's programmes, the curriculum is designed so that graduates pass on the first attempt at very high rates — typically above 95%.

## Career outcomes and salary

### Hospital Authority entry

The Hospital Authority is by far the largest employer of nurses in Hong Kong, recruiting the bulk of each graduating cohort. The HA runs a **centralised recruitment exercise** every year and graduates from the four bachelor programmes are typically all but guaranteed a place if they pass the licensing exam.

Starting salary for a Registered Nurse on the HA master pay scale is approximately **HK$40,000–46,000 per month**, including allowances. Average total compensation in the first year (with overtime, on-call and shift allowances) commonly reaches HK$55,000+ per month. Public-sector nurses also receive 21–28 days of annual leave, paid sick leave, an Examination Leave allowance for further qualifications, and an attractive non-contributory provident fund after vesting.

### Specialisation and career ladder

After 2–3 years of bedside experience, RNs can apply for specialisation in areas such as:

- **Critical care** — ICU, CCU, A&E
- **Operating theatre / perioperative**
- **Oncology**
- **Paediatric and neonatal**
- **Mental health and community psychiatric**
- **Midwifery** — requires additional 18-month training to qualify as a Registered Midwife
- **Community and public health nursing**

The HA career ladder progresses RN → Advanced Practice Nurse (APN) → Nursing Officer (NO) → Ward Manager (WM) → Department Operations Manager (DOM). A Nursing Officer typically earns HK$65,000–80,000 monthly, and Ward Managers HK$90,000–110,000+.

### Private sector and overseas

Private hospitals (Hong Kong Adventist, Matilda, Gleneagles, Hong Kong Sanatorium, etc.) offer comparable or slightly higher base salaries and more predictable hours. International work is well established — Hong Kong RN registration is highly regarded, and bridging routes into the UK NMC, Australian AHPRA and Canadian/US licensure are well documented.

## Choosing between the four programmes

For top-band applicants (Best 5 ~33+), **HKU** and **CUHK** are the prestige choices and offer the strongest research-track, postgraduate and overseas-mobility links. HKU's new Advanced Leadership Track is worth shortlisting for students considering hospital management or academic careers.

For applicants with strong subject scores and an interest in **specialisation**, **PolyU** has unmatched depth — its mental-health track is unique in Hong Kong, and its general programme has the broadest clinical-placement network across the territory. PolyU is also the strongest choice for students who want to start clinical exposure early, as the curriculum front-loads ward-based learning.

For mid-band-B applicants, **HKMU** is the realistic primary target. The SSSDP subsidy makes tuition essentially equivalent to UGC universities, the clinical training is rigorous and Council-accredited, and graduates are recruited by the Hospital Authority on the same terms as those from HKU/CUHK/PolyU. The qualification at the end is the same RN registration.

## Practical tips for DSE applicants

**Take Biology** — even where it is not strictly required (PolyU JS3648, CUHK JS4513), Biology is the single best preparation for the Year 1 anatomy and physiology load. Chemistry is the second-best choice. Avoid taking neither.

**Demonstrate genuine interest before the interview**. Volunteer at a hospital, elderly home or community-care NGO. Shadow a working nurse if family connections allow. Read widely about Hong Kong's healthcare system, the public-private mix and the role of NGOs. Interviewers ask "why nursing?" and the strongest answers come from real exposure.

**Prepare for shift work**. Five years of clinical placements include night shifts, weekend rotations and physically demanding wards. Realistic self-assessment matters — students who underestimate the physical and emotional demands often do not finish the programme.

**Consider the Higher Diploma route as a fallback**, not as a first choice. HKMU's HDN is a legitimate path to EN registration with later articulation to RN, but it adds 2–3 years compared to the direct bachelor's route. For most candidates capable of nursing, aiming for one of the four bachelor programmes is the better play.

## Conclusion

A nursing bachelor's degree in Hong Kong is one of the most reliable returns on five years of study available in the JUPAS system. Demand is locked in by demography, starting salaries are strong, the qualification travels internationally, and the clinical careers are deep — there are paths into management, research, education, midwifery and advanced practice for those who want them. Whether you target HKU's research-intensive programme, CUHK's broad-spectrum clinical training, PolyU's specialised tracks or HKMU's accessible SSSDP route, the destination is the same — registration as a Registered Nurse with the Nursing Council of Hong Kong, and a career with rare combination of meaning and security.

For applicants weighing nursing against medicine, dentistry or pharmacy, the trade-off is real but worth thinking through carefully — five years versus six, lower DSE entry threshold but a profession whose autonomy, scope of practice and earning ceiling have all been expanding for two decades. For the right student, nursing is not a fallback. It is the answer.

# Hong Kong Occupational Therapy Bachelor (PolyU JS3624) Complete Guide 2026

The Bachelor of Science (Honours) in Occupational Therapy at The Hong Kong Polytechnic University (PolyU) - JUPAS code **JS3624** - is the only undergraduate programme in Hong Kong that leads to direct registration as a Registered Occupational Therapist (Part I) with the Occupational Therapists Board. Together with Physiotherapy (JS3636) and Optometry (JS3290), it forms the so-called "PolyU Three Treasures" (理大三寶) - a trio of clinical degrees that combine guaranteed registration, six-figure starting salaries in the public sector, and statutory practice rights nowhere else available in the territory.

This guide walks through the 2026 admission picture: how the score is calculated, what the curriculum looks like across four years, how the 1,000+ hours of clinical placements are structured, what the Hospital Authority pays new graduates, and how the World Federation of Occupational Therapists (WFOT) recognition opens doors to overseas licensure. It also covers the Non-JUPAS routes that international and mainland applicants increasingly use, given that the JUPAS quota is fixed at roughly 70 places out of an annual intake of 100.

## What Occupational Therapists Actually Do

Occupational therapy (OT) is one of the four statutory allied health professions in Hong Kong, alongside physiotherapy, medical laboratory technology, and radiography. Where physiotherapists focus on movement, strength, and pain, occupational therapists work on **purposeful activity** - the everyday "occupations" of self-care, productivity, and leisure that give a person's life meaning. A stroke survivor relearning to button a shirt, a child with autism developing fine-motor skills for handwriting, an elderly resident adapting a kitchen for safe cooking after a hip fracture, a worker returning to a factory line after a hand injury - all of these fall within the OT scope.

In Hong Kong's clinical landscape, OTs are deployed across the Hospital Authority's seven clusters (acute hospitals, rehabilitation hospitals, infirmaries, psychiatric units, child assessment centres), the Department of Health, special schools and integrated programmes under the Education Bureau, elderly day-care centres and integrated rehabilitation centres operated by NGOs such as the Hong Kong Society for Rehabilitation, and a fast-growing private sector that includes paediatric clinics, ergonomic consultancies, and post-acute home rehabilitation services for the ageing population.

The profession is governed by the Occupational Therapists Board under the Supplementary Medical Professions Ordinance (Cap. 359). Practising OT in Hong Kong without registration is a criminal offence, which is why the supply of new practitioners is tightly controlled by PolyU's annual intake.

## JS3624 at a Glance

| Item | Details |
|------|---------|
| JUPAS code | JS3624 |
| Full title | Bachelor of Science (Honours) in Occupational Therapy |
| Offering school | Department of Rehabilitation Sciences, Faculty of Health and Social Sciences, PolyU |
| Duration | 4 years full-time |
| Annual intake | 100 places (JUPAS + Non-JUPAS combined) |
| Funding | UGC-funded |
| Tuition (local) | HK$47,000 per year (Year 1, 2025/26 reference) |
| Credits to graduate | 130 (including 24 credits of clinical fieldwork) |
| Clinical placement hours | 1,000+ hours across all four years |
| Professional registration | Direct registration with Occupational Therapists Board (Part I) |
| International recognition | WFOT-accredited; eligible for AU / UK / CA licensure pathways |

## 2026 JUPAS Admission Requirements

### Minimum entrance requirements

- **Chinese Language**: Level 3
- **English Language**: Level 3
- **Mathematics Compulsory Part**: Level 2
- **Citizenship and Social Development**: Attained
- **Two elective subjects** at Level 3, **OR** one elective at Level 3 plus Mathematics Extended Module (M1 or M2) at Level 3

There is **no compulsory elective subject**, but the programme strongly favours science background. Applicants without Biology, Chemistry or Physics among their electives compete at a structural disadvantage in the weighted score and will face harder questioning in any interview.

### Subject weightings (admission score calculation)

PolyU calculates the JS3624 admission score using **Best 5 subjects with subject weighting**. Under the published weighting scheme:

- **English Language**: weight ×1.5
- **Biology / Chemistry / Physics / Combined Science (with Biology, Chemistry or Physics)**: weight ×1.5 (one science subject is given the bonus)
- **Chinese Language, Mathematics Compulsory Part, M1, M2, and other electives**: weight ×1.0

Citizenship and Social Development is **not** counted in the score - it only needs to be Attained to satisfy the entrance bar.

### Recent admission scores

| Intake year | Average admission score (Best 5 with weighting) |
|-------------|------------------------------------------------|
| 2024/25 | 281.8 |
| 2025/26 | 285.6 |

For context, on the standard "Best 5 unweighted" basis these scores correspond to roughly **5*-level performance across four core subjects plus a 5 in a fifth**. The lower 25th percentile typically lands around 27 (in unweighted Best 5 terms), while the top end of the cohort regularly exceeds 32. JS3624 is not as competitive as Medicine or Physiotherapy, but it is comfortably above the average band cut-off for non-clinical PolyU programmes.

### Interview and OEA

The programme reserves the right to require an interview or test, and in practice interviews are conducted for borderline applicants and those whose Other Experiences and Achievements (OEA) profile or Student Learning Profile (SLP) signals strong motivation. Useful OEA evidence includes volunteering with persons with disabilities, hospital or elderly-home shadowing, sports-coaching of children with special educational needs, and any independent reading or community projects related to rehabilitation. The interview, when held, is typically a structured panel format of 15-20 minutes, sometimes with a short scenario task.

## Four-Year Curriculum Structure

The programme follows a "scheme" model under the Department of Rehabilitation Sciences. Year 1 is shared with Physiotherapy (JS3636) for the foundation science modules, with branching into OT-specific content from Year 2.

### Year 1 - Foundation Sciences

Anatomy, physiology, kinesiology, biomechanics, psychology, sociology, plus PolyU's General University Requirements (GUR): English, Chinese, service learning, and a leadership and intra-personal development cluster. Students earn around 30 credits and take a single-credit "Introduction to Occupational Therapy" module that includes hospital observation visits.

### Year 2 - Conditions and Assessment

Pathology, neurology, orthopaedics, paediatric development, mental health and psychiatry, occupational science theory, and the first OT-specific assessment courses (activity analysis, occupational performance assessment). Year 2 ends with the **first clinical placement (Level I, ~3 weeks)** in a supervised acute or rehabilitation setting.

### Year 3 - Intervention and Specialty Practice

Adult physical rehabilitation, mental health practice, paediatric intervention, hand therapy, splinting and orthotics, assistive technology, environmental modification, vocational rehabilitation. Year 3 contains the largest single placement block - typically **two Level II placements of 8-10 weeks each**, rotating through different clinical specialties (e.g., one acute physical, one psychiatric or paediatric).

### Year 4 - Capstone and Independent Practice

Honours research project (year-long), advanced practice electives (e.g., community-based rehabilitation, hand therapy specialisation, dementia care), professional ethics and law, healthcare management. The final clinical block is a **Level III "role-emerging" placement** of 8-10 weeks where students function with substantial autonomy under remote supervision, often in non-traditional settings such as schools, NGO community centres, or workplace ergonomics consultancies.

Across the four years students accumulate **at least 1,000 hours of clinical fieldwork**, the WFOT minimum. PolyU consistently exceeds this benchmark, which is part of why its degree is recognised internationally without bridging requirements in most jurisdictions.

## Tuition, Costs and Scholarships

For local UGC-funded students the 2025/26 first-year tuition is **HK$47,000**. Total degree cost (tuition only) over four years is in the order of HK$188,000 - identical to other UGC programmes and significantly less than self-financed alternatives.

Indirect costs to budget for include:

- Hostel fees if applicable: HK$10,000-18,000 per academic year for PolyU halls
- Textbooks, lab coats, professional shoes, and a clinical placement uniform: roughly HK$3,000-5,000 in Year 1, less thereafter
- Transport to placement sites across all 18 districts of Hong Kong during clinical blocks
- Optional WFOT student membership (~US$30/year) for international networking and conference discounts
- Professional indemnity insurance during Level III placement (often covered by PolyU)

PolyU offers an extensive range of scholarships including the Talent Development Scholarship (renewable, HK$30,000+), entrance scholarships for students with 5** in three or more subjects, and need-based bursaries through the Student Affairs Office. Mainland students who enter via Non-JUPAS at full overseas tuition (HK$145,000 in 2025/26) are eligible for the PolyU Mainland Scholarship, which can cover up to 100% of tuition for top-scoring Gaokao admittees.

## Clinical Placements - What to Expect

Placements are coordinated through the Department of Rehabilitation Sciences in partnership with all seven Hospital Authority clusters, the Department of Health's Child Assessment Service, the Education Bureau's special schools, and over 50 NGO and private-sector partners. Students typically complete:

- **One Level I placement** (Year 2): exposure-style, 3 weeks, focus on observation and basic assessment
- **Two Level II placements** (Year 3): full immersion, 8-10 weeks each, structured caseload progression
- **One Level III placement** (Year 4): role-emerging or advanced practice, 8-10 weeks, near-autonomous practice

Placements are unpaid (in line with the global norm for clinical training) and students are responsible for their own commute. A common rite of passage is being assigned a Tuen Mun Hospital or Castle Peak Hospital block while living in Hung Hom - the daily MTR commute becomes part of the learning curve. Performance is graded by the on-site clinical educator (a registered OT with at least three years' experience) using a national fieldwork assessment instrument; failure of any single placement requires repeating the block, which can delay graduation by a semester.

## Career Prospects and Salary

### Hospital Authority

The single largest employer of new graduates is the Hospital Authority, which absorbs roughly 60-70% of each cohort into its allied health workforce. New graduates enter as **Occupational Therapist II** on the Master Pay Scale (MPS) Point 16. After the April 2024 adjustment the OT II band runs from approximately MPS 16 to MPS 33, with monthly salaries starting around **HK$36,000** and reaching HK$60,000+ within the band over 6-8 years. Promotion to **Occupational Therapist I** (MPS 34-44, roughly HK$67,000-91,000/month) typically follows after another 3-5 years of solid performance, with senior and managerial grades stretching beyond MPS 45.

Allied health staff in the HA receive 13 months of salary, civil-service-style medical and dental coverage, generous leave entitlements (22+ days, rising with service), and a Mandatory Provident Fund top-up scheme. Total first-year compensation for a new OT II is comfortably in the **HK$470,000-500,000** range.

### Government, NGOs and private sector

Beyond the HA, OTs are recruited by:

- **Department of Health** - Child Assessment Service, Elderly Health Service, Centre for Health Protection
- **Education Bureau** - special schools, integrated education support teams
- **Social Welfare Department** and subsidised NGO operators - Hong Kong Society for Rehabilitation, Heep Hong Society, Caritas, Tung Wah Group of Hospitals, Po Leung Kuk
- **Private hospitals and clinics** - Hong Kong Sanatorium, Adventist, Matilda, plus the rapidly growing paediatric OT clinic sector in Causeway Bay, Tsim Sha Tsui and Sha Tin
- **Workplace ergonomics consultancies** serving banks, airlines and construction companies
- **Self-employment** as a registered OT, particularly in private paediatric practice and home-based geriatric care

Private-sector salaries for new graduates often start slightly above HA scales (HK$38,000-45,000/month) and can rise faster, but lack the long-service progression and pension benefits of the public sector.

## WFOT Recognition and Overseas Practice

PolyU's BSc (Hons) in Occupational Therapy has been continuously accredited by the **World Federation of Occupational Therapists (WFOT)** since the programme's founding. WFOT accreditation means the curriculum meets international minimum standards, which translates into materially easier overseas registration in three of the most popular destination markets:

- **Australia**: Eligible to apply for registration with the Occupational Therapy Board of Australia (AHPRA) without bridging coursework, subject to English-language proof and a competency assessment
- **United Kingdom**: Eligible for HCPC registration via the international application route, typically with a streamlined review of curriculum and clinical hours
- **Canada**: Eligible to sit the National Occupational Therapy Certification Examination (NOTCE) administered by CAOT and provincial regulators after credential review
- **United States**: Requires NBCOT examination plus state-by-state licensure; PolyU graduates have a strong track record of passing NBCOT, though additional documentation is needed
- **Singapore**: Direct recognition by the Allied Health Professions Council for restricted registration leading to full registration after supervised practice

This international portability is one of the strongest selling points of JS3624. Graduates who later emigrate, study overseas, or take a working holiday are not stranded in a non-transferable qualification.

## Non-JUPAS and International Pathways

Of the 100 first-year places, roughly 70 are filled through JUPAS and the remaining 30 through Non-JUPAS - a category that includes Hong Kong students with non-DSE qualifications (IB, GCE A-Level, SAT/AP, Gaokao), mainland Gaokao applicants, and international students. The most common entry profiles are:

- **GCE A-Level**: AAA in three subjects including at least one science
- **IB Diploma**: 38-40 points overall with HL 6/6/6 including HL Biology or Chemistry
- **Gaokao**: well above the first-tier line (一本線) for the applicant's province, typically 80+ points above the cut-off
- **Associate Degree / Higher Diploma in related fields**: rare entry into Year 1 (PolyU does not typically offer senior-year articulation into JS3624 due to clinical sequencing)

Non-JUPAS applicants apply directly through PolyU's eAdmission system, with rounds opening in September and closing typically in mid-November (early round) and January (main round). Interviews for Non-JUPAS shortlistees are essentially universal and are taken seriously - PolyU is checking for English fluency, ethical reasoning, and authentic interest in the profession.

International (non-local) tuition is **HK$145,000 per year** in 2025/26, with the same hostel and living-cost picture as local students.

## Comparison with the Master in Occupational Therapy (MOT)

PolyU also offers a **Master in Occupational Therapy** (programme code 51068), a 2.5-year postgraduate-entry programme for graduates who already hold a bachelor's degree in another discipline. The MOT also leads to registration with the Occupational Therapists Board and is WFOT-accredited, but:

- Tuition is much higher (self-financed, around HK$340,000+ for the full programme)
- Intake is smaller (typically 30-40 places per year)
- Competition includes mature applicants with biology, psychology or healthcare backgrounds

For school leavers the BSc route remains by far the more cost-effective path. The MOT is best viewed as a career-change option for graduates in their mid-20s onwards.

## How JS3624 Compares With JS3636 (Physiotherapy) and JS3290 (Optometry)

| | JS3624 OT | JS3636 PT | JS3290 Optometry |
|--|----------|-----------|------------------|
| Duration | 4 years | 4 years | 5 years |
| Intake | ~100 | ~75 | ~55 |
| 2025/26 average score | 285.6 | ~290+ | ~280+ |
| Registration | OT Board (Cap. 359) | PT Board (Cap. 359) | Optometrists Board (Cap. 359) |
| HA entry grade | OT II | PT II | Optometrist II |
| Practice setting | Hospital, school, community, home | Hospital, sports clinic, community | Hospital, private optical, refraction clinic |
| International portability | WFOT (AU/UK/CA) | WCPT (AU/UK/CA) | Variable, country-specific |

OT typically draws applicants who are interested in **holistic, person-centred rehabilitation** rather than the more biomechanical focus of PT or the more procedural focus of optometry. The work is intellectually broad - one week may involve hand therapy splinting, the next a cognitive rehabilitation group for early dementia, the next ergonomic redesign of an office workstation.

## Should You Apply?

Apply to JS3624 if:

- You are drawn to long-term, relationship-based care rather than acute or surgical work
- You are comfortable with both physical (anatomy, kinesiology) and psychosocial (mental health, group therapy) aspects of healthcare
- You want a guaranteed registration pathway and a clear public-sector salary ladder
- You value international portability of your qualification
- You can sustain four years of an academically demanding curriculum with substantial unpaid placement time

Think carefully before applying if:

- You are primarily attracted by the salary - PT and OT pay similarly, but Pharmacy or Medicine pay more if the financial calculus is dominant
- You dislike documentation - OT clinical work is paperwork-heavy
- You are uncertain about working with elderly, paediatric or mental-health populations - all three are unavoidable across the four-year placement schedule

For applicants who fit the profile, JS3624 remains one of Hong Kong's best-value undergraduate degrees: guaranteed professional registration, an internationally portable credential, a stable public-sector employer ready to absorb the cohort, and a starting salary in the territory's top quintile. For the 2026 JUPAS cycle it deserves a serious place in any health-sciences-focused Band A.

## Hong Kong Optometry Bachelor (PolyU JS3290) Complete Guide 2026: The City's Only Licensed Optometrist Pathway, Five-Year Curriculum, JUPAS Scoring and Career Outcomes

# Hong Kong Optometry Bachelor (PolyU JS3290) Complete Guide 2026

If you want to become a licensed optometrist in Hong Kong, there is exactly one undergraduate route: the **Bachelor of Science (Honours) in Optometry** at the Hong Kong Polytechnic University (PolyU), JUPAS code **JS3290**. No other UGC-funded university in Hong Kong runs an optometry degree, and no overseas optometry qualification is automatically recognised by the Optometrists Board for Part I registration without further assessment. This makes JS3290 the single most strategic — and most competitive — entry point into the profession.

This guide walks DSE candidates and Non-JUPAS applicants through everything that matters in 2026: admission scoring, the five-year curriculum, the Optometrists Board licensing system, clinical training, tuition, graduate salaries and overseas recognition.

## Why Optometry, and Why Only PolyU

In Hong Kong the optometry profession is regulated under the **Supplementary Medical Professions Ordinance (Cap. 359)**. The Optometrists Board maintains four parts on the licence register (Parts I–IV), with **Part I** being the highest tier. Only Part I optometrists are authorised to perform comprehensive eye examinations, use diagnostic pharmaceutical agents, and provide the full scope of primary eye-care services that include detection of ocular disease, binocular vision assessment and contact lens fitting.

The PolyU School of Optometry was established in 1979 and remains the only institution in Hong Kong whose undergraduates are eligible for **direct entry to Part I** of the Optometrists Register on graduation. Holders of overseas optometry degrees — even from accredited US, UK or Australian programmes — must apply individually and may be required to sit licensing examinations or complete supervised practice before being granted Part I status.

The practical consequence: if your goal is to practise as a licensed optometrist in Hong Kong before age 25, JS3290 is by far the fastest route.

## Programme Snapshot 2026

- **JUPAS code:** JS3290
- **Award:** Bachelor of Science (Honours) in Optometry
- **Duration:** 5 years full-time
- **Total credits:** 152 (including 20 clinical/field-experience credits)
- **Intake quota:** 60 places (combined JUPAS + Non-JUPAS + International)
- **Funding:** Government-funded (UGC)
- **2025/26 average HKDSE admission score:** 260.6 (Best 5 + 6th-subject bonus)
- **Entry type:** Direct entry to Year 1 (not a broad-based scheme)
- **Tuition (2026/27):** HK$44,500 per year for local government-funded students (subject to Government adjustment); non-local fees substantially higher
- **Professional outcome:** Eligible for direct registration as a Part I optometrist with the Optometrists Board of Hong Kong

The 60-place quota is one of the smallest among UGC-funded professional programmes in Hong Kong — comparable to CityU's Bachelor of Veterinary Medicine and significantly tighter than nursing or pharmacy. Combined with the fact that direct registration as a Part I optometrist is reserved for PolyU graduates, this scarcity drives admission scores up consistently to the high 250s and low 260s.

## JUPAS Admission Requirements

### Minimum requirements

JS3290 follows PolyU's **General Entrance Requirements**:

- Chinese Language: Level 3
- English Language: Level 3
- Mathematics (Compulsory Part): Level 2
- Citizenship and Social Development: Attained
- Two elective subjects: Level 3 each (M1/M2 counted as elective)

These minimums get you considered. They will not get you offered.

### Score calculation (2026)

PolyU calculates the JS3290 admission score using:

**Any best 5 subjects + bonus score for the 6th subject if at Level 3 or above.**

Conversion: Level 5** = 8.5, 5* = 7, 5 = 5.5, 4 = 4, 3 = 3, 2 = 2, 1 = 1. There are no compulsory subjects, but PolyU applies positive weighting on **preferred subjects**.

### Preferred subjects with positive weighting

- Chinese Language
- English Language
- Mathematics (Compulsory Part)
- Mathematics Extended Module 1 (Calculus and Statistics)
- Mathematics Extended Module 2 (Algebra and Calculus)
- Biology
- Chemistry
- Physics
- Combined Science (any two of Bio/Chem/Phys)

The strongest profiles take **two of Biology / Chemistry / Physics**, plus M1 or M2. Biology + Chemistry is the most common combination because both feed directly into the Year 1–2 visual science modules; Physics is highly useful for the optics components.

### Realistic competitive scores

For DSE 2025 admissions, the Best-5 + 6th-subject median score for offered candidates clustered around **27–30** under the standard 5**=7 conversion (or 260+ under the 8.5-scale). Practically, 5*5*5*55 across English, Chinese, Maths and two science subjects is a comfortable Band A1 profile. 5544 + 5 in Liberal Studies / CS will likely fall short of the cut-off in a typical year.

### Special physical and language requirements

PolyU explicitly requires applicants to "possess the sensory and motor skills necessary to perform an eye examination". This is not a screening filter at the JUPAS stage, but candidates with severe colour vision deficiency, significant tremor or motor impairment should consult the School of Optometry before applying — clinical training requires **fine bimanual coordination** for slit-lamp work, contact-lens fitting and instillation of eye drops.

The programme also expects students to develop **good Cantonese skills before starting clinical placements**, because the majority of clinic patients are Cantonese-speaking Hong Kong residents. International and Mainland students are admitted but should plan early Cantonese acquisition.

## Non-JUPAS and International Applicants

Non-local applicants apply directly to PolyU (not via JUPAS). Required components:

- **Academic credentials:** Gaokao with strong scores in Chinese, English, Maths and at least one science (typically 50+ above first-tier line); IB 36+ with HL sciences; A-Levels AAA including two of Bio/Chem/Phys/Maths; or equivalent
- **English proficiency:** IELTS 6.5 (no band below 6.0) or TOEFL iBT 80
- **Personal Statement:** Maximum 500 words explaining motivation for optometry
- **Reference letter:** Required for international candidates
- **Interview:** 15-minute individual interview conducted in English

The interview probes motivation, basic understanding of the optometric scope of practice, ethical reasoning around patient care, and manual dexterity awareness. Candidates are routinely asked the difference between an optometrist, an ophthalmologist and an optician — a surprising number of applicants conflate the three.

## Five-Year Curriculum: What You Actually Study

The 152-credit programme is divided into a science-foundation phase, a clinical-skills phase and a clinical-immersion phase.

### Year 1 — Foundation

- General University Requirements (English, Chinese, Service Learning, GE clusters)
- Human Anatomy and Physiology
- General and Visual Optics
- Geometric and Physical Optics
- Introduction to Optometry and Visual Science

Year 1 is heavy on optics: students learn how light refracts, how spherical and cylindrical lenses correct ametropia, and how the eye's optical system forms images on the retina. Expect mathematics-intensive problem sets.

### Year 2 — Visual Science

- Ocular Anatomy and Physiology
- Visual Perception and Neuroscience
- Optometric Instrumentation
- General Pathology and Microbiology
- Pharmacology for Optometrists

This is the year where the discipline narrows from "applied physics" to "applied biomedical science". Pharmacology is particularly important: Part I optometrists are authorised to instil diagnostic agents (mydriatics, cycloplegics, topical anaesthetics) and need to understand drug interactions, contraindications and adverse reactions.

### Year 3 — Clinical Techniques

- Refraction and Subjective Examination
- Binocular Vision and Orthoptics
- Contact Lens Theory and Fitting
- Ocular Disease I (anterior segment)
- Paediatric Optometry

Year 3 is where students first work on each other and on volunteer patients in the **Skills Laboratory** under tight supervision. Practical assessments are continuous — every clinical examination skill is signed off individually before students progress.

### Year 4 — Clinical Practice and Specialisation

- Ocular Disease II (posterior segment, glaucoma, retinal disease)
- Low Vision and Visual Rehabilitation
- Geriatric Optometry
- Public Health and Occupational Optometry
- Clinical Practice (real patients, supervised)

Students start their **clinical placements at the PolyU Optometry Clinic** — a fully operational primary-care eye clinic on the PolyU Hung Hom campus that sees thousands of public patients each year. Patient bookings span paediatric vision screening, contact lens fitting, low-vision assessment and ocular disease management.

### Year 5 — Internship and Capstone

- Five semesters of cumulative supervised clinical training (continued from Year 4)
- Honours Project (research thesis or extended clinical case study)
- Advanced Clinical Optometry
- Professional Practice Management
- Elective rotations: Hospital Authority eye clinics, paediatric specialty clinics, low-vision services, sports vision, satellite community clinics

Final-year students take primary responsibility for managing their own patient panels under faculty supervision. This is functionally a residency-light experience and is the reason PolyU graduates are deemed exam-ready for Part I registration on graduation rather than after a separate licensing year.

## The Optometrists Board Part I Registration

PolyU's BSc (Hons) in Optometry is recognised by the Optometrists Board of Hong Kong for **direct entry to Part I of the optometrist register** under the Supplementary Medical Professions Ordinance. Graduates apply via the eForm system (DH0208) administered by the Department of Health.

Required documentation:

- Original PolyU degree certificate and academic transcript
- Hong Kong ID copy
- Two passport-sized photos
- Application fee
- Continuing Professional Development undertaking

Most graduates receive Part I registration within 4–8 weeks of graduation, allowing them to start full clinical practice the same calendar year they finish the degree. There is no separate national licensing examination — the curriculum's clinical assessments serve that role.

## Clinical Training Infrastructure

Year 4–5 clinical training takes place at:

- **PolyU Optometry Clinic** (Hung Hom main campus) — the largest student-run eye clinic in Hong Kong
- **PolyU Satellite Clinics** in Kowloon and the New Territories serving lower-income communities
- **Hospital Authority eye departments** (rotation slots at Queen Elizabeth Hospital, Hong Kong Eye Hospital and others)
- **Paediatric specialty clinics** for myopia control and amblyopia management
- **Low-vision rehabilitation services** in collaboration with the Hong Kong Society for the Blind

The clinic operates on a real patient-fee model. Students are supervised by registered Part I optometrists and faculty ophthalmologists.

## Tuition, Scholarships and Cost of Study

- **Local UGC-funded tuition:** HK$44,500 per year (2026/27, subject to Government revision)
- **Non-local tuition:** HK$145,000–171,000 per year depending on cohort
- **Five-year total local cost of study:** approximately HK$222,500 in tuition + accommodation and living
- **Scholarships:** PolyU Entrance Scholarships (up to full tuition for top JUPAS scorers), Hong Kong Government's Student Finance Office TSFS/NLSFT loans, HKSAR Government Scholarship Fund, and a small number of dedicated Optometry alumni scholarships

Compared with overseas optometry — a four-year US OD typically costs US$120,000–200,000 in tuition alone — PolyU's local-fee track is a remarkable value proposition.

## Graduate Outcomes and Salaries

The PolyU School of Optometry consistently reports near-100% employment within three months of graduation. Typical first-job destinations:

- **Private optometry chains:** OPTICAL 88, Puyi Optical, Hong Kong Optical, Vision Express
- **Independent practices:** boutique clinics in Central, Causeway Bay, Sha Tin, Tseung Kwan O
- **Hospital Authority clinical optometrist posts:** salary point 16+ on the HA pay scale
- **In-house optometry roles** at international brands and contact lens manufacturers
- **Department of Health** (school health programme, public eye-care services)

Starting salaries for fresh graduates in 2025 ranged from **HK$25,000 to HK$35,000 per month** in private practice, with senior optometrists in established practices earning HK$50,000–80,000+ after 5–7 years. Hospital Authority optometrists start around point 16 of the HA Master Pay Scale (~HK$36,000 monthly) with structured progression.

A small but growing cohort pursue **postgraduate clinical specialisation**: PolyU offers a Doctor of Optometry (OD) and a residency programme in paediatric, primary care, low vision and ocular disease specialties. Some graduates also pursue a Master of Public Health, an MPhil/PhD in Visual Science, or an MBA for practice management.

## Overseas Recognition

PolyU's BSc (Hons) in Optometry is recognised for licensing — usually with additional examinations or supervised practice — in:

- **Australia** (via Optometry Council of Australia and New Zealand assessment, then OBA registration)
- **United Kingdom** (via the General Optical Council Overseas Registration assessment route)
- **Mainland China** (recognised at provincial registration level; specific bridge programmes in Guangdong)
- **Singapore** (through Allied Health Professions Council case-by-case assessment)

Direct US licensure (state-by-state) generally requires conversion to a Doctor of Optometry, but PolyU graduates routinely gain advanced standing in OD bridge programmes at US schools such as SUNY College of Optometry and the New England College of Optometry.

## Application Strategy and Timeline

For DSE candidates aiming at JS3290 in 2026:

- **Subject selection (Form 4):** lock in two of Biology, Chemistry, Physics, plus M1 or M2 if your school offers it
- **Year 5–6 sprint:** prioritise English, Chinese and the two preferred sciences for Level 5 or above; aim for at least 5*5*5*55 (29 in best-5 + bonus)
- **JUPAS Band A:** if your goal is optometry, JS3290 must sit in Band A (preferably A1). The score cutoff means it does not realistically appear in Band B offers
- **Backup choices:** Pharmacy at CUHK or HKU, Nursing at PolyU/HKU/CUHK, Biomedical Sciences at HKUST, Chinese Medicine at CUHK/HKBU/PolyU
- **Non-JUPAS deadline:** typically late November of the preceding year; secure references and IELTS/TOEFL scores by October

For interview preparation, study the **scope of practice** of a Hong Kong Part I optometrist, read the Optometrists Board Code of Practice, and be ready to articulate why optometry — not medicine, not nursing — fits your career goals.

## Common Misconceptions

**Optometrist vs. ophthalmologist.** An ophthalmologist is a registered medical doctor who has completed medicine, internship and ophthalmology specialty training (MBBS + 6+ years), and can perform eye surgery. An optometrist is a non-medical primary eye-care professional who diagnoses refractive errors and ocular disease and prescribes optical and pharmaceutical treatment, but does not perform surgery.

**Optometrist vs. optician.** Opticians (Parts III/IV) dispense glasses against a prescription written by a Part I optometrist or ophthalmologist; they do not perform full eye examinations.

**"I can study optometry overseas and come back to practise."** Not without the Optometrists Board's case-by-case assessment, possibly an examination, and possibly supervised practice. Students underestimate this barrier every year.

## Bottom Line

PolyU JS3290 is one of the most strategically valuable degrees in Hong Kong: a 60-place, government-funded, profession-licensing programme with near-universal employment and a clear path to a HK$25,000–80,000+ monthly career inside five years of starting Form 6. The trade-off is admission competitiveness — high-260s admission scores in 2025 — and an explicit physical-skills requirement. If your DSE profile is heading toward 5*5*5*55 in English, Chinese, Maths and two of Biology / Chemistry / Physics, and you are comfortable with bimanual clinical work in Cantonese, JS3290 is one of the highest-yield Band A choices on the JUPAS list.

# Hong Kong Pharmacy Bachelor Complete Guide 2026: HKU JS6494, CUHK JS4525, Four-Year BPharm, Pharmacy and Poisons Board Registration, Hospital Authority Pharmacist Salary Scales

Only two universities in Hong Kong currently offer a UGC-funded Bachelor of Pharmacy (BPharm) degree: **The Chinese University of Hong Kong School of Pharmacy** (JUPAS code **JS4525**) and **The University of Hong Kong Department of Pharmacology and Pharmacy** (JUPAS code **JS6494**). Both programmes run for four years full-time, both are accredited by the Pharmacy and Poisons Board of Hong Kong (PPBHK), and graduates of both — after passing the Board's registration examination and completing a one-year approved internship — are eligible to register as practising pharmacists in Hong Kong's public hospitals, private hospitals, community pharmacies (the registered counters at Mannings, Watsons, and CRC Care), pharmaceutical manufacturing, regulatory affairs, and academic research.

Pharmacy is one of the few healthcare degrees in Hong Kong with effectively 100% graduate employment. The Hospital Authority pharmacy departments have been expanding for several years, the 2024 amendments to the Pharmacy and Poisons Ordinance have widened pharmacist scope of practice, and the gradual rollout of the prescription-dispensing model in community pharmacies has created persistent vacancies. This guide breaks down both programmes in detail — admissions, curriculum, the registration pathway, salary, and overseas mobility — to help 2026 DSE candidates make informed JUPAS Band A choices.

## 1. Why pharmacy is a stable choice in Hong Kong

### 1.1 Statutory foundation — the Pharmacy and Poisons Ordinance (Cap. 138)

Under Cap. 138 of the laws of Hong Kong, **only individuals registered with the Pharmacy and Poisons Board of Hong Kong (PPBHK)** may practise as pharmacists in Hong Kong. To be entered on the Register of Pharmacists, an applicant must:

1. Hold a Board-recognised pharmacy degree;
2. Pass the Pharmacist Registration Examination administered by the Board;
3. Complete a Board-approved internship of at least one year;
4. Satisfy character and fitness checks, and pay the registration fee.

A registered pharmacist must also obtain an **Annual Practising Certificate** at the start of each calendar year before lawfully practising. Without registration, an individual cannot dispense Part 1 poisons (most prescription medicines), supervise a registered pharmacy, or sign a methadone dispensing record.

### 1.2 Why a local BPharm is the cleanest entry route

The PPBHK does recognise certain overseas pharmacy degrees (UK MPharm, Australian BPharm/MPharm, Canadian PharmD, etc.), but overseas-trained graduates still need to sit and pass the Hong Kong Registration Examination, which has historically pegged pass rates at around 50% per paper. By contrast, BPharm graduates of HKU and CUHK take the same examination but with a curriculum tailored to Hong Kong's drug schedules, dispensing law, and Cantonese-language patient counselling. Both schools also embed Board-approved internship rotations into the final year, so by graduation candidates are typically only a few months of further internship away from full registration. This is the cleanest route for any local DSE student set on a pharmacy career in Hong Kong.

## 2. Programme snapshot

| Item | HKU BPharm (JS6494) | CUHK BPharm (JS4525) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Awarding faculty | LKS Faculty of Medicine, Department of Pharmacology and Pharmacy | Faculty of Medicine, School of Pharmacy |
| Duration | 4 years, full-time, 258 credit-units | 4 years, full-time |
| Annual intake | ~35 first-year places | ~30 first-year places |
| Degree | Bachelor of Pharmacy (BPharm) | Bachelor of Pharmacy (Honours) |
| Accreditation | Pharmacy and Poisons Board of Hong Kong | Pharmacy and Poisons Board of Hong Kong |
| Teaching sites | Sassoon Road Campus; Queen Mary Hospital; Gleneagles Hong Kong Hospital | Lo Kwee-Seong Integrated Biomedical Sciences Building (Sha Tin); Prince of Wales Hospital |
| Internship structure | Pharmacy Experiential Education Programme (PEEP) embedded across years | Clinical clerkships in Year 4; one-year post-graduation internship typical |
| Tuition (local students) | HK$44,500 / year (UGC-funded rate) | HK$44,500 / year (UGC-funded rate) |

Combined intake across the two universities is roughly **65 places per year** — fewer than dentistry (90 BDS places at HKU) and far fewer than the ~590 MBBS/MBChB seats. This makes pharmacy one of the smaller and tighter healthcare cohorts in Hong Kong.

## 3. JUPAS admission requirements

### 3.1 General DSE requirement (both universities)

Both HKU and CUHK require the standard "**3-3-2-2-3-3**" minimum to be considered: Level 3 in Chinese Language, Level 3 in English Language, Level 2 in Mathematics Compulsory Part, Level 2 in Citizenship and Social Development, and Level 3 in two elective subjects.

For pharmacy, however, hitting the floor is nowhere near enough. Both schools weight Chemistry and Biology as effective prerequisites, and successful applicants typically present **Level 5 to 5\* averages** across the four core plus two best electives.

### 3.2 Subject combination expectations

- **Chemistry** is treated as a de-facto prerequisite at both universities. Without Chemistry it is extremely difficult to be shortlisted, and impossible to follow the first-year pharmaceutical chemistry curriculum.
- **Biology** is strongly preferred as the second science elective. Students who present Physics or Mathematics M1/M2 instead are not strictly excluded, but Biology applicants tend to fare better in interview because the curriculum builds rapidly into anatomy, physiology and pharmacology.
- **Mathematics Extended Module M1 or M2** can be counted as the seventh subject in HKU's "best 6 subjects" formula and CUHK's flexible weighting, and is useful for pharmacokinetics calculations later on.

### 3.3 Indicative admission scores (2024–2025 entry, for 2026 reference)

Best-six DSE scores for the median admitted student have hovered around:

- **HKU JS6494**: median ~33 – 34 (best 6, 4-2-2-2-2-2 weighting, with science subjects at full weight)
- **CUHK JS4525**: median ~33 – 35 (best 5 weighted on the relevant subject formula, with bonus for Chemistry)

The lower-quartile admit is typically around 30–31 for both. Realistically, Band A applicants should aim for **5 or 5\* in Chemistry and Biology** plus **5\* in English** to be safely competitive, since both schools interview shortlisted candidates.

### 3.4 Interviews

- **HKU** runs group discussion + short individual interview, conducted in English, focused on ethical scenarios, communication, and motivation. Topics commonly include drug pricing, generic substitution, medication safety, and the role of community pharmacy.
- **CUHK** uses a similar group + individual format and is also conducted in English with some Cantonese sections to test patient-counselling potential. Expect questions on local healthcare policy and on why CUHK rather than HKU.

Strong candidates spend serious time before the interview reading the Department of Health drug office circulars, the Consumer Council medication articles, and the Hospital Authority Drug Formulary news.

## 4. Four-year curriculum structure

### 4.1 HKU BPharm

HKU's 258-credit programme is structured as follows:

- **Year 1 — Foundations**: General chemistry, organic chemistry, human anatomy and physiology, introduction to pharmacy practice, communication skills, and a common-core curriculum of HKU general education courses.
- **Year 2 — Pharmaceutical sciences**: Pharmaceutical chemistry, pharmaceutics (formulation), pharmacology I, biochemistry, microbiology and immunology.
- **Year 3 — Clinical and applied**: Clinical pharmacy, pharmacotherapeutics across body systems, pharmacokinetics, pharmacoepidemiology, drug regulatory affairs, and the start of the **Pharmacy Experiential Education Programme (PEEP)** placements.
- **Year 4 — Capstone and clerkships**: Advanced pharmacotherapeutics, hospital clerkships at Queen Mary and Gleneagles, community-pharmacy rotations, a research-based final-year project, and Hong Kong pharmacy law and ethics in preparation for the Board examination.

### 4.2 CUHK BPharm

CUHK's curriculum follows a similar four-year arc but with somewhat heavier early emphasis on biomedical fundamentals (because the School of Pharmacy sits within the Faculty of Medicine and shares first-year basic science teaching with medicine and Chinese medicine students):

- **Year 1**: Core sciences shared with the medical faculty; introduction to pharmacy.
- **Year 2**: Drug discovery and design, medicinal chemistry, pharmaceutics, applied physiology.
- **Year 3**: Pharmacology and therapeutics, biopharmaceutics, clinical pharmacy I, drug information and patient counselling.
- **Year 4**: Clinical clerkships at Prince of Wales Hospital and selected community pharmacies, pharmacy management, research project, and law and ethics.

### 4.3 Experiential learning

Both programmes embed multiple weeks of supervised practice. HKU's PEEP, for instance, places students in a structured rotation across hospital pharmacy, community pharmacy, and pharmaceutical industry settings, supervised by registered pharmacist preceptors. These placements **do not** by themselves satisfy the post-graduation one-year internship — they are educational rotations during the degree — but they significantly accelerate clinical confidence.

## 5. The Pharmacist Registration Examination

After graduation, both HKU and CUHK BPharm holders must sit the **Pharmacist Registration Examination** administered by the PPBHK to be eligible for full registration. Key facts:

- **Three papers, each three hours**: (1) Pharmacy Legislation, (2) Pharmacy Practice, (3) Pharmacology.
- **Examination windows**: Held twice a year, typically in **June and December**. Application deadlines for new entrants are 28 February (June sitting) and 31 August (December sitting). Re-sit deadlines are 31 March and 30 September respectively.
- **Cohort size**: Approximately 80–100 candidates per paper, drawn from local BPharm graduates and overseas-trained pharmacists.
- **Pass rate**: Roughly **50% per paper**, on average. Pharmacy Legislation has historically been the most failed paper for overseas candidates because of the depth of Hong Kong-specific drug schedule and ordinance content.

After passing all three papers, the candidate must complete (or have completed) the one-year approved internship before being added to the Register of Pharmacists. Most local BPharm graduates start their internship immediately after graduation in a Hospital Authority pharmacy or a major community-pharmacy chain, sit the registration exams during or just after that year, and qualify within roughly 12–18 months of degree completion.

## 6. Career pathways and salary in Hong Kong

### 6.1 Hospital Authority — the largest employer

The Hospital Authority is by far the largest employer of pharmacists in Hong Kong, operating pharmacy departments across all 43 public hospitals and a centralised drug procurement and compounding unit.

- **Resident Pharmacist (intern)**: Roughly **HK$36,000 – HK$40,000 / month** during the one-year internship year.
- **Pharmacist I**: Entry rank for fully registered pharmacists. Pegged at approximately **Master Pay Scale Point 27**, equivalent to roughly **HK$60,000 / month** in 2026. With incremental rises through the scale, mid-career Pharmacist I salaries reach Point 33+ within several years.
- **Senior Pharmacist / Senior Pharmacist (Specialist)**: Mid-to-senior rank, MPS Point 34 onwards, typically reached within 6–10 years of registration depending on departmental vacancies.
- **Department Manager / Chief Pharmacist**: MPS Point 45+ at the top end of the Hospital Authority pharmacist career ladder.

The HA also has dedicated **clinical pharmacy specialty tracks** in oncology, infectious diseases, anticoagulation, total parenteral nutrition, and ambulatory care.

### 6.2 Department of Health and government

The Department of Health employs Pharmacists within the **Drug Office** (regulatory affairs, GMP inspection, clinical-trial certification) and the **Government Pharmacist** grade. Pay broadly tracks the Hospital Authority's MPS pegging. The Drug Office pathway is typically chosen by graduates with an interest in regulatory science and pharmaceutical law rather than direct patient care.

### 6.3 Community pharmacy

Major community-pharmacy chains — Mannings, Watsons, the Hospital Authority Drug Formulary affiliated pharmacies, and the smaller registered-pharmacy operators — recruit BPharm graduates as **store pharmacists** at starting salaries of around **HK$45,000 – HK$55,000 / month**, often with retention bonuses to compensate for the salary gap with the Hospital Authority. Pharmacist-in-charge roles at flagship outlets reach HK$65,000+ within a few years.

The community-pharmacy sector is set to grow further as Hong Kong rolls out the **Primary Healthcare Blueprint** and the **District Health Centre** scheme, both of which assume a larger role for community pharmacists in chronic-disease management and minor ailment counselling.

### 6.4 Industry and other sectors

Beyond hospital and community practice, BPharm graduates also enter:

- **Pharmaceutical industry**: Regulatory affairs, medical affairs, drug safety/pharmacovigilance, and clinical research at the Hong Kong offices of multinational pharmaceutical firms.
- **Academia and research**: PhD pathways at HKU, CUHK, and overseas, often via the Hong Kong PhD Fellowship Scheme.
- **Government and NGOs**: Department of Health, Hospital Authority Head Office, Consumer Council, and HK Pharmacy Council secretariat.

Effectively all BPharm graduates are placed in a pharmacy-related role within months of graduation. Hong Kong has been classified as having a chronic pharmacist shortage by Hospital Authority workforce reviews for over a decade.

## 7. Overseas registration pathways

A Hong Kong BPharm degree is well-recognised internationally, but no jurisdiction grants automatic mutual recognition — every country requires additional examinations or supervised practice.

### 7.1 United Kingdom — General Pharmaceutical Council (GPhC)

The GPhC requires non-UK pharmacy graduates to complete the **Overseas Pharmacist Assessment Programme (OSPAP)** — a one-year postgraduate diploma at an accredited UK university — followed by the standard 52-week pre-registration training (Foundation Training Year) and the **GPhC Registration Assessment**. Total time-to-licence for a Hong Kong BPharm graduate is typically 2–3 years from arrival in the UK.

### 7.2 Australia — Australian Pharmacy Council (APC)

The APC operates a competency-based pathway. Hong Kong BPharm graduates apply for **Skills Assessment**, then complete an Australian internship (around 1,824 hours) under a registered preceptor, sit the **Pharmacy Board of Australia oral and written examinations**, and then register with **AHPRA**. Time-to-licence is around 1.5–2 years.

### 7.3 Canada — Pharmacy Examining Board of Canada (PEBC)

The PEBC operates an evaluation pathway that includes the **Document Evaluation**, **Evaluating Examination**, **Qualifying Examination Part I (MCQ) and Part II (OSCE)**, plus structured practical training (length varies by province). Provincial regulators (e.g. OCP in Ontario) layer their own jurisprudence examinations on top. Time-to-licence is typically 2–4 years.

### 7.4 United States — NABP

US pharmacy is now a doctoral-entry profession (PharmD). A Hong Kong BPharm holder applies to the **NABP FPGEC** for the Foreign Pharmacy Graduate Equivalency Certificate, then sits the **FPGEE** and **TOEFL iBT**, completes US internship hours, and takes the **NAPLEX** plus state-specific MPJE jurisprudence exam. Most US states still effectively expect a PharmD for clinical roles, so many Hong Kong graduates aiming at the US instead go via a US PharmD bridge programme.

### 7.5 Singapore — Singapore Pharmacy Council (SPC)

The SPC accredits selected overseas pharmacy programmes and historically has been receptive to HKU and CUHK BPharm holders, who must still complete a Singapore pre-registration training programme and sit the SPC's registration assessments. Time-to-licence is around 1–1.5 years.

### 7.6 Mainland China

Mainland China runs its own **Licensed Pharmacist** examination (执业药师). A Hong Kong BPharm graduate planning to practise across the border typically sits the mainland licensing examination, which is conducted in Chinese, and registers via the relevant provincial pharmaceutical administration. Career mobility into the Greater Bay Area is increasingly common, and CUHK Shenzhen has been signalling closer cross-boundary pharmacy collaboration.

## 8. HKU vs CUHK — how to choose

| Dimension | HKU JS6494 | CUHK JS4525 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Teaching language | Predominantly English | Predominantly English |
| Hospital base | Queen Mary, Gleneagles HK | Prince of Wales Hospital |
| Class size | ~35 | ~30 |
| Strengths | Drug discovery, pharmaceutical chemistry, longer-established department, deep links to Queen Mary | Clinical pharmacy emphasis, integrated biomedical campus, strong community-pharmacy linkages |
| Geography | Pok Fu Lam / Sassoon Road | Sha Tin |
| First-year experience | Common Core HKU general education; bigger broad-based campus feel | Faculty of Medicine common first year; tighter cohort within a focused medical campus |

Neither programme is "better" in absolute terms — both are PPBHK-accredited, both produce graduates who fully populate the Hospital Authority pharmacy departments, and both lead to identical professional registration. The honest practical questions for a 2026 candidate are:

1. **Which campus geography fits your home?** Sha Tin vs Pok Fu Lam is a real one-hour-a-day commute difference for many students.
2. **Do you prefer a more discovery-and-chemistry feel (HKU) or a more clinical-faculty feel (CUHK)?**
3. **Which interview format do you perform better in?** Sit a mock interview with both styles before locking your Band A choice.

Most Band A applicants pick one as Band A1 and the other as A2 — that combination protects against single-school interview variance and is the standard strategy among 5\*\* DSE candidates.

## 9. Application timeline for 2026 entry

| Date (approx.) | Action |
| --- | --- |
| Sep – early Dec 2025 | Open JUPAS account, submit programme choices |
| 4 Dec 2025 (deadline) | JUPAS Programme Choices initial deadline |
| Late Apr – mid May 2026 | DSE examinations |
| Late May 2026 (deadline) | JUPAS Programme Choices final amendment deadline |
| Mid-Jul 2026 | DSE results released |
| Late Jul 2026 | JUPAS Main Round offers; HKU and CUHK BPharm interviews held |
| Early Aug 2026 | Final pharmacy offers issued |
| Sep 2026 | Programme commences |

Both faculties typically interview in late July, immediately after results release. Block out the week after results day for interview preparation — it is too late to start preparing then if you have not already practised.

## 10. Final notes — is BPharm right for you?

Pharmacy in Hong Kong is a **very stable, very specialised** career. The trade-off is that the day-to-day work is more focused than medicine — you will not run a clinic and you will not perform surgery — but you will own the medication-safety and counselling layer of patient care, and you will build deep expertise in pharmacotherapy. Public-sector pharmacist hours are also dramatically more humane than HA medical officer rotations.

If you enjoy chemistry and biology equally, want a healthcare profession with a clear registration pathway and clear salary scale, and value work-life balance over the prestige of an MBBS letterhead, BPharm is a strong Band A choice for 2026. With only 65 places between HKU and CUHK, it is selective — but the funnel is narrower than medicine and the rewards (in employment certainty and overseas mobility) compare favourably.

For a deeper look at the JUPAS scoring formulas referenced above, see our [JUPAS scoring and calculation complete guide](/en/admission/jupas-scoring-and-calculation-complete-guide-2026.html). For comparison with other healthcare degrees in Hong Kong, see our complete guides to [Nursing](/en/majors/hong-kong-nursing-bachelor-degree-complete-guide-2026.html), [Physiotherapy](/en/majors/hong-kong-physiotherapy-bachelor-polyu-complete-guide-2026.html), [Dental Surgery](/en/majors/hong-kong-dental-surgery-bachelor-hku-complete-guide-2026.html), and [Speech-Language Pathology](/en/majors/hong-kong-speech-language-pathology-bachelor-hku-complete-guide-2026.html).
