title: "Italy Pathway for DSE Students: Marco Polo, English-Taught Bachelor's, Universitaly and Post-Study Residence Permit Guide 2026"
description: "Complete 2026 guide for Hong Kong DSE students applying to Italian public universities — Marco Polo programme context, English-taught bachelor's degrees, Universitaly pre-enrolment, tuition fees, visa Type D, residence permit and the 12-month post-graduation job-seeking permit."
lang: en
category: overseas
date: 2026-05-03
author: DSE Knowledge Hub Editorial Team
---

Italy is one of Europe's most underrated study destinations for Hong Kong DSE students. The country hosts some of the oldest universities in the world (Bologna was founded in 1088), public tuition is dramatically lower than in the UK or US, and a growing share of bachelor's programmes are now delivered entirely in English. For DSE students who want a continental European experience without the German numerus clausus or the French dossier marathon, Italy offers a comparatively flexible path — provided you understand the difference between the Marco Polo channel, the regular international track, and the Universitaly pre-enrolment system.

This guide walks through the full 2026 application cycle: what Marco Polo actually is (and why most HK DSE students should not use it), how DSE results map to admission requirements, the Universitaly portal, tuition and ISEE-based fee discounts, the visa Type D and residence permit process, work rights during studies, and the 12-month post-graduation job-seeking permit that lets you stay in Italy to find work.

## Why Italy for DSE students

The case for Italy rests on four pillars.

**Cost.** Public university tuition typically ranges from €300 to €4,000 per academic year, and many students from low- and middle-income households pay the floor of that range after submitting an ISEE-Parificato (income equivalent) declaration. Compared to £21,000–£38,000 a year at a UK Russell Group university, the savings over a three-year bachelor's degree are substantial.

**English-taught programmes.** While Italian-language degrees still dominate the catalogue, the number of fully English-taught bachelor's (Lauree Triennali) has grown sharply over the past decade. Politecnico di Milano, Bocconi, Sapienza Università di Roma, Università di Bologna, Politecnico di Torino, Università di Padova and Università di Trento all run multiple English-medium undergraduate degrees in business, engineering, computer science, design, economics and international relations.

**Schengen mobility and lifestyle.** A residence permit issued in Italy gives you Schengen-area travel rights, which makes weekend trips, internships abroad and Erasmus+ exchanges straightforward.

**Post-study options.** Italy offers a 12-month residence permit for graduates to look for work, which can then be converted into a work permit when you find an employer.

The trade-offs are real: bureaucracy is heavy, the job market for non-Italian speakers is narrower than in the Netherlands or Germany, and salary levels in Italy are below the EU average. Italy is a strong choice for students who genuinely want to learn Italian and integrate locally, or who plan to use Italy as a low-cost EU launchpad.

## Marco Polo vs the regular international track

Most online articles aimed at Chinese students describe the **Marco Polo programme** as the standard route into Italian universities. For Hong Kong DSE students, the picture is more nuanced.

Marco Polo is a bilateral agreement signed in 2006 between the Italian and Chinese (PRC) governments specifically to facilitate Chinese students entering Italian universities. Two features matter:

1. **It is designed for PRC nationals.** Hong Kong SAR passport holders applying with DSE results are processed through the standard non-EU international student channel, not Marco Polo, even though the application portal (Universitaly) is the same.
2. **Marco Polo students must enrol in Italian-taught degrees.** Marco Polo includes a mandatory pre-academic year of intensive Italian language study (usually 10–11 months at B1/B2 level). If you intend to study in English, Marco Polo is not the right channel — you apply directly as a regular international (non-EU) student to the English-taught programme of your choice.

In practice, almost all HK DSE students choose **the regular international track with English-taught programmes**. Marco Polo only becomes relevant if you specifically want an Italian-taught degree and need a structured language preparation year — and even then, HK candidates would need to verify whether the host university extends the Marco Polo framework to non-PRC applicants on a case-by-case basis.

## DSE entry requirements

Italian public universities recognise the HKDSE as a valid secondary school qualification. Typical baseline requirements:

- **Minimum subjects.** At least four DSE subjects, including Chinese Language, English Language, Mathematics, and Liberal Studies / Citizenship and Social Development. Some universities also require at least one elective.
- **Minimum grades.** Most universities require a minimum of Level 3 in each core subject and Level 3 in two electives. More selective programmes (Bocconi, Politecnico di Milano engineering and design) may expect Level 4 or Level 5 in subjects relevant to the programme.
- **English proficiency.** For English-taught programmes, expect IELTS 6.0–6.5 overall (Bocconi: IELTS 6.5; Politecnico di Milano: IELTS 6.0 or TOEFL iBT 78). DSE English Level 4 is sometimes accepted in lieu of IELTS, but always confirm with the specific admissions office because policies vary by institution.
- **Mathematics for STEM.** STEM programmes typically require a recognised mathematics qualification. Most accept DSE Mathematics Compulsory Part at Level 4 or above; some programmes require an entrance test (TOLC) administered by CISIA.
- **Portfolio for design/architecture.** Politecnico di Milano's design school and IUAV Venezia require a portfolio and may interview candidates.

DSE results must be submitted via the official HKEAA transcript service to the Italian university's admissions office, and a **Dichiarazione di Valore (DoV)** — a declaration of equivalence issued by the Italian Consulate-General in Hong Kong — is normally required. CIMEA Diplome attestation is increasingly accepted as an alternative to the DoV, and some universities now process equivalence internally.

## The Universitaly pre-enrolment portal

Universitaly (universitaly.it) is the official MIUR portal through which all non-EU candidates submit their pre-enrolment application before applying for a visa. The flow is:

1. Receive a conditional or unconditional offer from your chosen Italian university (each university runs its own admissions cycle, often opening in November and closing between March and June 2026 for September 2026 entry).
2. Log into Universitaly and submit a pre-enrolment application linked to that offer, selecting the **regular international student** option (not Marco Polo) and the chosen programme.
3. The university validates your pre-enrolment online; the Italian Consulate-General in Hong Kong then receives your file and invites you for the visa interview.
4. Submit your visa application at the Consulate-General with the supporting documents (offer letter, DoV/CIMEA, proof of accommodation, financial means, health insurance).

Universitaly pre-enrolment for the 2026/2027 academic year typically opens in spring 2026 and closes in mid-July 2026 for most universities, though specific deadlines vary by institution. Start early: the bottleneck is almost never the academic decision — it is the consular appointment slot.

## Tuition fees, ISEE and scholarships

Italian public university tuition is income-tested through the **ISEE** (Indicatore della Situazione Economica Equivalente). For non-EU students, an ISEE-Parificato is calculated by an Italian patronato (welfare assistance office) based on documented family income and assets in Hong Kong.

Indicative annual tuition at major public universities for 2026/2027:

- **Sapienza Roma:** €0–€3,000 (means-tested), with the lowest band reserved for ISEE under €23,000.
- **Università di Bologna:** €0–€3,500 depending on ISEE and programme.
- **Politecnico di Milano:** €900–€4,000.
- **Università di Padova:** €0–€2,800.
- **Bocconi (private):** approximately €16,000–€17,000 — Bocconi is private and charges higher fees; generous merit scholarships available.

Key scholarships for HK DSE students:

- **DSU regional scholarships** (e.g. ER-GO in Emilia-Romagna, EDISU in Piemonte, LazioDisco in Lazio) — full tuition waiver plus a stipend of €5,000–€7,000 for low-income international students who meet academic milestones.
- **MAECI scholarships** from the Italian Ministry of Foreign Affairs — competitive scholarships for international students, awarded for 6 to 9 months.
- **University-specific merit awards** — Bocconi, Bologna and Politecnico di Milano all offer entrance scholarships of €6,000–€12,000 for top international applicants.

Always submit the ISEE-Parificato application as early as possible after enrolment; missing the deadline means you will be charged the maximum tuition band for that year regardless of family income.

## Visa Type D and the residence permit

Once your pre-enrolment is validated, apply for a **Visto per Studio Tipo D (long-stay study visa)** at the Italian Consulate-General in Hong Kong. Required documents typically include:

- Passport valid at least three months beyond intended stay
- Confirmed offer and Universitaly pre-enrolment receipt
- Proof of accommodation in Italy
- Proof of financial means (approximately €6,500–€7,000 per year)
- Health insurance valid in Italy and Schengen
- Round-trip flight booking and travel insurance
- DoV or CIMEA certificate

Within **8 working days of arrival in Italy**, you must apply for the **permesso di soggiorno per studio** (study residence permit) at the local post office (sportello amici dell'immigrazione) using the kit giallo. You will receive a receipt, attend a fingerprinting appointment at the Questura, and the physical permit arrives within 1–4 months. Keep the receipt safe — it is your legal proof of regular stay until the permit is issued.

The study residence permit must be renewed annually before expiry, with proof of academic progress (a minimum number of ECTS credits earned in the previous year, set by each university).

## Working during studies

Holders of the study residence permit are entitled to work **up to 20 hours per week during term** and **up to 40 hours per week during academic holidays**, capped at 1,040 hours per calendar year. Common student jobs in Italy include tutoring, hospitality, retail and English-language teaching assistance. Wages are modest — €7–€10 per hour is typical outside major cities, slightly higher in Milan and Rome — so part-time work covers small living expenses but rarely tuition.

Internships (tirocini) are widely available and often integrated into the curriculum. Paid internships with companies like Ferrari, Pirelli, Eni and Generali are competitive but accessible to international students with strong academic records and basic Italian.

## Post-graduation: the 12-month job-seeking residence permit

After completing your degree, Italy allows you to convert your study permit into a **permesso di soggiorno per attesa occupazione** (residence permit awaiting employment), which gives you up to 12 months in Italy to find work matching your qualifications. Key conditions:

- The degree must be from a MIUR-recognised Italian institution (all public universities and most accredited private universities qualify).
- You must register with the local Centro per l'Impiego (employment centre) within the application window.
- You must demonstrate financial means above the social allowance threshold (approximately €6,000 per year) and have valid health insurance.
- The permit is generally **non-renewable**; you have one year to convert to a work permit through an employer's Nulla Osta application.

Once you secure a job offer, your employer files a Nulla Osta (work authorisation) request, which converts your permit to a **permesso di soggiorno per lavoro subordinato**. After five years of legal residence in Italy (study years count partially toward this total under recent reforms), you may apply for **EU long-term residence**; after ten years of continuous legal residence, you may apply for **Italian citizenship**.

For HK DSE graduates planning to stay in Italy, the realistic strategy is:

1. **Learn Italian.** Even at English-taught programmes, conversational Italian (B1+) dramatically expands the job market beyond multinationals and tourism.
2. **Choose a sector with demand for English speakers.** Tech (Milan and Turin), fashion (Milan and Florence), automotive (Modena/Bologna), tourism management, and international business consulting are the strongest entry points.
3. **Use the university career service.** Most major Italian universities have dedicated career services with corporate relationships — Bocconi and Politecnico di Milano are particularly strong on graduate placement.

## Strengths and challenges, summarised

**Strengths**

- Public tuition often under €3,000/year, with ISEE-based discounts available
- Strong English-taught bachelor's catalogue at top universities
- Schengen mobility and Erasmus+ access during studies
- 12-month post-study residence permit with conversion path to work permit and eventual EU long-term residence
- Lower cost of living than UK, France or Netherlands in most cities outside Milan and Rome

**Challenges**

- Heavy bureaucracy: DoV/CIMEA, codice fiscale, permesso di soggiorno, ISEE-Parificato, annual permit renewals
- Job market outside multinationals expects working Italian
- Salary levels below EU average (entry-level €25,000–€32,000)
- Marco Polo branding can be misleading for HK students — the regular international track is what most DSE candidates should use

## Action checklist for the 2026/2027 cycle

1. **By September 2025:** shortlist 4–6 programmes, confirm DSE/IELTS requirements with each admissions office in writing.
2. **November 2025 – March 2026:** submit university applications (deadlines vary; Bocconi and Politecnico di Milano open earliest).
3. **After receiving offers (March–May 2026):** complete Universitaly pre-enrolment as a regular international student.
4. **April–June 2026:** request DoV from the Italian Consulate-General in Hong Kong, or apply for a CIMEA Diplome attestation.
5. **June–July 2026:** book the visa appointment at the Consulate-General, prepare financial proof and accommodation booking.
6. **August–September 2026:** travel to Italy, apply for the codice fiscale and submit the kit giallo for the residence permit within 8 working days of arrival.
7. **October 2026 onwards:** submit ISEE-Parificato application via an Italian patronato to lock in the lowest tuition band.

Italy rewards students who plan early and accept a learning curve on bureaucracy. The combination of low tuition, English-taught programmes, Schengen mobility and a structured post-study work pathway makes it one of the most cost-effective European destinations for HK DSE graduates willing to invest in the Italian context.

# Japan University Pathway for DSE Students: EJU, English-Taught Programmes, MEXT Scholarship and Visa Guide 2026

Japan has quietly become one of the most attractive overseas destinations for Hong Kong DSE graduates. National university tuition is roughly HK$30,000 a year — cheaper than local self-financed degrees in Hong Kong. English-taught programmes at Waseda, Keio, Sophia, and Tokyo have grown rapidly. Post-graduation work visas are generous, and the salary outlook in Tokyo for bilingual graduates is competitive with Singapore. Yet the application path is unfamiliar to most DSE students — there are two parallel admission systems (Japanese-medium via EJU, English-medium via direct application), and the documentation sits somewhere between the UCAS-style system and the US essay-driven model.

This guide breaks down everything a DSE student needs: the two application tracks, the EJU exam, top English-taught programmes, MEXT and JASSO scholarships, costs, visa procedure, and what happens after graduation.

## The Two Admission Tracks

Japanese universities admit international undergraduates through two largely separate channels. Choose one before you build your timeline — they have different exams, different deadlines, and different language requirements.

**Track 1: Japanese-medium degree (via EJU).** This is the traditional path. You sit the Examination for Japanese University Admission for International Students (EJU), and most universities then call you for a written test, interview, or both. Instruction is in Japanese, so you typically need JLPT N2 or above by enrolment. Cheapest option (especially at national universities), broadest programme choice, and strongest integration into Japanese society — but the language barrier is real.

**Track 2: English-medium degree (direct application).** A growing list of programmes — most famously Waseda's School of International Liberal Studies (SILS), Keio's PEARL and GIGA, Sophia's FLA, Tokyo's PEAK, Kyoto's iUP, and Osaka's Human Sciences — teach the entire degree in English. You apply directly with TOEFL/IELTS, SAT, transcripts, essays, and reference letters, much like a US application. No Japanese language requirement at entry (though courses are often available alongside the degree). More expensive, but accessible to DSE students with no Japanese background.

Most DSE students should target Track 2 unless they have already reached JLPT N3 by Form 6, in which case Track 1 with another year of language school becomes realistic.

## Track 1: The EJU Exam Explained

The EJU is run by the Japan Student Services Organization (JASSO) twice a year — June and November — at exam centres including Hong Kong. The 2026 second session application window is 6–30 July, with the test itself in November. The test is structured around four subjects:

- **Japanese as a Foreign Language** (compulsory for all Japanese-medium applicants; tests reading, listening, listening-reading, and writing)
- **Science** (Physics, Chemistry, Biology — choose two; required for science/engineering programmes)
- **Japan and the World** (a social-studies paper covering Japanese geography, history, politics, economics, and contemporary issues; required for arts/humanities/social-science programmes)
- **Mathematics** (Course 1 for arts/humanities, Course 2 for science/engineering)

Subjects other than Japanese can be sat in either Japanese or English, which sounds helpful but is misleading: nearly every selective Japanese-medium programme requires you to sit them in Japanese, because the receiving department needs evidence you can study in Japanese. Revised syllabuses for Science, Japan and the World, and Mathematics apply from the 2026 first session, so use up-to-date past papers from the JASSO website rather than older Chinese-language prep books.

After the EJU, top universities (Tokyo, Kyoto, Osaka, Hitotsubashi, Tsukuba) hold a second-stage internal exam and interview between January and March. This is where competition really happens — EJU scores get you into the pool, but the secondary screening decides the outcome.

A practical timeline for a DSE student going Track 1 is two years: complete DSE in May, enrol in a Japanese language school (語学学校) in Tokyo or Osaka in October, sit JLPT N3 in December and N2 the following July, sit EJU in June and November of that gap year, then apply to universities for an April or September entry the year after.

## Track 2: English-Taught Undergraduate Programmes

The English-medium track has expanded enormously over the past decade. Below are the programmes most relevant for DSE students.

**Waseda University — School of International Liberal Studies (SILS).** Waseda's flagship English-taught programme, with around 600 international students. Liberal-arts curriculum, strong in international relations, business, and cultural studies. Application requires SAT or equivalent, TOEFL 95+ or IELTS 7.0+, two recommendation letters, and an essay. Annual tuition around ¥1.6m (~HK$83,000). Two intakes per year (April and September).

**Keio University — PEARL (Economics) and GIGA (Policy Management / Environment).** Keio is Japan's most prestigious private university for business and economics. PEARL is the English-taught Economics degree at Mita campus. GIGA programmes sit at the Shonan Fujisawa campus and lean toward technology, policy, and design. Tuition ¥1.5–1.7m. SAT or A-Levels accepted; TOEFL 90+ or IELTS 7.0+.

**Sophia University — Faculty of Liberal Arts (FLA).** Catholic university in central Tokyo. FLA is one of Japan's oldest English-taught programmes, with majors in international business, social studies, and comparative culture. Smaller and more pastoral than Waseda. Tuition ~¥1.4m.

**University of Tokyo — PEAK (Programs in English at Komaba).** Two tracks: International Programme on Japan in East Asia, and International Programme on Environmental Sciences. Highly selective — comparable to HKU Medicine in admit rate. SAT 1450+, TOEFL 100+, two strong references, research-flavoured personal statement. As a national university, tuition is only ¥535,800 (~HK$28,000) per year. September intake.

**Kyoto University — iUP (International Undergraduate Program).** Six-month preparatory term followed by a regular Japanese-medium degree, with strong scholarship support (full tuition waiver plus monthly stipend for ~10 students per cycle). Suits academically strong DSE students willing to learn Japanese intensively in their first year. National university tuition.

**Other strong options.** Osaka University Human Sciences (English degree), Akita International University (full-English liberal arts in regional Japan, generous scholarships), Ritsumeikan APU in Beppu (truly bilingual campus, ~50% international students), Tohoku University FGL (science and engineering in English), Nagoya University G30 programmes (engineering, science, humanities).

Application materials for Track 2 typically include: high school transcript (DSE predicted grades for early rounds, actual results after July), DSE certificate or HKEAA result slip, TOEFL/IELTS score, SAT or ACT for top universities, two reference letters, a personal statement of 800–1,500 words, and sometimes a recorded video interview. Deadlines cluster between October and February for the September intake.

## DSE Grade Conversion and Subject Requirements

Most Japanese universities accept the HKDSE as a recognised secondary qualification without needing additional foundation years. There is no fixed conversion, but a working benchmark from past admits:

- **Top tier (Tokyo PEAK, Kyoto iUP, Waseda SILS competitive majors):** 5*5* in core plus 5* in two electives, equivalent to Best Five 32–35.
- **Selective private universities (Keio PEARL, Sophia FLA, Waseda SILS standard):** Best Five 25–30, with strong English (Level 5 or above) and consistent humanities/economics electives.
- **Regional national universities and APU-style programmes:** Best Five 20–24 with English Level 4 and a clear motivation letter.

Mathematics M1/M2 is a strong signal for economics, engineering, and PEAK applications. For SILS and FLA, depth in English Language and a humanities elective (History, Geography, Economics, Liberal Studies/Citizenship) matters more than the science subjects.

## MEXT and JASSO Scholarships

Japan funds international students more generously than most assume. The two main schemes for DSE graduates are:

**MEXT Scholarship (Embassy Recommendation).** Run by Japan's Ministry of Education through the Consulate-General of Japan in Hong Kong, administered in partnership with the Hong Kong Working Family and Student Financial Assistance Agency (WFSFAA). Covers full tuition, return airfare, and a monthly stipend of around ¥117,000 for undergraduates. Eligibility: HKID and HKSAR passport holder, born on or after 2 April 2001, completion of Form 6, with strong academic results. Application is once a year (typically May–June for the following April entry), followed by a written test and interview. Highly competitive — usually fewer than ten Hong Kong undergraduates selected per year — but worth attempting.

**JASSO Honors Scholarship.** ¥48,000 per month for international students already enrolled in Japan, awarded after the first year based on academic performance. Most international students at major universities receive this for at least part of their degree.

**University-specific scholarships.** Waseda, Keio, Sophia, APU, Akita International, and most national universities run additional tuition-waiver and stipend programmes. APU in particular awards 30%, 50%, 65%, 80%, or 100% tuition waivers automatically based on application strength — no separate application required.

A student who lands MEXT effectively pays nothing for the degree. A student who lands a 50% APU waiver plus JASSO Honors brings the total cost close to studying at a self-financed Hong Kong programme.

## Costs and Cost-of-Living

Realistic cost ranges for 2026 entry, based on JASSO and consulate guidance:

**National universities (Tokyo, Kyoto, Osaka, Tohoku, Nagoya, etc.).** Tuition ¥535,800/year (~HK$28,000). Add admission fee ¥282,000 in the first year. Total tuition over four years: ~HK$155,000.

**Private universities (Waseda, Keio, Sophia, Rikkyo, ICU).** Tuition ¥1.4–1.7m/year (~HK$73,000–88,000). Engineering and medicine higher.

**Living costs.** Tokyo: ¥120,000–180,000/month all-in for student dorm, food, transport, and National Health Insurance. Kyoto, Osaka, Nagoya: ¥90,000–130,000/month. Regional cities (Sendai, Fukuoka, Beppu): ¥70,000–100,000/month. National Health Insurance for students is heavily subsidised at ¥1,500–2,000 per month.

**Total four-year budget.** A DSE student at a national university with a dorm room in a regional city: HK$500,000–650,000 all-in. At a Tokyo private university with no scholarship: HK$1.0–1.3m. Considerably cheaper than the UK (£140,000+) or US (US$280,000+) for a comparable academic profile.

## Student Visa and Certificate of Eligibility

Once you have an unconditional offer, the university applies on your behalf for a Certificate of Eligibility (CoE) from the Japanese immigration authority. Processing takes one to three months — apply early. Once the CoE arrives, you submit it with your passport, application form, photo, and offer letter to the Consulate-General of Japan in Hong Kong (visa fee ¥3,000–6,000) for the actual student visa, which normally takes 5–7 working days.

For 2026, financial proof has been tightened: applicants are expected to show a consistent banking history (typically three to six months of statements) demonstrating funds of at least ¥2,000,000 (~HK$104,000), or equivalent sponsor letters and fixed deposit certificates. Spotty bank statements with last-minute large deposits are flagged.

The student visa permits up to 28 hours per week of part-time work once you obtain a "permission to engage in activity other than that permitted under the status of residence previously granted" stamp at immigration on arrival. Hourly wages of ¥1,100–1,300 are typical in Tokyo, enough to offset food and transport but not tuition.

## After Graduation: Job-Hunting and Visa Conversion

Japan's "shukatsu" (job-hunting) cycle starts in March of your third year and typically ends with informal offers in spring of your fourth year. Major employers — banks, trading houses, consulting firms, tech — recruit international students aggressively, especially those with bilingual ability. Starting salaries for new graduates are ¥250,000–350,000/month (~HK$13,000–18,000), lower than Hong Kong nominally but with strong career progression and lower cost of living.

After graduation, you can convert your student visa to a "Designated Activities" visa for up to one year of continued job-hunting if needed, then to an "Engineer/Specialist in Humanities/International Services" working visa once you have an offer. After ten years of residence (with five on a working visa), permanent residence becomes available; the highly skilled professional track can shorten this to as little as one year.

For a DSE student weighing pathways, Japan offers something distinctive: a top-30 global academic system, low tuition by developed-country standards, a clear post-graduation work pipeline, and a culture that — while different from Hong Kong — is geographically close (four hours by flight) and increasingly accessible in English. The two-track system rewards early planning. Decide which track fits, build the right test portfolio (EJU vs SAT/TOEFL), and begin researching specific programmes in Form 5 rather than after results day.

# Korea University Pathway for DSE Students: TOPIK, English-Taught Programmes, GKS Scholarship and D-2 Visa Guide 2026

Korea has rapidly climbed the wishlist of Hong Kong DSE graduates over the last five years. The K-culture wave is part of it, but the practical case is stronger: tuition at top private universities like Yonsei or Korea University runs roughly HK$60,000–90,000 per year, English-taught degree programmes have multiplied at the SKY universities (Seoul National, Korea, Yonsei), the Global Korea Scholarship covers full tuition plus a stipend, and the post-graduation D-10 job-seeking visa lets you stay on for up to two years to find work. From 2025 onward the HKEAA added Korean as a Category B Other Language subject in the DSE — a signal that the bilateral student pipeline is now formally recognised.

This guide walks through both application tracks (English-medium and Korean-medium), TOPIK requirements, the SKY universities and rising alternatives, the GKS scholarship process, costs, the D-2 visa, and what happens after graduation.

## The two application tracks

Korean universities admit international undergraduates through a dedicated *foreign student* track, typically called 외국인특별전형 (foreign student special admission). The simplifying detail for DSE students: this track does not compete against Korean nationals taking the Suneung (CSAT) — you are evaluated on your high school record and language proficiency only.

There are then two routes within that track:

**Korean-medium degrees** — the bulk of programmes, taught entirely in Korean. You will need a TOPIK score (usually Level 3 or 4 minimum, Level 5 or 6 for competitive majors) by application time, or you can sometimes be conditionally admitted and complete a year at the university's Korean Language Centre first.

**English-medium degrees (English-Taught Programmes, ETP)** — a smaller but high-quality set of programmes where instruction is in English. You submit IELTS or TOEFL instead of TOPIK. Most ETPs sit in business, international studies, engineering, and life sciences.

Pick the track first, because it dictates your two-year preparation plan. If you have any meaningful Korean already, the Korean-medium track opens vastly more programmes; if you don't, the ETP track is realistic but narrower.

## Top universities and what they want

### The SKY universities

**Seoul National University (SNU)** — the prestige choice and the hardest to enter. Foreign student admission is highly competitive, with most applicants holding strong AP / IB / A-Level results in addition to DSE. For Korean-medium programmes, expect to need TOPIK Level 5–6 in practice (though Level 3 is the formal minimum for some colleges). English-taught options are limited to a handful of programmes, including the College of Liberal Studies and parts of the College of Engineering and Business.

**Korea University (KU)** — strong international intake and a well-developed Division of International Studies (DIS) taught entirely in English. KU's foreign student track typically requires TOPIK Level 4 or higher for Korean-medium admission (Level 3 minimum, but Level 4 is more competitive). The Korea University Business School (KUBS) and DIS are the two flagship English-taught entry points.

**Yonsei University** — runs the Underwood International College (UIC), one of the largest English-taught liberal arts programmes in Asia. UIC has multiple admission rounds, accepts DSE results directly, and has a broad curriculum spanning humanities, social sciences, life sciences, and quantitative economics. Outside UIC, Yonsei's main campus also offers the foreign student track for Korean-medium degrees.

### Strong second-tier options

**Sungkyunkwan University (SKKU)** — top-ranked in engineering and business, partnered with Samsung. Has substantial English-taught content in business, computing, and natural sciences.

**Hanyang University** — engineering powerhouse, strong industry links, generous foreign student scholarships.

**Ewha Womans University** — long-standing reputation, large international division (Scranton College and Division of International Studies), generous needs-based aid.

**KAIST and POSTECH** — Korea's MIT and Caltech equivalents. KAIST teaches almost everything in English at undergraduate level and is essentially free for admitted international students through the KAIST International Scholarship. Highly selective in mathematics, physics, and engineering; expect strong DSE Maths Extended Module results to be persuasive.

**Chung-Ang, Konkuk, Kyung Hee, Hongik** — solid mid-tier private universities, more accessible TOPIK thresholds, popular with Hong Kong students aiming for media, design, hospitality, or arts programmes.

## TOPIK: what level and when

The TOPIK (Test of Proficiency in Korean) has six levels divided into two papers:

- **TOPIK I** — covers Levels 1–2 (beginner). Not enough for degree admission.
- **TOPIK II** — covers Levels 3–6. Level 3 is conversational; Level 6 is near-native.

For most foreign student admissions, the formal minimum is TOPIK Level 3, with Level 4 considered competitive and Level 5–6 expected for top programmes in humanities, law, or business at SKY-level universities. Some universities accept conditional admission with Level 2 if you commit to a year at their Korean Language Centre before starting your degree — useful if your Korean isn't there yet but you want to lock in a place.

Test logistics: TOPIK is held roughly six times a year, with sessions in Hong Kong (usually Hong Kong Korean International School or designated centres). Register through the official TOPIK Hong Kong portal at least two months ahead. Results take about a month. Build your timeline so you have a usable score *before* the application deadline, not after — universities don't wait.

If you're starting from zero in S5, a realistic path is one year of Korean classes (Sejong Institute, Korean Cultural Centre, or self-study) to reach Level 2, then intensive prep through S6 to push to Level 3 or 4 before final-year applications. Aiming higher than Level 4 from a cold start in two years is ambitious but feasible if you can do a summer language course in Korea between S5 and S6.

## English-taught route: IELTS, TOEFL and what's substitutable

For ETP admissions, most universities ask for one of:

- IELTS 6.0–6.5 (some flagship programmes ask 7.0)
- TOEFL iBT 79–90
- DSE English Language Level 4 or 5 — increasingly accepted in lieu of IELTS at Korea University, Yonsei UIC, and several others, but always check the current admission guide for your target programme.

DSE English at Level 5 typically maps to IELTS 6.5–7.0 for these admission purposes. If your DSE English is solid, you may not need to sit IELTS at all — but confirm this in writing before relying on it.

## Application timing

Korean universities have two intakes:

- **Spring intake** — March start. Applications open from August/September of the previous year and close around October–November.
- **Fall intake** — September start. Applications open from March–April and close around May–June.

Most DSE students target the **Fall intake of the year they sit DSE** (apply March–June, results released July, start September). Some students with stronger overseas paperwork target the following Spring (extra prep time, but six months of gap to fill).

Many universities have multiple application rounds within an intake (Round 1 / Round 2 / Round 3) — earlier rounds usually have more places and slightly easier thresholds. If you're confident, apply early.

## Documents you'll need

The standard foreign student application bundle for Korean universities:

1. Online application form
2. DSE results (predicted grades for early-round applications, plus official statement of results when available — HKEAA can issue verified result statements)
3. Full secondary school transcripts (S4–S6, often with school stamp and a sealed-envelope certified version)
4. Certificate of Graduation or expected graduation letter
5. Language proficiency — TOPIK (Korean track) or IELTS/TOEFL/DSE English (English track)
6. Personal statement / Study plan (1–2 pages, in Korean or English depending on track)
7. Letter of recommendation (usually one from a teacher or principal)
8. Passport copy (yours and both parents')
9. Family relationship documents — proving both you and your parents are non-Korean citizens
10. Financial documents — bank statement, sponsor's income proof, often showing roughly USD 18,000–20,000 in liquid funds for one year
11. Application fee — around USD 80–130 per university

Note the *both parents non-Korean* requirement: if either parent holds Korean citizenship, you generally cannot apply through the foreign student track and must compete in the regular admission with Suneung. This is a hard rule at most universities.

## Global Korea Scholarship (GKS)

The GKS is the Korean government's flagship scholarship, fully funding 280 undergraduate students per year (2026 cycle) from 71 countries. Hong Kong is eligible.

**What it covers:**
- Full tuition (up to a generous cap)
- One year of Korean language training at a designated language institution before starting the degree
- Monthly stipend of around KRW 900,000 (~HK$5,400)
- Round-trip airfare
- Settlement and research allowances
- Korean medical insurance

**Headline 2026 eligibility:**
- Under 25 years old at time of entry (born after a cut-off date in 2001 for the 2026 cycle — verify against the current call)
- Completed or about to complete secondary school by 31 December 2025
- Top 20% of class, or CGPA above 80% on your school's scale
- Both you and your parents non-Korean citizens
- Sound health

**How to apply:** GKS undergraduate applications open through the Study in Korea website (studyinkorea.go.kr) typically in September of the year before entry. There are two tracks: *Embassy track* (apply via the Korean embassy or consulate in your country — Hong Kong applicants apply via the Consulate General of the Republic of Korea in Hong Kong) and *University track* (apply directly through a designated university). The embassy track has more flexibility; the university track is faster.

The GKS is highly competitive — more so than direct admission to most universities — but the financial package transforms the cost equation completely.

### Other scholarships worth chasing

- **University-internal foreign student scholarships** — almost every university (Korea, Yonsei, SNU, KAIST, Hanyang, etc.) offers tuition reductions of 30–100% based on academic merit. These are awarded automatically with admission at most schools; check each university's foreign student admission guide.
- **KAIST International Scholarship** — full tuition + stipend for admitted international undergraduates at KAIST.
- **Posco TJ Park Foundation Scholarship** — for Asian students; competitive.
- **Korean Government Self-Finance Scholarship** — partial support, lower bar than GKS.

## Costs: tuition and living

### Tuition (per year, 2026 estimates)

- **National universities (SNU, Pusan National, KAIST, etc.)** — KRW 4,000,000–10,000,000 (~HK$23,000–58,000) for humanities/social sciences; engineering and natural sciences higher.
- **Private universities (Yonsei, Korea, SKKU, Hanyang)** — KRW 8,000,000–16,000,000 (~HK$46,000–93,000) for most programmes; medical and dental significantly higher and largely closed to foreigners.
- **English-taught flagship programmes** — typically priced at the higher end of the private university range.

For comparison, a self-financed local degree in Hong Kong runs roughly HK$120,000–180,000 a year — Korea is meaningfully cheaper even at private universities.

### Living costs in Seoul

Realistic monthly budget for a student living in Seoul:

- Accommodation: KRW 400,000–700,000 (~HK$2,300–4,100) for a goshiwon or shared one-room; on-campus dorm is cheaper at around KRW 200,000–400,000
- Food: KRW 300,000–450,000 (~HK$1,750–2,600)
- Transport: KRW 60,000 (~HK$350) for a transit pass
- National Health Insurance: KRW 40,000–55,000 (mandatory after six months)
- Phone, internet, laundry, social: KRW 200,000–300,000

Total roughly KRW 1,000,000–1,500,000 per month (~HK$5,800–8,700). Outside Seoul (Busan, Daejeon, Daegu), shave 20–30% off.

Annual all-in cost for a self-funded student at a private Seoul university: roughly HK$200,000–270,000 a year. With GKS or a major university scholarship, this can drop to nearly zero.

## D-2 student visa

Once you have an admission letter you apply for the **D-2 student visa** at the Consulate General of the Republic of Korea in Hong Kong.

**Requirements:**
- Standard Admission Letter from the Korean university
- Proof of financial capacity — at least KRW 20,000,000 (~HK$120,000) in your or sponsor's bank account, demonstrated through a recent bank certificate (some embassies want the funds parked for several months)
- Passport with at least six months remaining
- Visa application form, photo
- Application fee — around USD 80 (single entry) or USD 120 (multiple entry)
- Sometimes: chest X-ray (TB screening), depending on the year and programme

**Processing time:** typically 2–4 weeks. Apply at least six weeks before your intended departure; longer if you also need to finalise dormitory paperwork.

**Work rights on D-2:** after six months of legal stay, you can apply for permission to work part-time — up to 20 hours per week during semester, unlimited during vacations. You'll need a TOPIK level requirement (Level 3 for most jobs, Level 4 for some) and approval from your university's international office.

## Living and studying in Korea: what DSE students should know

**Dorm vs off-campus:** Dorms are cheaper but have curfews and roommate placements. Off-campus *one-room* (원룸) studios near campus run KRW 500,000–800,000 with a key money deposit (보증금) of KRW 5–10 million — the deposit is returned at the end. Many students use *goshiwon* or *goshitel* for the first semester until they understand the rental market.

**Weather and clothing:** Seoul winters are seriously cold (regularly -10°C to -15°C with windchill). Hong Kong students consistently underbudget for winter clothing — plan HK$3,000–5,000 for a proper coat, boots, and layers in your first year.

**Healthcare:** National Health Insurance enrolment is mandatory after six months of stay. Coverage is good and premiums are reasonable. Carry your Alien Registration Card (ARC) for clinic visits.

**Banking:** Open a Korean bank account in your first month — most universities will help with this through partnered banks (KB, Woori, Shinhan). You'll need it for stipend, part-time wages, and rent.

**Korean society:** Hierarchical workplace and university norms (선배/후배 senior-junior dynamics) take time. Drinking culture is real but easier to navigate than reputation suggests — you can decline politely without social cost in most international-friendly settings.

## After graduation: the D-10 and beyond

Korea has been actively expanding post-study work options:

**D-10 job-seeking visa** — up to two years to find graduate-level employment. Eligibility hinges on graduating from an accredited Korean university with a points-based threshold (academic record, language ability, age, university ranking).

**E-7 specialised employment visa** — for graduates who land a professional job. Increasingly common for foreign graduates in IT, biotech, design, and language-related fields.

**F-2-7 long-term residence (points-based)** — accumulate enough points (income, Korean ability, education) over your D-10/E-7 period and you can transition to a renewable long-term residence permit, then eventually to F-5 permanent residence.

For Hong Kong students who learn Korean well, the post-graduation labour market in Seoul has steadily opened — Naver, Kakao, Coupang, the major chaebol's international divisions, and the growing English-content industries all hire foreign graduates.

## How does Korea compare to other overseas pathways?

- **Versus Japan** — Korea is more language-front-loaded (TOPIK is harder than EJU's Japanese paper for cold starters in some respects, though both are demanding). Korean private university tuition is lower than top Japanese privates. Job-seeking visa is more generous in Korea (2 years vs Japan's 1 year typical).
- **Versus Taiwan** — Taiwan is cheaper still (NTU tuition is HK$15,000–25,000/year), but Korea's brand recognition for global employment is stronger.
- **Versus Singapore / UK / US** — Korea is dramatically cheaper than all three. Brand prestige from SKY universities is regionally strong but doesn't yet match Oxbridge or Ivy globally.
- **Versus staying in HK** — for self-financed JUPAS students paying HK$120,000+ at lower-banded local programmes, a top Korean private with a partial scholarship can be cheaper *and* offer a different career trajectory.

## A 24-month plan if you start in S5

**S5 first semester (Sep–Dec):** Decide track (Korean-medium vs ETP). If Korean-medium, start lessons immediately — Sejong Institute, Korean Cultural Centre Hong Kong, or online (Talk To Me In Korean, How To Study Korean). Target TOPIK I Level 2 by year end.

**S5 second semester (Jan–Jun):** Push toward TOPIK II Level 3 prep. Sit IELTS by spring if going ETP. Shortlist 5–8 universities, read each foreign student admission guide carefully.

**Summer between S5 and S6:** Korean language summer programme in Seoul if budget allows (Yonsei KLI, Sogang KLEC, Korea University KLC). Hugely effective for jumping a TOPIK level. Visit campuses while there.

**S6 first semester (Sep–Dec):** Sit TOPIK in October or November to lock in a usable score. Draft personal statements. Approach teachers for recommendation letters early — don't wait until December. Submit GKS application in September if pursuing it.

**S6 second semester (Jan–Apr):** Submit Spring-after-DSE university applications (mostly fall-intake deadlines fall here). Sit DSE in March–April. Confirm offers as they arrive.

**Post-DSE (May–Aug):** Final document submission, official DSE result statements, accept offer, apply for D-2 visa, arrange dormitory or housing, fly out for August orientation.

## Final thoughts

Korea sits in a sweet spot for DSE students who want a strong overseas degree without the UK or US price tag, who are open to learning Korean (or are happy with one of the well-developed English-taught programmes), and who see East Asian career markets as viable. The infrastructure for international students is mature, the scholarships are real, and the post-graduation visa lets you actually use your degree on the ground. The hardest part is the language commitment for Korean-medium programmes — start early, take it seriously, and the rest of the pathway is more straightforward than it looks from Hong Kong.

# Macau Pathway for DSE Students: University of Macau, MUST, Macao Polytechnic English-Taught Programmes and Stay Permit Guide 2026

For most Hong Kong DSE candidates, "studying overseas" usually means London, Sydney, Toronto or Singapore. Macau rarely appears on the shortlist, yet it is one of the most underrated pathways available. The Special Administrative Region sits an hour by ferry or across the Hong Kong-Zhuhai-Macao Bridge, Cantonese works on every campus, the University of Macau is ranked in the QS global top 300, and full four-year tuition can come in cheaper than a single year in the UK. Crucially, time spent studying in Macau does not break Hong Kong permanent residency, so graduates can return to Hong Kong with their HKID intact and skip the "non-local graduate" label entirely.

This guide walks through every realistic option for a 2026 DSE leaver: admission requirements at the six main Macau universities, English-medium provision, tuition and scholarships, the non-resident student stay permit (學生逗留證), accommodation, and what happens after graduation if you want to return to Hong Kong, work in Macau, or move into the Greater Bay Area.

## 1. Why Macau Deserves a Place on Your Non-JUPAS Shortlist

**Friendlier admission thresholds.** The University of Macau (UM) accepts DSE 2024 candidates with 3-3-2 in core subjects plus Level 3 in two Category A electives. Compared with JUPAS Band A programmes at HKU/CUHK/HKUST, where actual cut-offs typically run at 5*5*4 or higher for competitive majors, Macau is roughly one tier easier across the board. MUST and Macao Polytechnic are looser still.

**Genuine English-medium teaching.** UM operates almost entirely in English. MUST teaches the majority of its undergraduate programmes in English, and the University of Saint Joseph (USJ) is fully English-taught. Students who scored DSE English Level 4-5 will not face a sudden Mandarin lecture wall the way they might at most mainland universities.

**Affordable total cost.** UM tuition for non-Macau residents sits at roughly MOP 122,600 per year (around HKD 134,000); MUST mainstream programmes are about MOP 170,000. Living costs run HKD 5,000-7,000 a month including hall fees. Four years total comes in around HKD 700,000-900,000 — less than a single UK year for some London business schools.

**You keep your Hong Kong PR.** Studying in Macau counts as absence from Hong Kong, but under the Immigration Ordinance, leaving for full-time study at a recognised institution does not by itself trigger loss of permanent resident status. You can return regularly, retain your HKID, and after graduation walk into Hong Kong's job market as a Hong Kong permanent resident — no IANG visa required, no employer sponsorship pain, no "non-local graduate" status.

**Independent admissions, no JUPAS slots used.** Macau universities run their own admissions outside the JUPAS system, so applying does not consume any of your 20 JUPAS choices. It is a clean parallel application.

## 2. The Six Universities Worth Considering

Macau has ten higher-education institutions; six are realistic targets for DSE students.

| Institution | Type | English-medium share | QS World 2026 | Strongest faculties |
|-------------|------|----------------------|---------------|---------------------|
| **University of Macau (UM)** | Public | ~100% | 285 | Law, Computer Science, Business, Portuguese Studies |
| **Macau University of Science and Technology (MUST)** | Private | 80%+ | 251 | Chinese Medicine, Hospitality, Medicine, Communication |
| **Macao Polytechnic University (MPU)** | Public | Mixed EN/ZH/PT | Unranked | Translation, Design, Health Sciences, Public Administration |
| **City University of Macau (CityU Macau)** | Private | EN/ZH | Unranked | Business, Education, Psychology |
| **University of Saint Joseph (USJ)** | Private (Catholic) | 100% English | Unranked | Psychology, Architecture, Religious Studies |
| **Macao University of Tourism (UTM)** | Public | EN/ZH/PT | Top 10 globally for Hospitality & Leisure | Tourism, Hotel, Gaming Management |

If global ranking and a fully English campus matter most, UM is the obvious target. If you want medicine, Chinese medicine, or media at a less competitive school, MUST is excellent value. For design, translation or nursing, look at MPU. For tourism and hospitality, UTM is one of the strongest brands in Asia.

## 3. University of Macau (UM): Admission Requirements in Detail

UM is the only Macau university in the QS top 300 and the most international option. Its DSE rules (applicable from the 2024 examination onward) are:

- **English Language: Level 3 or above**
- **Chinese Language: Level 3 or above**
- **Mathematics (Compulsory Part): Level 2 or above**
- **Citizenship and Social Development: Attained**
- **Two Category A electives: Level 3 or above each**

Programme-specific overlays:

- **Faculty of Science and Technology** (Computer Science, Engineering, Maths, Physics): one of the two electives must be Physics at Level 3 or above.
- **Faculty of Health Sciences** (Biomedical Sciences, Pharmaceutical Sciences): Chemistry at Level 3 or above is required among the electives.
- **Faculty of Business Administration**: no specific elective is mandated, but Mathematics M1/M2 at Level 3 strengthens applications.
- **Law (LLB)**: Chinese Language Level 4 is strongly recommended given Chinese-language case material.

Application window for the 2026/27 intake runs from **3 February to 9 April 2026**. Applicants submit through the UM Registry online portal, pay the application fee (around MOP 250), upload predicted grades, and may be invited to an interview for selected programmes (Law, English Studies, Communication). DSE results are released in mid-July; conditional offers are then converted to firm offers, with registration in late August.

## 4. Macau University of Science and Technology (MUST): Strongest Private Option

MUST is the largest private university in Macau and the highest-ranked private institution in the city. For DSE candidates the baseline requirement is **Level 3 in English, Chinese and Mathematics, plus Level 2 in any two electives** — meaningfully easier than UM.

Key programmes:

- **Faculty of Medicine** (MBBS, 6 years): the most competitive at MUST; expect Level 4+ in English and Biology/Chemistry, plus an interview.
- **Faculty of Chinese Medicine**: a flagship programme, registered globally. Bilingual Chinese/English instruction.
- **School of Business**: largest faculty, English-taught, strong in hospitality finance and gaming management.
- **Faculty of Hospitality and Tourism Management**: ranked top 30 globally for hospitality.

MUST runs a rolling admission system; the 2026/27 main window opens **November 2025 and closes around 31 May 2026**, with later waves running into July for unfilled seats. DSE candidates can apply with predicted grades and convert with results in mid-July. Tuition for most programmes is MOP 165,000-185,000 per year; medicine sits at around MOP 250,000.

## 5. Macao Polytechnic University, City University of Macau, USJ and UTM

**Macao Polytechnic University (MPU)** is public, applied-focused, and admits DSE candidates with Level 2 in core subjects. Translation (Chinese-English-Portuguese), nursing, art design and computing are the standout programmes. Tuition for non-residents sits at MOP 28,000-42,000 per year, the cheapest serious option in the region.

**City University of Macau** is private and known for business, education and psychology. Admission is generous (Level 2 across cores), tuition runs MOP 80,000-100,000 per year, and the campus is the most central in Macau peninsula.

**University of Saint Joseph (USJ)** is the only fully English-medium Catholic university in Macau. Strong for psychology, architecture and design. Class sizes are small and the atmosphere is closer to a UK liberal-arts college than a research university. Tuition around MOP 70,000-90,000.

**Macao University of Tourism (UTM)** — formerly the Institute for Tourism Studies (IFT) — is the place to be if hospitality, event management, or gaming management is the goal. UTM ranks top 10 globally in QS Hospitality and runs strong industry placements at Macau's integrated resorts.

## 6. English Requirements and Language Reality

UM, USJ and most MUST programmes accept DSE English Level 3 as meeting the language requirement. There is no separate IELTS requirement for DSE candidates at UM. MUST sometimes asks for IELTS 5.5-6.0 if DSE English is below Level 4, especially for medicine.

The lived reality is that Macau is trilingual — Cantonese is the working language outside lecture halls, Mandarin is increasingly common, Portuguese is ceremonial. DSE candidates already speak Cantonese, so social adjustment is near zero. Picking up working Mandarin is sensible, since most postgraduate or career options reach into the mainland Greater Bay Area.

## 7. Tuition, Scholarships and Living Costs

A realistic 2026/27 budget for a non-Macau-resident DSE student:

| Item | UM | MUST | MPU | UTM |
|------|-----|------|-----|-----|
| Tuition | MOP 122,600 | MOP 170,000 | MOP 32,000 | MOP 41,500 |
| Hall (shared room) | MOP 16,000 | MOP 18,000 | MOP 12,000 | MOP 13,000 |
| Food and transport | MOP 36,000 | MOP 36,000 | MOP 36,000 | MOP 36,000 |
| Books, insurance, misc | MOP 12,000 | MOP 12,000 | MOP 10,000 | MOP 10,000 |
| **Annual total (MOP)** | **186,600** | **236,000** | **90,000** | **100,500** |
| **Approx. HKD** | **204,000** | **258,000** | **98,000** | **110,000** |

**Scholarships.** UM offers entrance scholarships of MOP 30,000-122,600 (full tuition) for top-tier admissions, awarded automatically based on DSE results — Level 5* or above in core subjects and electives is competitive. MUST runs the "Macau Foundation Scholarship" and "MUST Excellence Scholarship", up to MOP 100,000 per year. The Macao SAR Government Tertiary Education Office (DSEDJ) also has a Special Scholarship Scheme open to non-Macau students. Apply early — most close in May.

## 8. The Non-Resident Student Stay Permit (學生逗留證)

Hong Kong students do **not** need a visa to enter Macau, but anyone studying full-time for more than 180 days needs a **Non-Resident Student Stay Permit (Autorização de Permanência para Estudante)** issued by the Macao Public Security Police Force (CPSP) Immigration Department.

**How it works:**

1. Once you accept your offer, the university issues an admission letter and submits your file to CPSP.
2. You attend the CPSP Immigration Department in Pac On with your HKID, HKSAR passport, admission letter, accommodation proof and a passport-size photo.
3. The permit is issued as a sticker in your passport and is valid for one academic year, renewed annually.
4. Holders may enter and exit Macau freely during the validity period.

There is no work component to this permit — students cannot legally work full-time in Macau, although unpaid internships and university teaching assistantships are permitted.

## 9. Accommodation: On-Campus, Off-Campus, or Commute from Zhuhai

UM has the most comprehensive halls in Macau — the Hengqin campus has 10 residential colleges modelled on Oxbridge, and first-year non-Macau students are guaranteed a place. MUST and MPU offer halls but with limited capacity, so apply within two weeks of your offer.

Off-campus rentals in Taipa or central Macau run MOP 6,000-9,000 per month for a shared two-bedroom flat. A growing number of UM students live in Zhuhai's Hengqin and walk through the dedicated UM-Hengqin tunnel — Hengqin rents are 30-40% cheaper, but the tunnel closes at midnight.

Commuting from Hong Kong is impractical for most students because of the time and ferry/bridge cost, but quarterly weekend trips home are easy: TurboJET ferry runs HKD 175 one-way and the bridge bus is HKD 80.

## 10. After Graduation: Three Realistic Routes

**Route A — Return to Hong Kong as a permanent resident.** This is the simplest path. You retain your HKID, walk into the Hong Kong job market with no visa restriction, and your overseas degree is recognised by HKQF (assuming it is from a recognised university — all six listed here are). UM, MUST and UTM degrees are well-known among Hong Kong employers in finance, hospitality, law and Chinese medicine.

**Route B — Stay in Macau on a work permit.** Macau employers must apply for a Non-Resident Worker's Identification Card (the "blue card") on your behalf. The Macau labour market is heavily concentrated in gaming, hospitality, finance and government, so non-Macau-resident graduates without local connections find it harder to land their first job locally than in Hong Kong. Realistic salaries: MOP 18,000-28,000 entry-level for hospitality and business graduates.

**Route C — Move into the Greater Bay Area.** Zhuhai, Shenzhen and Guangzhou increasingly recruit Macau graduates for cross-border roles. The Hengqin Cooperation Zone offers tax incentives and a streamlined Macau-resident-status track. UM's Hengqin campus location makes this route especially natural for tech and biotech graduates.

## 11. Application Timeline at a Glance

- **November 2025:** MUST and CityU Macau open early-bird applications.
- **3 February 2026:** UM application opens.
- **9 April 2026:** UM application deadline.
- **April–May 2026:** UM and MUST interviews for selected programmes.
- **31 May 2026:** Most MUST and MPU windows close.
- **Early July 2026:** DSE results released.
- **Mid-July 2026:** Conditional offers converted to firm offers; scholarship decisions issued.
- **Late July 2026:** Stay permit application starts.
- **Late August 2026:** Move-in and orientation; semester begins early September.

## 12. Common Pitfalls

- Treating Macau as a JUPAS substitute instead of a parallel non-JUPAS application — you can apply to both. Most Macau universities accept results well into August.
- Missing the UM 9 April deadline — UM is strict and does not run a major late round.
- Not budgeting for the stay permit and annual renewal fee (MOP 300).
- Assuming your HKID protects you in Macau — for everything from a SIM card to a hall booking, you need either the stay permit or your HKSAR passport.
- Picking a private university with weak global recognition for a portable career. UM, MUST and UTM are well-recognised; some smaller private colleges are not.

## 13. Final Verdict

For a Hong Kong DSE candidate weighing options outside the JUPAS top tier, Macau hits a rare combination: cheap, English-taught, geographically close, ranked respectably, and crucially compatible with Hong Kong permanent residency. The University of Macau is competitive with mid-tier Hong Kong universities on academic outcomes; MUST and UTM offer specialist strengths that are hard to replicate cheaply in Hong Kong. Add Macau to your non-JUPAS shortlist alongside one or two UK or Singapore options and you walk into August with a genuine portfolio of choices rather than a single bet on JUPAS allocation day.
